01 / QA FOUNDATIONS

Quality engineering foundations

Testing is a risk-reduction activity. The useful question is not “how many tests do we have?” but “what important failure could still reach a user, and what evidence do we have that it will not?”

Foundation

Quality Assurance, software testing, SDLC, and STLC

Quality Assurance is broader than executing tests. QA improves the process that creates software: requirement review, risk analysis, testability, environments, data, automation, release controls, and feedback. Software testing evaluates a system and gathers evidence about its behavior.

SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle) is the complete lifecycle used to plan, build, verify, release, operate, and eventually retire software. A typical SDLC includes discovery or planning, requirements analysis, architecture and design, implementation, testing/verification, deployment, operation, maintenance, and retirement. The exact names and boundaries vary by organization and methodology.

STLC (Software Testing Life Cycle) is the testing-focused lifecycle inside the broader SDLC. It organizes activities such as requirement analysis, test planning and estimation, test design, environment and test-data preparation, execution, defect management, reporting, and test closure. STLC is not a competing lifecycle: it is the quality/testing perspective that runs through the SDLC.

In a sequential model these activities may appear as distinct phases; in Agile and DevOps environments they overlap continuously. QA can review requirements before code exists, developers can run unit tests during implementation, automated regression can execute in CI/CD, and monitoring can provide quality feedback after release.

Mental model: risk → expected behavior → oracle → evidence → decision.
Quality AssuranceSoftware TestingTest PlanningTest Strategy

Related: Risk-based testing · Requirements analysis

Back to contents ↑
Foundation → Intermediate

Risk-based testing, coverage, planning, and strategy

When time is limited, prioritize by business impact, likelihood of failure, scope of change, technical complexity, detectability, and historical defects. A duplicate payment risk deserves more attention than a cosmetic spacing defect.

A test strategy defines the principles and layers used to control quality: unit, API, integration, UI, performance, security, acceptance, automation, environments, data, and release evidence. A test plan applies that strategy to a release or project with scope, owners, schedule, entry/exit criteria, and reporting.

Coverage should describe behaviors and risks, not raw test counts. A huge suite with shallow assertions can provide less assurance than a smaller suite built around critical journeys and failure modes.

Test StrategyTest PlanningRegression TestingAcceptance Testing

Related: Automation strategy · Quality gates

Foundation

Test scenarios, test cases, and design techniques

A test scenario is a high-level behavior or journey. A test case is executable: preconditions, data, steps, expected result, and evidence. Acceptance criteria describe the business conditions that make a story complete.

Core techniques include equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision tables, and state-transition testing. Good coverage includes happy paths, negative paths, validation failures, permissions, boundaries, state changes, and recovery.

Example: login

Valid login, invalid password, locked user, expired session, missing MFA, rate limiting, safe error messages.

Example: payment

Valid payment, insufficient balance, duplicate click, retry, provider failure, rollback, reconciliation.

Exploratory TestingAcceptance TestingAuthentication Testing
Foundation

Unit, integration, E2E, regression, exploratory, and acceptance testing

Unit testing validates small logic units. Integration testing verifies boundaries between components. End-to-end testing exercises a realistic journey across layers. Regression testing ensures existing behavior still works after change and can exist at any layer.

Exploratory testing combines learning, test design, and execution to discover unknown risks. Acceptance testing/UAT verifies business suitability, often with product owners or users. Push deterministic checks down to the cheapest reliable layer and keep E2E focused on critical integrated journeys.

Unit TestingIntegration TestingEnd-to-End TestingRegression TestingExploratory TestingAcceptance Testing

Related: Test pyramid · API testing

Foundation → Intermediate

Defect lifecycle, severity, priority, and non-reproducible bugs

A typical lifecycle is new → triaged → assigned → fixed → retested → verified → closed, with reopening when needed. Severity is technical/user impact; priority is business urgency.

For intermittent bugs, preserve build/version, environment, test data, timestamps, screenshots/video, network traces, request IDs, console/server logs, and reproduction frequency. Change one variable at a time and build hypotheses instead of repeatedly rerunning without evidence.

Defect TrackingTroubleshootingRoot Cause Analysis

Related: Flaky tests · Observability

Intermediate

Traceability, reporting, and Allure

Traceability connects requirements or risks to tests, execution evidence, and defects. It answers what is covered, what failed, which requirement is affected, and what evidence exists.

A useful test report includes scope, build, environment, pass/fail/blocked status, known defects, residual risk, and a release recommendation. Allure is one reporting system that can aggregate steps, attachments, history, categories, and links. The tool matters less than stable test identity and actionable evidence.

Test TraceabilityTest ReportingAllure

Related: Playwright evidence · CI/CD

02 / AUTOMATION ARCHITECTURE

Automation that remains maintainable

Automation is software engineering applied to quality. The goal is fast, trustworthy feedback—not a collection of scripts.

Foundation

What to automate and the test pyramid

Automate checks that are repeatable, valuable, stable enough to interpret, and executed often enough to justify maintenance. Keep human exploration for discovery, ambiguity, and one-off judgment.

Use the lowest layer that can prove the behavior. Business-rule permutations usually belong in unit or API tests; critical user journeys belong in E2E. UI checks are expensive because they cross more moving parts.

Test AutomationAutomationBrowser Automation
Intermediate → Advanced

Framework design, Page Object Model, and fixtures

A scalable framework separates test intent, domain helpers, page/API adapters, fixtures, data builders, assertions, configuration, and reporting. Avoid one giant helper file and deep inheritance trees.

Page Object Model centralizes UI interaction knowledge. Fixtures create controlled dependencies such as authenticated pages, API clients, temporary users, and cleanup. This makes failures easier to localize.

TypeScript / Page Object
export class LoginPage {
  constructor(private page: Page) {}

  async login(email: string, password: string) {
    await this.page.getByLabel('Email').fill(email);
    await this.page.getByLabel('Password').fill(password);
    await this.page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
  }
}
Page Object ModelTest FixturesTest Automation
Intermediate

Test data management and isolation

Prefer unique data per worker/run, API setup helpers, controlled pools with ownership, and deterministic cleanup. Shared mutable accounts are a common source of flakiness.

Protect sensitive production data: use synthetic or masked data. Test setup should be idempotent when possible so retries and reruns do not create duplicate state.

Test Data ManagementData Validation
Advanced

Flaky tests, retries, and failure diagnosis

Common causes of flakiness include timing assumptions, shared state, eventual consistency, unstable data, environment pressure, weak selectors, and uncontrolled dependencies. Distinguish product defects from flaky tests using traces, logs, network evidence, data state, and controlled repetition.

Retries are a diagnostic safety net, not a mechanism to turn failures into passes. Preserve each attempt and track tests that only pass on retry.

Test AutomationTroubleshootingRoot Cause Analysis
Intermediate

BDD, Gherkin, and Cucumber

BDD (Behavior-Driven Development) is a collaborative software-development approach that describes expected system behavior through concrete examples written from the perspective of users and business outcomes. Its purpose is to improve shared understanding between product, QA, and engineering before and during implementation.

BDD is broader than a syntax or test framework. Given / When / Then is a common structure for examples: Given establishes context, When describes an action or event, and Then describes the observable outcome. Gherkin is the structured language commonly used to write those scenarios, while Cucumber is a tool that can execute them by mapping steps to automation code.

BDD works best when examples clarify business rules and become a shared specification. It adds little value when feature files merely rewrite low-level UI actions such as “click this button” or when nobody outside the automation team reads them.

Gherkin
Feature: Transfer funds
  Scenario: Reject transfer above available balance
    Given an account with a balance of 100 USD
    When the customer attempts to transfer 150 USD
    Then the transfer is rejected
    And the balance remains 100 USD
BDDCucumber

Technology profiles in this section

The concepts above are implemented or encountered through the following technologies: Gherkin, Cucumber. Each profile explains what the technology is, its defining characteristics, how it is used in QA/automation, and what its name or acronym means.

Gherkin
BDD specification language

Definition: A structured, human-readable language used to express behavior as Features, Scenarios, and Given/When/Then steps.

Main characteristics

  • Business-readable examples
  • Supports Scenario Outlines and Examples tables
  • Can be localized into multiple human languages
  • Designed to describe behavior rather than implementation detail
QA / automation relevance: Used with Cucumber and other BDD tools when executable examples are genuinely shared between business and engineering.

Name / acronym: Gherkin is a name, not an acronym.

Cucumber
BDD automation tool

Definition: A family of tools that execute Gherkin scenarios by mapping natural-language steps to automation code.

Main characteristics

  • Feature files written in Gherkin
  • Step definitions connect scenarios to code
  • Supports tags, hooks, tables, and reports
  • Available for multiple programming ecosystems
QA / automation relevance: Useful when business-readable executable specifications provide shared value; avoid using it merely as an extra wrapper around low-level UI steps.

Name / acronym: Cucumber is a project name, not an acronym.

03 / PLAYWRIGHT

Playwright deep dive

Understand the execution model—browser, context, page, locators, fixtures, projects, and evidence—rather than memorizing isolated commands.

Foundation

Browser, BrowserContext, Page, and isolation

A Browser is the browser process. A BrowserContext is an isolated session with its own cookies/storage. A Page is a tab. Playwright Test creates isolated contexts by default, preventing state leakage between tests.

Reusing one context across unrelated tests can make order matter. When authentication is expensive, reuse validated storage state, not mutable browser state.

PlaywrightEnd-to-End TestingBrowser Automation

Technology profiles in this section

The concepts above are implemented or encountered through the following technologies: Playwright. Each profile explains what the technology is, its defining characteristics, how it is used in QA/automation, and what its name or acronym means.

Playwright
Browser automation and testing framework

Definition: An open-source framework for automating Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit with a modern test runner and browser-control APIs.

Main characteristics

  • BrowserContext isolation
  • Auto-waiting and actionability checks
  • Semantic locators
  • Fixtures, projects, retries, sharding, and parallel workers
  • Network interception and direct API requests
  • Trace Viewer, screenshots, video, and reporters
QA / automation relevance: Useful for E2E, browser regression, authentication flows, API-assisted setup, cross-browser coverage, mobile emulation, and debugging CI failures.

Name / acronym: Playwright is a project name, not an acronym.

Foundation

Locators, semantic selection, and strictness

Prefer getByRole, getByLabel, text, and stable test IDs. They reflect user-visible semantics and survive CSS/layout changes better than deep selectors or absolute XPath.

TypeScript
const row = page.getByRole('row').filter({ hasText: 'Order #1042' });
await row.getByRole('button', { name: 'Refund' }).click();

If multiple elements match, narrow the locator using the business container or filter instead of blindly using first().

PlaywrightAccessibility Testing
Foundation → Intermediate

Auto-waiting and actionability

Before actions such as click(), Playwright checks that the target resolves correctly, is visible, stable, enabled where relevant, and can receive pointer events. Assertions also retry until the condition or timeout.

Avoid fixed sleeps. Wait for the state that actually matters: URL, network response, message, disabled/enabled state, or persisted data. state: 'hidden' can complete when an element is hidden or detached; opacity alone does not necessarily mean hidden.

PlaywrightTest Automation
Intermediate

Fixtures, worker scope, and authenticated state

Fixtures model dependencies and cleanup. Test-scoped fixtures are recreated per test; worker-scoped fixtures are created once per worker and should only hold state safe to share within that worker.

TypeScript
export const test = base.extend<{ userId: string }>({
  userId: async ({ request }, use) => {
    const id = await createUser(request);
    await use(id);
    await deleteUser(request, id);
  }
});
Test FixturesAuthentication TestingPlaywright
Intermediate

Network interception and APIRequestContext

Intercept requests to observe, modify, block, or fulfill controlled dependency behavior. This is useful for deterministic outage/error scenarios but must not replace real integration or contract coverage.

TypeScript
await page.route('**/api/rates', route => route.fulfill({
  status: 503,
  contentType: 'application/json',
  body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'temporarily_unavailable' })
}));

Playwright's request context also supports direct API testing and fast test setup/teardown.

Network InterceptionAPI TestingPlaywright
Intermediate

Projects, cross-browser execution, and mobile emulation

projects defines different execution configurations: Chromium, Firefox, WebKit, device profiles, locales, permissions, and environment-specific settings. Device emulation validates viewport, touch, user agent, and responsive behavior but is not a full replacement for real devices.

playwright.config.ts
projects: [
  { name: 'chromium', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } },
  { name: 'mobile', use: { ...devices['Pixel 5'] } }
]
Cross-Browser TestingMobile TestingResponsive Web Design
Intermediate

Trace Viewer, screenshots, video, reporters, and codegen

Trace Viewer captures actions, DOM snapshots, console, network, timing, and source context. trace: 'on-first-retry' is a practical CI setting. video: 'retain-on-failure' keeps evidence only for failed tests.

JUnit reporters create XML for CI; HTML and Allure provide human-friendly views. npx playwright codegen records interactions and produces starter code—refactor generated selectors and assertions before treating it as production automation.

playwright.config.ts
export default defineConfig({
  retries: 1,
  reporter: [['html'], ['junit', { outputFile: 'results.xml' }]],
  use: { trace: 'on-first-retry', video: 'retain-on-failure' }
});
Test ReportingAllurePlaywright
04 / APIS & DATA

REST APIs, Postman, contracts, SQL, and data quality

A 200 response proves transport success, not business correctness. Quality at this layer includes protocol, schema, permissions, side effects, persistence, resilience, and data meaning.

Foundation

APIs, REST, HTTP methods, status codes, and authentication

API (Application Programming Interface) is a defined interface that allows one software component to communicate with another. An API specifies how a consumer can request data or behavior and what the provider promises in return. APIs can exist as web APIs over HTTP, library or operating-system interfaces, database interfaces, messaging interfaces, and other software boundaries.

For QA and automation, an API is valuable because it exposes behavior below the user interface. API tests can validate business rules, authentication and authorization, data contracts, error handling, idempotency, and integrations faster and more directly than many browser tests. API calls are also useful for creating test data and cleaning up state around UI automation.

GET reads, POST creates or triggers processing, PUT replaces a representation, and PATCH changes part of a resource. Know common 2xx, 4xx, 429, and 5xx codes, but always validate the body and resulting state.

Authentication answers “who are you?” and authorization answers “what may you do?”. Test expiry, scopes, resource ownership, role boundaries, safe errors, and session/logout behavior.

REST APIsAPI TestingAuthentication Testing

Technology profiles in this section

The concepts above are implemented or encountered through the following technologies: REST, HTTP / HTTPS, OAuth 2.0. Each profile explains what the technology is, its defining characteristics, how it is used in QA/automation, and what its name or acronym means.

REST
Architectural style

Definition: Representational State Transfer is an architectural style for networked systems centered on resources, representations, stateless interactions, cacheability, and a uniform interface.

Main characteristics

  • Resource-oriented identifiers
  • Uses standard HTTP semantics in common web APIs
  • Stateless requests are a core constraint
  • Representations such as JSON encode resource state
  • REST is not synonymous with “any HTTP API”
QA / automation relevance: REST-aware API tests validate method semantics, status/error behavior, idempotency, caching, resource ownership, and representations.

Name / acronym: REST = Representational State Transfer.

HTTP / HTTPS
Application-layer protocol

Definition: HTTP is the Hypertext Transfer Protocol used for requests and responses on the web. HTTPS is HTTP protected by TLS encryption and server authentication (and optionally client authentication).

Main characteristics

  • Methods, status codes, headers, body, caching, content negotiation
  • Stateless request/response semantics
  • Modern versions include HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 with different transport/multiplexing behavior
  • HTTPS protects data in transit but does not make application logic secure
QA / automation relevance: API and browser tests inspect methods, status codes, headers, cookies, redirects, caching, TLS behavior, and failure mappings.

Name / acronym: HTTP = Hypertext Transfer Protocol. HTTPS is commonly read as Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure; technically it is HTTP over TLS.

OAuth 2.0
Authorization framework

Definition: A framework for delegated authorization that allows a client to obtain scoped access to protected resources without receiving the resource owner’s password.

Main characteristics

  • Uses access tokens rather than sharing user passwords
  • Defines roles such as resource owner, client, authorization server, and resource server
  • Supports multiple grant/flow patterns for different client types
  • Scopes can restrict delegated permissions
  • Authentication is commonly added through OpenID Connect (OIDC)
QA / automation relevance: Test redirect/callback behavior, scopes, token expiry/refresh, invalid tokens, consent, client configuration, and authorization boundaries.

Name / acronym: OAuth is the framework name rather than a strict acronym. It is often informally described as “Open Authorization.”

Foundation → Intermediate

Postman, collections, scripts, and command-line execution

Postman organizes requests, environments, variables, examples, and scripts. Collections can represent real workflows such as login → create → fetch → update → delete.

Postman test script
pm.test('returns an order', () => {
  pm.response.to.have.status(200);
  const body = pm.response.json();
  pm.expect(body.id).to.be.a('string');
  pm.expect(body.total).to.be.above(0);
});

For CI, run collections with the current Postman CLI when possible; Newman remains common in existing pipelines.

PostmanJavaScriptCI/CD

Technology profiles in this section

The concepts above are implemented or encountered through the following technologies: Postman, Rest Assured. Each profile explains what the technology is, its defining characteristics, how it is used in QA/automation, and what its name or acronym means.

Postman
API development and testing platform

Definition: A platform for designing, sending, organizing, documenting, mocking, and testing API requests.

Main characteristics

  • Collections and folders organize requests
  • Environment/collection variables support configuration and chaining
  • JavaScript-based pre-request and test scripts
  • Supports REST, GraphQL, WebSocket and other API workflows
  • CLI execution integrates collections with CI
QA / automation relevance: Useful for exploratory API testing, reproducible collections, contract/business assertions, authentication flows, and CI smoke suites.

Name / acronym: Postman is a product name, not an acronym.

Rest Assured
Java API testing library

Definition: A Java domain-specific library for testing REST-style HTTP APIs with fluent request and assertion syntax.

Main characteristics

  • Fluent given/when/then style
  • JSON/XML parsing and assertions
  • Authentication and request specification helpers
  • Integrates with Java test frameworks
QA / automation relevance: Common in Java QA automation stacks for service-level API tests.

Name / acronym: REST = Representational State Transfer; “Assured” is part of the library name.

Intermediate

JSON, JSON Schema, API contract testing, and integrations

JSON is only a representation. JSON Schema defines allowed structure, required fields, types, formats, ranges, and enums. Contract tests protect consumers from breaking producer changes.

JSON Schema
{
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["id", "status"],
  "properties": {
    "id": { "type": "string" },
    "status": { "enum": ["pending", "paid", "cancelled"] }
  }
}

Schema compatibility is not enough: business meaning can change while types remain valid. Add targeted invariants and integrated coverage.

JSONJSON SchemaAPI Contract TestingAPI IntegrationSystem Integration

Technology profiles in this section

The concepts above are implemented or encountered through the following technologies: JSON, JSON Schema, OpenAPI, GraphQL, WebSocket. Each profile explains what the technology is, its defining characteristics, how it is used in QA/automation, and what its name or acronym means.

JSON
Data-interchange format

Definition: JavaScript Object Notation is a lightweight text format for structured data using objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null.

Main characteristics

  • Human-readable and language-independent data representation
  • Common default format for REST APIs
  • No comments in the standard format
  • Does not itself enforce types, required fields, or business rules
QA / automation relevance: QA engineers validate JSON payloads, compare expected fields and values, and combine JSON with schema or domain assertions.

Name / acronym: JSON = JavaScript Object Notation.

JSON Schema
Schema / validation specification

Definition: A declarative vocabulary for describing and validating the structure and constraints of JSON documents.

Main characteristics

  • Defines types, required properties, enums, formats, numeric/string limits, and nested schemas
  • Supports reusable definitions and composition
  • Can forbid unexpected properties
  • Useful as an executable interface contract
QA / automation relevance: Used for API contract tests, structured LLM output validation, config validation, and detecting breaking payload changes.

Name / acronym: JSON is the acronym inside the name; “Schema” is not an acronym.

OpenAPI
API description specification

Definition: A standard machine-readable format for describing HTTP APIs, including endpoints, operations, parameters, request bodies, responses, schemas, and security schemes.

Main characteristics

  • Usually represented as YAML or JSON
  • Supports reusable schemas/components
  • Can generate documentation, clients, server stubs, and test inputs
  • Useful as a contract but still requires semantic/business assertions
QA / automation relevance: Compare implementation responses with the OpenAPI contract, detect breaking changes, generate test cases, and validate required/optional fields and error shapes.

Name / acronym: OpenAPI is a specification name, not an acronym.

GraphQL
API query language and runtime

Definition: A typed API query language and execution model in which clients select the exact fields they need from a schema.

Main characteristics

  • Strongly typed schema
  • Queries, mutations, and subscriptions
  • Nested graph-shaped selection sets
  • A single endpoint is common, unlike resource-per-URL REST conventions
  • Field-level authorization and resolver performance require careful design
QA / automation relevance: Test schema contracts, required/optional fields, authorization at nested fields, query complexity, error arrays, nullability, batching, and resolver/data consistency.

Name / acronym: GraphQL is a product/language name, not an acronym.

WebSocket
Bidirectional communication protocol

Definition: A protocol that upgrades an HTTP connection into a persistent full-duplex channel where client and server can send messages independently.

Main characteristics

  • Persistent connection
  • Bidirectional messages without request-per-message polling
  • Text and binary frames
  • Requires reconnect/heartbeat/backpressure strategies in real systems
QA / automation relevance: Test connection establishment, authentication, ordering, duplicates, reconnects, network interruption, message validation, and server cleanup.

Name / acronym: WebSocket is a protocol name, not an acronym.

Advanced

Chaining, idempotency, rate limiting, and downstream failures

Chained API tests pass explicit values from one response into the next. Idempotency is critical for retries and payments: repeated requests should not create duplicate side effects. Test duplicate clicks at UI, API, and persistent data layers.

Simulate dependency outages, latency, malformed responses, and 429/5xx behavior with controlled stubs or fault injection. Validate timeouts, retries, fallback, safe errors, and telemetry. Rate-limit tests should check threshold, headers, reset behavior, fairness, and recovery.

API TestingAPI IntegrationSecurity Testing
Foundation → Intermediate

SQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL, and Redis

QA commonly uses SQL to filter, join, aggregate, reconcile, and validate state. PostgreSQL and MySQL are server databases with different operational features; SQLite is embedded/file-based. Understand transactions, indexes, and concurrency at a practical level.

Redis is typically used for cache, sessions, queues, locks, and ephemeral state. When API/UI/database values disagree, stale cache or TTL behavior may be part of the problem.

SQL
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS payments
FROM payments
WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
SQLPostgreSQLSQLiteMySQLRedis

Technology profiles in this section

The concepts above are implemented or encountered through the following technologies: SQL, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, Redis. Each profile explains what the technology is, its defining characteristics, how it is used in QA/automation, and what its name or acronym means.

SQL
Declarative query language

Definition: Structured Query Language is the standard family of languages used to define, query, manipulate, and control relational data.

Main characteristics

  • Declarative: specify the desired result rather than an algorithm
  • Core operations include SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, JOIN, GROUP BY, and transactions
  • Implementations vary between database engines
  • Indexes and query plans strongly affect performance
QA / automation relevance: QA uses SQL for setup, reconciliation, data-quality checks, persistence verification, and debugging discrepancies between database, API, and UI.

Name / acronym: SQL = Structured Query Language.

PostgreSQL
Relational database

Definition: An open-source object-relational database management system known for standards support, extensibility, transactions, and advanced SQL features.

Main characteristics

  • Strong ACID transaction support
  • Rich indexing and query capabilities
  • JSON/JSONB support alongside relational data
  • Extensions, functions, and advanced data types
  • Client-server architecture
QA / automation relevance: Useful for persistence checks, SQL reconciliation, test data setup, transaction testing, and backend debugging.

Name / acronym: PostgreSQL is a product/project name, not an acronym.

MySQL
Relational database

Definition: A widely used client-server relational database management system using SQL.

Main characteristics

  • Transactional storage engines such as InnoDB
  • Indexes, joins, constraints, replication options
  • Large web-hosting and application ecosystem
QA / automation relevance: QA engineers commonly validate application persistence, migrations, constraints, and query results in MySQL-backed systems.

Name / acronym: MySQL is a product name. SQL = Structured Query Language.

SQLite
Embedded relational database

Definition: A serverless, self-contained relational database engine that stores a database in a file and is embedded directly into the application process.

Main characteristics

  • No separate database server
  • Very small operational footprint
  • Transactional and SQL-capable
  • Excellent for local tools, mobile/desktop apps, prototypes, and tests
  • Concurrency model differs from server databases
QA / automation relevance: Useful for lightweight automation systems, fixtures, local test stores, and validating file-backed applications.

Name / acronym: SQLite is a product name; “SQL” inside the name refers to Structured Query Language.

Redis
In-memory data store

Definition: An in-memory data-structure server used for caching, sessions, queues/streams, counters, locks, and ephemeral state.

Main characteristics

  • Very low-latency memory-first access
  • Data structures such as strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, and streams
  • TTL/expiration support
  • Optional persistence and replication depending on deployment
QA / automation relevance: When debugging inconsistent systems, QA should consider stale caches, TTLs, race conditions, session state, and rate-limit counters.

Name / acronym: Redis historically expanded to “REmote DIctionary Server,” though it is generally treated as the product name today.

Foundation → Advanced

Data quality and data validation

Core dimensions are accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, and uniqueness. Define rules against business meaning, not vague “clean data”.

Validate ingestion, transformation, persistence, API, and reporting boundaries. Each rule needs an owner, threshold, evidence, severity, and remediation path.

Data QualityData ValidationData Analysis
Intermediate

Data pipelines, ETL, processing, webhooks, and documentation

ETL extracts, transforms, and loads. Reliable pipelines also need schema checks, idempotency, ordering rules, duplicate handling, retries, lineage, observability, and safe reprocessing.

Webhooks are untrusted inbound events: verify signatures, validate schema, acknowledge quickly, process idempotently, persist failures, and retry safely. Data documentation should record field meaning, source, owner, refresh cadence, transformations, privacy classification, and limitations.

Data PipelinesData ProcessingETLWebhooksData DocumentationData Visualization

Programming and web foundations for automation engineers

You need enough programming depth to design frameworks, debug async systems, validate runtime data, and understand the products you test.

Foundation → Intermediate

JavaScript fundamentals

Prefer const unless rebinding is needed; use let for block-scoped reassignment. The event loop coordinates synchronous code, promise microtasks, timers, and I/O callbacks. async/await is syntax over promises; errors still need deliberate handling.

Understand closures, modules, arrays, map, event delegation, strict equality, and shared mutable state. These concepts directly affect Playwright and Node-based test code.

JavaScript
async function loadOrder(id) {
  const response = await fetch('/api/orders/' + id);
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error('HTTP ' + response.status);
  return response.json();
}
JavaScriptNode.js

Intermediate

TypeScript: interfaces, unions, generics, narrowing, and strict mode

TypeScript catches many mismatches before runtime. unknown is safer than any because values must be narrowed. Generics preserve type relationships. Discriminated unions model state safely. readonly communicates compile-time ownership expectations.

Type assertions do not validate external data. API and LLM boundaries still require runtime validation such as JSON Schema or Pydantic.

TypeScript

TypeScript
Programming language / static type system

Definition: A language developed by Microsoft that extends JavaScript with static type checking and additional syntax. TypeScript code is transformed into JavaScript for execution.

Main characteristics

  • Structural type system
  • Interfaces, type aliases, unions, generics, enums, and type narrowing
  • Strict compiler options can catch nullability and unsafe assumptions
  • Interoperates with existing JavaScript libraries
  • Types are erased at runtime, so external data still needs runtime validation
QA / automation relevance: A strong fit for large Playwright suites because types improve editor support, refactoring safety, fixture contracts, and test-data modeling.

Name / acronym: TypeScript is not an acronym. “TS” is a common abbreviation.

Foundation → Intermediate

Python, pytest, generators, exceptions, context managers, and Pydantic

Lists are mutable; tuples are immutable sequences. Generators yield lazily. Virtual environments isolate dependencies. Decorators wrap behavior. Context managers guarantee setup/cleanup.

pytest fixtures provide reusable setup/teardown and scopes. Pydantic turns untrusted dicts into validated models or explicit errors—useful for APIs and LLM outputs. The CPython GIL matters mainly for CPU-bound threads, not all forms of concurrency.

Python / pytest
@pytest.fixture
def user(api):
    created = api.create_user()
    yield created
    api.delete_user(created['id'])

06 / DELIVERY & INFRASTRUCTURE

Git, CI/CD, containers, Linux, and cloud delivery

Automation becomes valuable when it runs repeatedly in the delivery system and produces evidence teams can act on.

Foundation

Git and GitHub

fetch downloads remote refs; pull fetches and integrates. merge preserves branch history; rebase rewrites commits onto a new base. Resolve conflicts by understanding both changes, testing the result, and staging the intended resolution.

Before push: inspect status/diff, verify, stage only intended files, commit clearly, and push the correct branch. GitHub adds collaboration through pull requests, reviews, Actions, issues, and repository controls.

GitGitHub

Distributed version-control system

Main characteristics

CI/CD, GitHub Actions, Jenkins, and quality gates

Continuous Integration validates changes frequently with automated build/test/lint/security checks. Continuous Delivery/Deployment extends this into releasable or automatically deployed software.

GitHub Actions uses workflows → jobs → steps. Jenkins pipelines solve similar orchestration problems. When tests pass locally but fail in CI, compare browser/runtime versions, environment variables, resources, timing, parallelism, data, and artifacts.

GitHub Actions
name: qa
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps
      - run: npx playwright test

07 / SPECIALIZED TESTING

Web, mobile, visual, accessibility, performance, and security

Functional correctness is only one quality dimension. Products must work across environments, remain usable, perform under load, and resist misuse.

Intermediate

Cross-browser, mobile, and responsive testing

Choose browser/device coverage from analytics and risk. Emulation is useful for viewport, touch, user agent, and responsive behavior, but real devices remain necessary for some OS, hardware, network, webview, and native-integration risks.

Cross-Browser TestingMobile TestingResponsive Web Design
Intermediate

Visual regression testing

Visual testing compares rendered output to a trusted baseline. Control viewport, fonts, animations, data, and time to reduce false positives. Review baseline changes like code changes; never “accept all” without understanding the diff.

Visual Regression Testing
Foundation → Advanced

Accessibility testing

Accessibility covers keyboard operation, focus order, semantic roles/names, labels, contrast, zoom/reflow, screen-reader behavior, and more. Automated tools such as Lighthouse or axe detect many issues but cannot prove real usability.

Semantic HTML improves both accessibility and reliable locator strategies.

Accessibility Testing
Intermediate → Advanced

Performance testing

Measure latency, throughput, concurrency, resource use, and errors under expected load, spikes, endurance, and capacity limits. Correlate client results with server metrics, databases, queues, caches, and dependencies. Watch tail latency, not only averages.

Performance Testing
Intermediate

Security and authentication testing

Test authentication (identity) and authorization (permission) independently. Cover expiry, logout, token refresh, MFA, lockout/rate limits, horizontal access, vertical privilege, input validation, secret exposure, and safe failure behavior.

Never treat hidden UI controls as access control; verify the API itself rejects unauthorized requests.

Security TestingAuthentication Testing
08 / AI AUTOMATION

LLMs, agents, orchestration, RAG, MCP, and evaluation

AI introduces probabilistic behavior. Reliable systems place deterministic validation, authorization, observability, and human judgment around model behavior.

Foundation

LLMs, provider APIs, and prompt engineering

An LLM predicts tokens from context; it does not inherently know truth, permissions, or business policy. Good prompts define task, relevant context, constraints, examples where useful, and required output format.

OpenAI, Gemini, Groq, and OpenRouter differ in model families, latency, price, context length, structured-output features, and safety behavior. Hide provider differences behind adapters when portability matters.

An agent combines model reasoning with state, tools, and control flow. Define allowed capabilities, stop conditions, budgets, retries, and validation. Use deterministic workflow steps for policies, payments, and irreversible actions; use models where interpretation adds value.

Memory can mean conversation history, durable task state, retrieved knowledge, or user preferences. Scope memory to the task and privacy need.

Choose the simplest orchestration model that explains the workflow. Multi-agent systems add cost, latency, coordination failure modes, and evaluation complexity; they are useful only when specialization or delegation materially improves results.

Definition: A framework/ecosystem for composing language-model calls with prompts, tools, retrieval, structured output, and application logic.

Main characteristics

  • Model/provider abstractions
  • Tools and tool calling
  • Retrievers and document pipelines
  • Composable runnable interfaces
  • Integrates with LangGraph for stateful orchestration
QA / automation relevance: Relevant for testing prompt/tool contracts, retrieval behavior, provider substitutions, and deterministic boundaries around LLM calls.

Name / acronym: LangChain is a project name, not an acronym.

LangGraph
Agent/workflow orchestration framework

Definition: A framework for building stateful, graph-based LLM/agent workflows with explicit nodes, transitions, state, persistence, and human-interruption patterns.

Main characteristics

  • Graph/state-machine style control flow
  • Persistent state/checkpointing patterns
  • Cycles and conditional transitions
  • Human-in-the-loop and resumable workflows
  • Works with LangChain ecosystem but can model explicit workflow state
QA / automation relevance: Makes agent flows more testable when each node/transition has clear contracts and state can be inspected and replayed.

Name / acronym: LangGraph is a project name, not an acronym.

CrewAI
Multi-agent orchestration framework

Definition: A framework centered on agents, roles, tasks, crews, and process orchestration for collaborative AI workflows.

Main characteristics

  • Role/task-oriented abstractions
  • Sequential and collaborative process patterns
  • Tool integration
  • Agent delegation and coordination
QA / automation relevance: Useful for experimenting with multi-agent workflows, but additional agents increase evaluation, cost, latency, and failure modes.

Name / acronym: CrewAI is a project name; AI = Artificial Intelligence.

Extended v9 coverage: Framework selection · OpenAI orchestration

Intermediate → Advanced

Model Context Protocol and MCP server development

MCP standardizes how AI applications discover external capabilities. Servers can expose tools for actions, resources for context, and prompts for reusable templates.

Design narrow, typed, least-privilege capabilities. Prefer get_sensor_status(sensor_id) over a generic execute_sql(query). Validate arguments and perform authorization server-side.

Intermediate

RAG, embeddings, and vector retrieval

RAG retrieves external information before generation. Embeddings map text to vectors for semantic similarity. Retrieval quality depends on chunking, metadata, filters, embedding model, query formulation, and ranking.

Evaluate retrieval separately from generation: did the system fetch the right evidence, and did the model use it faithfully?

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
AI architecture pattern

Definition: A pattern that retrieves relevant external information and supplies it to a generative model as context before producing an answer.

Main characteristics

  • Separates retrieval from generation
  • Often uses embeddings/vector or hybrid search
  • Can apply metadata filters and reranking
  • Requires evaluation of both retrieval quality and answer grounding
QA / automation relevance: Test chunking, recall, ranking, stale documents, permissions, citations, hallucination despite correct retrieval, and failure when relevant evidence is absent.

Name / acronym: RAG = Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

Advanced

AI evaluation: deterministic vs probabilistic testing

Traditional software often has an exact oracle. LLM outputs may have multiple acceptable forms, so evaluate with rubric scores, semantic measures, task success, factuality, safety labels, latency/cost, and human review.

Build a versioned golden/evaluation set with representative normal cases, boundaries, historical failures, adversarial inputs, and high-risk scenarios. Use deterministic checks wherever possible: schema validity, tool authorization, exact calculations, required citations, and no duplicate side effects.

AI EvaluationTest StrategyLangSmith

Extended v9 coverage: Agent observability and feedback

Advanced

AI safety, prompt injection, human review, and observability

Treat retrieved webpages, documents, emails, and user content as untrusted data, not trusted instructions. Use least-privilege tools, sandboxing, allowlists, validation, data minimization, and explicit approval for high-impact actions.

Human review is useful when confidence is low, consequences are high, or policy is ambiguous. Agent observability should capture model calls, prompt/version, retrieved context, tool calls, state transitions, latency, token/cost, and final outcomes.

09 / OPERATIONS, RELIABILITY & IOT

Operate systems that can be understood and recovered

Reliability comes from observable behavior, actionable alerts, safe change, tested recovery, and learning from incidents.

Foundation → Advanced

Observability, logging, metrics, and traces

Logs record events, metrics show numerical trends, and traces connect work across services. Structured logs should include timestamps, severity, correlation/request IDs, entity IDs, and useful context—without secrets.

ObservabilityLogging
Intermediate

Monitoring, alerting, infrastructure monitoring, and dashboards

A useful alert is actionable, owned, tied to meaningful impact or leading risk, and includes enough context to investigate. Tune thresholds, deduplicate correlated events, and distinguish warnings from page-worthy incidents.

Dashboards should answer: Is the service healthy? What changed? Who is affected? Which dependency is failing?

AlertingOperational MonitoringInfrastructure MonitoringDashboard Design
Advanced

Reliability engineering, SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, and capacity

An SLI measures behavior such as success rate or latency. An SLO sets a target. The error budget is the allowed unreliability within the objective window. These concepts balance feature delivery against reliability risk.

Capacity planning models load, queue depth, storage, CPU/memory, dependency limits, and growth. Monitor the user-visible path—not only server uptime.

Reliability Engineering
Advanced

Incident management, troubleshooting, root cause analysis, and runbooks

During an incident, reduce user impact first: contain, fail over, disable, roll back, or restore. Communicate clearly and preserve evidence. After stabilization, perform blameless RCA that asks why the system allowed the failure to reach users.

Runbooks describe triggers, prerequisites, diagnostic commands, safe actions, rollback, escalation, and verification. Repeated manual recovery is a candidate for automation.

Incident ManagementTroubleshootingRoot Cause AnalysisRunbooksTechnical Operations
Foundation → Advanced

IoT, Home Assistant, MQTT, sensors, Tuya, and hardware integration

IoT failures can originate in power, radio/network, firmware, protocol, cloud service, configuration, calibration, or application logic. Diagnostics therefore cross hardware and software boundaries.

MQTT uses publish/subscribe topics through a broker, which makes it lightweight and decoupled. Home Assistant integrates devices and services into entities, automations, dashboards, and APIs. Tuya devices may use cloud, gateways, or local paths depending on hardware/integration.

For physical automation, define safe startup state, maximum run time, timeout behavior, interlocks, manual override, sensor plausibility checks, and behavior during connectivity loss.

Internet of Things (IoT)Home AssistantMQTTSensorsTuyaHardware IntegrationHome AutomationAutomation Systems

10 / PROFESSIONAL PRACTICE

Communicating quality, risk, and technical evidence

Senior QA work is not just finding bugs; it is turning ambiguous product behavior into evidence and decisions that developers, product owners, and operators can act on.

Professional practice

Explaining a project and your responsibilities

Describe product context, users, architecture at the level relevant to your work, major risks, your ownership, tools, collaboration model, difficult problems, and outcomes. Do not recite technologies—explain what each one enabled.

Professional practice

From requirements to acceptance criteria and tests

Read requirements for actors, preconditions, data, business rules, permissions, state transitions, integrations, failure behavior, and non-functional constraints. Turn ambiguity into questions before implementation finishes. Trace acceptance criteria to automated and manual coverage.

Professional practice

Evidence-driven debugging

Separate observation from hypothesis. “POST /payments returned 409 with request ID X after two rapid clicks” is evidence; “the database is broken” is a hypothesis. Report the smallest reproducible path, environment/build, data, expected vs actual behavior, impact, and artifacts.

11 / DEEP DIVE

Test Design & Quality Management

A deeper layer for the QA topics repeated throughout the question bank: how to transform ambiguous requirements into systematic coverage, how to estimate and operate testing, and how to make release decisions under uncertainty.

Foundation → Intermediate

Requirements analysis and testability

Before designing tests, turn a requirement into a model of actors, preconditions, inputs, business rules, state changes, outputs, integrations, permissions, and failure behavior. The objective is not to "understand the ticket" informally; it is to expose assumptions before they become defects.

A requirement is testable when it defines observable behavior. Statements such as “the page should be fast” or “the recommendation should be relevant” need measurable criteria. Ask what the user does, what the system must do, what data is used, and what would count as failure.

Good QA contributes during refinement: identify missing edge cases, contradictory rules, hidden dependencies, unclear ownership, and requirements that cannot be verified. This is defect prevention, not just defect detection.

  • Functional questions: What inputs are accepted? What states can the entity reach? What happens on failure?
  • Data questions: Which system is the source of truth? Are fields required, unique, or time-sensitive?
  • Security questions: Which roles can perform the action? What must never be exposed?
  • Operational questions: What should be logged, monitored, retried, or recoverable?
INTERVIEW LENS

A strong answer explains how you convert a vague story into risks and observable acceptance criteria before writing test cases.

Skills covered

Requirements AnalysisQuality AssuranceTest Planning

Related: SDLC & STLC · Acceptance criteria · Risk-based strategy

Back to contents ↑
Foundation

Acceptance criteria and examples

Acceptance criteria describe the conditions under which a feature provides the expected business behavior. They should be specific enough to test but should not prescribe unnecessary implementation detail.

Examples are often more precise than abstract prose. A transfer rule that says “do not allow overdrafts” becomes clearer when expressed with concrete balances, amounts, currencies, and expected final state. This naturally connects to BDD/Gherkin.

Acceptance criteria should include important negative behavior. If a payment fails, define whether the order remains pending, whether a retry is allowed, whether the user sees a safe message, and whether duplicate charging is impossible.

Behavior example
Given an account balance of 100 USD
When the user requests a 150 USD transfer
Then the transfer is rejected
And no ledger entry is created
And the balance remains 100 USD
INTERVIEW LENS

Explain that acceptance criteria are a contract for expected business behavior and a source for tests—not a complete test suite by themselves.

Skills covered

Acceptance TestingTest TraceabilityBDD

Related: BDD & Cucumber · Traceability

Back to contents ↑
Foundation

Equivalence partitioning

Equivalence partitioning reduces redundant testing by grouping inputs expected to behave the same. Instead of testing every possible age, amount, or string length, identify classes such as valid, invalid-low, invalid-high, missing, malformed, or unauthorized.

The technique assumes that one representative value can provide confidence about the rest of the partition. That assumption should be challenged when the implementation has special cases or data-dependent rules.

  • Example: a quantity field accepts 1–99. Partitions might be <1, 1–99, and >99.
  • Also consider type/format partitions: null, empty string, non-numeric text, decimals, Unicode, or unexpected JSON types.
INTERVIEW LENS

State the partitions first, then choose representative values. Interviewers often care more about the reasoning than the number of cases.

Skills covered

Test PlanningQuality Assurance

Related: Boundary values · Decision tables

Back to contents ↑
Foundation

Boundary value analysis

Defects cluster around edges because conditions often use <, <=, array limits, date cutoffs, or rounding. Boundary value analysis tests values immediately below, at, and immediately above important limits.

For a range 1–99, a compact set might include 0, 1, 2, 98, 99, and 100. For dates, consider exact cutoff timestamps and timezone conversions. For files, consider the size limit and just above it.

INTERVIEW LENS

Give concrete values around the boundary and explain why they reveal off-by-one and comparison defects.

Skills covered

Test PlanningData Validation

Related: Equivalence partitioning · State transitions

Intermediate

Decision tables and business-rule combinations

Decision tables model combinations of conditions and the resulting action. They are useful when multiple independent rules interact—for example account status, balance, fraud flag, and transfer amount.

List conditions, enumerate meaningful combinations, eliminate impossible combinations, and define expected outcomes. This avoids accidentally testing each rule in isolation while missing interactions.

Decision table
| Verified | Balance sufficient | Fraud flag | Expected |
| yes      | yes                | no         | approve  |
| yes      | no                 | no         | reject   |
| no       | yes                | no         | reject   |
| yes      | yes                | yes        | review   |
INTERVIEW LENS

Use decision tables when “if A and B unless C” starts becoming hard to reason about in prose.

Skills covered

Intermediate

State-transition testing

Many systems behave differently based on current state. A payment might move created → authorized → captured → refunded. A support ticket might move open → assigned → resolved → reopened. State-transition testing validates both allowed and forbidden moves.

Test the transition, resulting state, side effects, and behavior when the same action is repeated. Invalid transitions should fail safely and should not leave partial state.

State model
const allowed = {
  pending: ['paid', 'cancelled'],
  paid: ['refunded'],
  cancelled: [],
  refunded: []
};
INTERVIEW LENS

Model the state machine explicitly. Then test valid transitions, invalid transitions, repeated events, and recovery after partial failure.

Intermediate

Test estimation and planning under uncertainty

Test estimates should reflect scope, risk, environments, data, dependencies, automation work, defect turnaround, and uncertainty—not just the number of test cases. A new integration with an unstable third party can require more effort than a large but isolated UI change.

Break work into activities such as requirement analysis, test design, setup, automation, execution, investigation, retest, and reporting. Explicitly identify assumptions and external dependencies.

When time is fixed, reduce scope by risk rather than pretending the original plan still fits. Communicate what will remain untested and the consequence of that decision.

INTERVIEW LENS

Explain the dimensions you estimate and how you communicate uncertainty. Avoid giving a formula that ignores risk.

Intermediate

Test environment management

A test result is only meaningful if the environment is understood. Record application version, service versions, feature flags, browser/runtime versions, database state, external dependencies, credentials/roles, and relevant configuration.

Environment drift is a common reason tests pass locally and fail in CI. Prefer reproducible setup through containers, infrastructure-as-code, seeded data, and versioned configuration. When full parity with production is impossible, document the differences and risks.

Test data should be separate from environment configuration. Changing a test account is not the same as changing the runtime environment.

Defect triage and prioritization

Triage decides whether a report represents a defect, its impact, urgency, ownership, and release consequence. Good triage uses evidence and business context rather than arguing about labels.

Consider severity, frequency, affected users, workaround, data/security impact, regulatory implications, detectability, and proximity to release. Duplicate reports should be linked without losing additional evidence.

A rejected bug should have a reason: expected behavior, cannot reproduce with current evidence, duplicate, configuration issue, or requirement decision. “Works on my machine” is not a sufficient resolution.

Advanced

Release readiness and residual risk

Release readiness is a decision supported by evidence. It combines test results, known defects, change scope, production observability, rollback capability, migration readiness, dependency health, and unresolved risk.

Not every failure must block a release, and not every green pipeline means the release is safe. Define blocking criteria before the deadline. Exceptions should be explicit, owned, documented, and time-bounded.

For high-risk changes, validate deployment and rollback procedures. A feature that works only when deployment succeeds perfectly is operationally fragile.

INTERVIEW LENS

Explain what evidence you would bring to a go/no-go decision and how you communicate residual risk rather than simply saying “QA approved.”

UAT collaboration and business process testing

User Acceptance Testing validates whether the system supports real business work. QA can prepare scenarios/data, explain expected behavior, observe failures, and translate business feedback into actionable defects or requirement changes.

UAT should not be the first time basic functionality is exercised. Engineering tests should already cover deterministic behavior; UAT focuses on business fit, workflow, policy, and acceptance.

For complex operational workflows, shadowing users and mapping the real process often reveals states and exceptions that are absent from written requirements.

Intermediate → Advanced

When database, API, and UI disagree: source of truth, freshness, transformations, and eventual consistency

When the database, API, and UI display different values, do not immediately decide that one layer is wrong. First identify the authoritative source of truth for that field and the expected propagation path from write to read.

Record timestamps, request IDs, entity IDs, cache keys, database row/version information, and the exact API payload. A difference can come from stale cache, asynchronous replication, eventual consistency, transformation/rounding, timezone conversion, formatting, authorization filtering, or a genuine mapping defect.

Trace the value in order: write event → persistent state → service/domain transformation → API representation → frontend state/cache → rendered UI. Compare the same entity and point in time at every boundary.

A UI assertion should not bypass the system's architecture. If the product contract explicitly allows eventual consistency, test the allowed convergence window rather than asserting immediate equality.

INTERVIEW LENS

Start by establishing ownership and freshness. “The database is always correct” is not a safe assumption in distributed systems.

Related: Evidence-driven debugging · API resilience · Data validation

Skills covered

Data ValidationAPI TestingSQLTroubleshootingRoot Cause Analysis

Intermediate → Advanced

Quality metrics, defect escapes, and signal quality

Metrics are useful only when they change a decision. Raw test count and pass percentage are weak proxies for product quality because they do not describe what risk was covered or what escaped to users.

Track trends such as escaped defects, severity distribution, flaky rate, time-to-detect, time-to-resolve, execution duration, failure cause, coverage of critical journeys, and release change-failure rate. Segment metrics by product area and risk so averages do not hide critical failures.

Avoid rewarding teams for numbers they can game. If success is “more tests,” low-value tests multiply. If success is “100% pass,” teams may quarantine meaningful failures. Prefer metrics tied to customer and engineering outcomes.

Quality AssuranceTest ReportingTest Strategy

12 / DEEP DIVE

Advanced Browser Automation & Playwright

A reference layer for advanced Playwright and Selenium interview topics: race-free browser events, fixtures, sharding, emulation, API setup, reports, and current guidance such as the deprecation of layout selectors.

Intermediate

Playwright vs Selenium: execution model and trade-offs

Selenium and Playwright both automate browsers, but they encourage different synchronization and isolation patterns. Selenium traditionally exposes WebDriver objects and explicit waits; Playwright centers Locator, auto-waiting, browser contexts, web-first assertions, and an integrated test runner.

The right choice depends on ecosystem, language, legacy infrastructure, browser requirements, and team skills. Existing enterprise suites may favor Selenium; new JavaScript/TypeScript web automation often benefits from Playwright’s integrated capabilities.

Concepts transfer: stable locators, isolated state, meaningful assertions, deterministic data, parallel safety, and evidence are more important than framework syntax.

INTERVIEW LENS

Do not answer that one tool is universally “better.” Compare architecture, team ecosystem, and maintainability.

Skills covered

Test AutomationPlaywrightBrowser Automation

Selenium
Browser automation ecosystem

Definition: An open-source browser automation ecosystem centered on WebDriver, which drives browsers through standardized automation interfaces.

Main characteristics

  • Broad browser/language support
  • WebDriver-based client/server model
  • Explicit waits are important for synchronization
  • Large mature ecosystem and enterprise adoption
  • Selenium Grid supports distributed browser execution

Related: Playwright auto-waiting · Selenium waits

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate

Selenium waits, stale elements, and ThreadLocal

An explicit Selenium wait targets a specific condition such as visibility, clickability, URL, or custom state. Broad implicit waits can make timing harder to reason about, especially when mixed with explicit waits.

A stale element means the DOM node referenced by an Element object was replaced or detached. Re-find the element after the update instead of holding long-lived references.

For parallel Java tests, ThreadLocal<WebDriver> can isolate one driver per thread. Clean it up after execution; thread-local state that is never removed can leak resources across reused worker threads.

Java / Selenium
private static final ThreadLocal<WebDriver> DRIVER = new ThreadLocal<>();

public static WebDriver driver() {
    return DRIVER.get();
}

@AfterEach
void cleanup() {
    if (DRIVER.get() != null) DRIVER.get().quit();
    DRIVER.remove();
}
INTERVIEW LENS

Connect stale-element handling and waits to dynamic DOM behavior, not to arbitrary sleeps.

Skills covered

Test Automation

Related: Playwright auto-waiting · Flakiness

Intermediate

Layout selectors and why :right-of() is deprecated

Playwright supports layout pseudo-classes such as :right-of(), :left-of(), :above(), :below(), and :near(), but current Playwright documentation marks layout selectors as deprecated because one-pixel layout changes can select a different element.

Prefer accessible roles, labels, text, test IDs, and locator filtering. If layout matching is unavoidable, combine it with a strong element selector and understand that first() chooses the closest match, not necessarily the semantically correct one.

This is an example of why interview questions can test legacy or edge APIs even when production guidance has evolved. Know the API, but also know the recommended modern alternative.

INTERVIEW LENS

Mention the deprecation proactively. That demonstrates current knowledge rather than simply memorizing selector syntax.

Skills covered

PlaywrightAccessibility Testing

Related: Locators · Accessibility

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate

textContent vs innerText, Locator vs ElementHandle, and JSHandle

textContent() reflects DOM text content and can include text from hidden descendants. innerText() is closer to rendered text and accounts for layout/visibility. For assertions, prefer web-first locator assertions such as toHaveText() when possible.

Locator stores the logic for finding an element and re-resolves it on use. ElementHandle points to one DOM node and can become stale; Playwright discourages handles for normal actions/assertions.

JSHandle retains a browser-side JavaScript object from garbage collection until the frame/context goes away or you call dispose(). Use handles only when page-evaluation work genuinely needs them.

TypeScript / Playwright
const locator = page.getByTestId('hidden-metadata');
const raw = await locator.textContent();
await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText('Ready');

const handle = await page.evaluateHandle(() => window.someLargeObject);
try {
  // inspect the browser-side object
} finally {
  await handle.dispose();
}
INTERVIEW LENS

Explain semantics first: DOM text vs rendered text, re-resolving locator vs fixed element reference.

Skills covered

PlaywrightBrowser Automation

Related: Locators · Assertions

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate

iframes, dialogs, popups, and new tabs

For iframes, use frameLocator() to keep locator semantics inside the frame. Avoid jumping to raw frame objects unless you need lower-level frame control.

Browser dialogs such as alert/confirm/prompt block the page. Register the dialog handler before triggering the action, then accept or dismiss intentionally.

For popups/new tabs, begin waiting for the page event before the click that creates it. This avoids a race where the new page appears before the listener is active.

TypeScript / Playwright
const popupPromise = page.waitForEvent('popup');
await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Open invoice' }).click();
const popup = await popupPromise;
await expect(popup).toHaveURL(/invoice/);

await page.frameLocator('#payment-frame')
  .getByLabel('Card number')
  .fill('4111111111111111');
INTERVIEW LENS

The key idea is race-free event waiting and scoping locators to the correct browsing context.

Skills covered

Intermediate

File uploads and downloads

Use setInputFiles() for file inputs and validate both client-side behavior and server-side result. Include wrong type, zero-byte file, maximum size, duplicate names, Unicode names, and cancellation where relevant.

For downloads, start waiting for the download event before the action. Validate suggested filename, failure state, and file contents when the business risk justifies it. Temporary paths are cleaned up with the context.

TypeScript / Playwright
await page.getByLabel('Upload document').setInputFiles('fixtures/report.pdf');

const downloadPromise = page.waitForEvent('download');
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Export CSV' }).click();
const download = await downloadPromise;
expect(download.suggestedFilename()).toMatch(/\.csv$/);

Permissions, geolocation, locale, timezone, and environment emulation

Playwright can configure browser permissions, geolocation, locale, timezone, color scheme, user agent, viewport, and touch behavior. These are useful for deterministic scenarios that would otherwise depend on the developer machine.

Emulation is not the same as a physical device. OS-level behavior, native permissions, hardware sensors, mobile webviews, push notifications, and some rendering/input differences still require real-device testing.

playwright.config.ts
use: {
  locale: 'es-AR',
  timezoneId: 'America/Argentina/Buenos_Aires',
  geolocation: { latitude: -34.60, longitude: -58.38 },

Intermediate

APIRequestContext for service testing and setup

Playwright Test provides an API request context that shares familiar test-runner features with browser tests. It is useful for direct API validation and for fast setup/teardown around UI tests.

A common pattern is: create state through an API, exercise the critical browser workflow, then verify the final API/database state. This keeps UI setup fast while preserving end-to-end confidence in the behavior that matters.

Do not hide all business validation behind UI tests. Keep dedicated service-level tests for contracts, errors, authorization, and data invariants.

TypeScript / Playwright
test('refund appears in UI', async ({ request, page }) => {
  const order = await request.post('/api/orders', { data: { total: 25 } });
  const { id } = await order.json();
  await page.goto('/orders/' + id);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Refund' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Refunded')).toBeVisible();
});

Describe the test layer intentionally: setup through API, user-visible behavior through UI, final state through API if needed.

Tags and annotations let teams select suites by purpose: smoke, critical, payments, accessibility, or environment constraints. Keep tags meaningful and governed; hundreds of ad-hoc tags become another source of entropy.

Sharding splits a suite across CI machines, while multiple workers parallelize inside a machine. Both require tests to be isolated. Balance shards by historical duration if one shard consistently receives all the slow tests.

Parallelism increases demand on databases, rate limits, test accounts, and external services. Capacity of the test environment can become the bottleneck before CPU does.

INTERVIEW LENS

Differentiate workers from shards and explain the isolation/capacity requirements of each.

Project dependencies, setup projects, and authenticated state

Projects can depend on a setup project that prepares shared prerequisites such as authentication state. Unlike opaque global setup hooks, project dependencies are visible in reports and can use fixtures and tracing.

Keep setup deterministic and minimize cross-project mutable state. A setup project that creates one shared account for hundreds of parallel tests can become a bottleneck or source of conflicts.

playwright.config.ts
projects: [
  { name: 'setup', testMatch: /.*\.setup\.ts/ },
  {
    name: 'chromium',
    use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'], storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json' },
    dependencies: ['setup']
  }
]

Visual snapshots and automated accessibility scans

Visual snapshot tests compare screenshots against baselines. Stabilize viewport, fonts, animations, data, time, and dynamic content before relying on pixel diffs. Review baseline changes as code changes.

Automated accessibility scans can catch missing names, invalid roles, contrast issues, and structural violations, but they cannot prove the complete user experience. Pair them with keyboard navigation, focus checks, zoom/reflow, and representative screen-reader testing.

Keep visual and accessibility checks targeted. A full-page screenshot for every state can be expensive and noisy; component- or critical-page baselines are often more maintainable.

Allure can organize test results into steps, attachments, categories, history, trends, and environment information. Attach only evidence that helps diagnosis: screenshots, logs, HTTP exchanges, videos, and traces.

Historical data is useful for identifying unstable tests and regressions across builds. Current Allure versions differ in how history is stored, so treat report-version configuration as implementation detail and preserve stable test identity across runs.

Categories can separate product failures from test/framework failures. This makes a dashboard more actionable than a single red/green total.

Intermediate → Advanced

Selenium dynamic UI: WebDriverWait, relative XPath, stale elements, windows, nested iframes, sticky headers, and virtualized tables

WebDriverWait is Selenium's explicit-wait mechanism. Wait for a specific observable condition—visibility, clickability, URL/title change, frame availability, element count, or a custom predicate—rather than inserting fixed sleeps.

For dynamic XPath, anchor the selector to a stable business container and then use a relative relationship. For example, locate the product card by product name and find its rating inside that card. Avoid absolute XPath such as /html/body/div[3]/..., which couples the test to incidental DOM structure.

A StaleElementReferenceException means the previously located DOM element was detached or replaced. Wait for the update and locate the element again. Refreshing the whole page can hide the real synchronization problem.

For multiple windows/tabs, save the original handle, trigger the new window, wait until the expected number of handles exists, identify the new tab by expected URL/title/content, switch deliberately, and return to the original handle. Window-handle order is not a stable contract.

For nested iframes, switch one frame level at a time after waiting for frame availability. Use parentFrame() to move one level up and defaultContent() to return to the top document.

Sticky headers and virtualized tables need viewport-aware tests. Scroll the actual table/container, validate the sticky header separately, and re-locate rows after scrolling because virtualization may recycle DOM nodes for different data.

Selenium dynamic-state patterns
WebDriverWait wait = new WebDriverWait(driver, Duration.ofSeconds(10));

WebElement card = wait.until(ExpectedConditions.visibilityOfElementLocated(
    By.xpath("//article[.//h3[normalize-space()='Laptop Pro']]")
));

String rating = card.findElement(
    By.xpath(".//*[@aria-label[contains(., 'rating')]]")
).getAttribute("aria-label");

// Nested frame
wait.until(ExpectedConditions.frameToBeAvailableAndSwitchToIt(By.id("outer")));
wait.until(ExpectedConditions.frameToBeAvailableAndSwitchToIt(By.id("inner")));
// ... assertions ...
driver.switchTo().parentFrame();
driver.switchTo().defaultContent();
INTERVIEW LENS

Connect the technique to browser state: re-query replaced DOM nodes, identify tabs by behavior rather than index, and treat virtualized rows as transient views of data.

COMMON TRAP: Mixing large implicit waits with explicit waits can create confusing compounded timing.

Skills covered

SeleniumTest AutomationBrowser Automation

Advanced

Playwright BrowserContext versus Selenium WebDriver session, ThreadLocal, waits, and parallel isolation

A Playwright BrowserContext is a lightweight isolated browser profile inside a browser process. Each context has its own cookies, local storage, permissions, and pages. It is cheap enough to create per test in many suites.

A Selenium WebDriver session represents a browser automation session controlled through the WebDriver protocol. Parallel Selenium suites typically create separate driver sessions; sharing one driver across concurrent tests is unsafe.

In Java/TestNG frameworks, ThreadLocal<WebDriver> can bind one driver to each worker thread. The same principle applies to wait/helper objects that carry driver-specific state. Always call remove() during teardown because thread-pool workers can be reused.

ThreadLocal only solves in-process object ownership. It does not isolate shared accounts, test records, downloads, database rows, queues, or external service state.

Thread-local WebDriver lifecycle
private static final ThreadLocal<WebDriver> DRIVER = new ThreadLocal<>();

public static WebDriver driver() {
    return DRIVER.get();
}

@BeforeMethod
public void setUp() {
    DRIVER.set(new ChromeDriver());
}

@AfterMethod(alwaysRun = true)
public void tearDown() {
    WebDriver d = DRIVER.get();
    if (d != null) d.quit();
    DRIVER.remove();
}
INTERVIEW LENS

Browser isolation and test-data isolation are separate problems.

Skills covered

SeleniumPlaywrightTestNGParallel Testing

Intermediate → Advanced

Capturing screenshots and evidence automatically on TestNG failure

TestNG listeners such as ITestListener can observe test success/failure and capture evidence before the driver is destroyed. Failure hooks are useful for screenshots, page URL/title, browser logs, network/trace references, and report attachments.

Name evidence with test ID/name, timestamp, worker/thread, browser, and build/run ID so parallel executions never overwrite each other.

Capture the screenshot before teardown. If the framework closes the browser first, the most useful state is already gone.

A screenshot is only one signal. For intermittent failures, retain enough context to correlate the UI image with logs, network calls, test data, and the CI build.

ITestListener failure hook
public class FailureListener implements ITestListener {
    @Override
    public void onTestFailure(ITestResult result) {
        WebDriver driver = DriverManager.driver();
        if (driver instanceof TakesScreenshot shot) {
            byte[] png = shot.getScreenshotAs(OutputType.BYTES);
            ReportAttachments.attachPng(result.getName(), png);
        }
    }
}
INTERVIEW LENS

Listeners centralize cross-cutting evidence collection without duplicating try/catch blocks in every test.
