Advanced

Measuring an LLM-assisted test-generation pipeline without guessing

Treat the generator as a product with a versioned evaluation set. Establish a baseline, change one variable at a time, compare against the baseline/control, and inspect failure categories rather than relying only on average quality.

Useful metrics include semantic agreement with the source test/requirement, approved-step reuse rate, duplicate/new-step rate, schema-valid rate, compile/type-check rate, first-run execution success, stable rerun rate, reviewer acceptance rate, reviewer editing time, defect/value contribution, latency, token cost, and infrastructure cost.

Segment by test type and difficulty. A high compile rate can hide weak assertions; a high execution rate can hide incorrect semantics. Keep catastrophic errors—wrong account, destructive action, false pass, leaked secret—as separate high-severity measures.

Use human labels for a representative sample and calibrate any LLM-as-judge against them. Retain historical failures in the eval set so improvements do not reintroduce previously fixed errors.

Pipeline evaluation example
Example experiment table:
version | semantic_accept | step_reuse | compile | stable_run | review_min | cost
v1      | 0.71            | 0.62       | 0.78    | 0.59       | 8.4        | $...
v2      | 0.83            | 0.79       | 0.91    | 0.77       | 4.9        | $...

Promote v2 only if high-severity failure categories also improve or remain within threshold.

A pipeline is improved by evidence: baseline → controlled change → labeled evaluation → failure analysis → retain only reproducible gains.

Agentic AI engineering: agent loops, SDKs, runtimes, protocols, sandboxes, and production systems

This chapter fills the gaps found by comparing v8 with the full Agentic AI Engineering course. It moves from framework-neutral agent design into current OpenAI Agents SDK, CrewAI, LangChain/LangGraph, Deep Agents, Google ADK/A2A, Strands, PydanticAI, Microsoft Agent Framework, Agno, Mastra, advanced MCP, deployment, evaluation, and reusable project architectures.

Foundation

Agentic AI project setup: uv, virtual environments, .env files, API keys, Git, Cursor, and cost awareness

uv is a fast Python package and project manager from Astral. It can initialize projects, manage Python versions and virtual environments, resolve and lock dependencies, run commands, and install tools. In agent projects it provides a reproducible alternative to a loose combination of pip, venv, pipx, and ad-hoc requirements files.

Keep model/provider credentials outside source code. A local .env file is convenient for development when it is excluded from Git, while production should use the deployment platform's secret store. Validate required variables on startup and fail clearly when one is missing.

Cursor is an AI-oriented code editor. It is useful as a development surface, but it is not part of the runtime architecture. The same agent project should remain runnable from a terminal and CI.

Agent costs are operational behavior. Record provider/model, token usage, tool-call counts, latency, retries, and external API costs. A prototype that works only because it silently makes dozens of expensive calls is not production-ready.

Reproducible Python agent project
uv init agent-lab
cd agent-lab
uv add openai python-dotenv pydantic
uv run python app.py

# .gitignore
.env
.venv/

Foundation → Intermediate

Agents versus workflows and core design patterns: chaining, routing, parallelization, and orchestrator-worker

A workflow has an explicit control path chosen by code or configuration. An agent delegates at least some control decisions—typically tool selection, subtask planning, or next-step choice—to a model. Use a normal function or workflow when the process is known and deterministic.

Chaining passes one model call's output into the next. Routing chooses a specialist/model/path based on the request. Parallelization runs independent work concurrently. Orchestrator-worker patterns let one component decompose a task and assign parts to workers before synthesizing the result.

The word 'autonomous' should not imply unlimited freedom. Production autonomy is bounded by tool permissions, stop conditions, budgets, guardrails, human approvals, and durable state.

INTERVIEW LENS

A strong design starts by asking whether an agent is needed at all. Explicit workflows are easier to reason about when the steps are known.

Provider abstraction, OpenAI-compatible APIs, Claude, Gemini, Groq, Ollama, and local models

Agent systems should separate the model-provider adapter from business logic. Provider choice affects model quality, context window, tool calling, structured output, latency, cost, data policy, and regional availability.

Many providers expose an OpenAI-compatible API, allowing similar client code with a different base URL and credential. Compatibility is not equivalence: supported parameters, tool semantics, streaming, structured output, and error behavior can differ.

Ollama runs supported models locally and exposes an API for model invocation. Local inference can improve privacy and remove per-request cloud costs, but hardware capacity, model quality, startup time, memory usage, and operations become your responsibility.

Comparing eight models is not useful unless the evaluation task and rubric are stable. Use a versioned evaluation set and capture model IDs, parameters, latency, and cost.

INTERVIEW LENS

Do not promise provider portability based only on an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Verify the exact capabilities your application uses.

LLM-as-a-judge as an orchestration component

An LLM judge evaluates another model's output against a rubric. It can rank candidate answers, score dimensions, classify failures, or provide feedback to an orchestrator.

Judges introduce their own bias, stochasticity, model dependency, and position/style preferences. Calibrate them against human labels, randomize candidate order when comparing outputs, use structured rubrics, and track agreement over time.

A judge is most useful as one signal inside an evaluation system. Deterministic checks—schema validity, exact calculations, required citations, forbidden actions—should remain deterministic.

The agent ecosystem: model API, framework, runtime, harness, tool, protocol, builder, and deployment surface

A model API provides inference. An agent framework/SDK provides abstractions such as agents, tools, memory, handoffs, and workflows. A runtime executes and persists the work. An agent harness adds opinionated capabilities for long-running tasks such as planning, files, subagents, compaction, approvals, and observability.

A tool is a capability the agent can invoke. A protocol, such as MCP or A2A, standardizes communication. A builder or studio provides a UI for authoring/testing. A deployment surface hosts the application.

These layers are often bundled by products, which makes comparisons confusing. Compare frameworks at the layer you actually need rather than by marketing labels.

Intermediate

Build the agent loop from scratch: model → tool call → validation → execution → observation → repeat

A tool-using agent loop is conceptually simple: send instructions, conversation state, and tool schemas to a model; inspect the response; validate requested tool calls; execute authorized tools; append tool results; and call the model again until it returns a final answer or a stop condition fires.

Support multiple tool calls in one turn rather than assuming exactly one. Dispatch by an explicit registry, not unrestricted dynamic access to arbitrary Python globals. Validate every argument and normalize tool errors into structured results the model can reason about.

Set maximum turns, token/cost budgets, deadlines, and recursion limits. Persist checkpoints for long tasks. A visible checklist/to-do tool can externalize the plan and make long-running work auditable.

Framework-neutral agent loop
TOOLS = {
    "get_order": get_order,
    "create_ticket": create_ticket,
}

for turn in range(MAX_TURNS):
    response = model_call(messages, tool_schemas)

    if not response.tool_calls:
        return response.final_text

    for call in response.tool_calls:
        fn = TOOLS.get(call.name)
        if fn is None:
            result = {"error": "unknown_tool"}
        else:
            args = validate(call.name, call.arguments)
            result = fn(**args)
        messages.append(tool_result(call.id, result))

raise RuntimeError("agent exceeded turn budget")
INTERVIEW LENS

The model proposes an action; application code authorizes, validates, executes, and records it.

COMMON TRAP: Using `globals()` or eval-like dynamic dispatch without a strict allowlist creates an unnecessarily broad execution surface.

Advanced

Context engineering: system prompts, conversation state, memory, RAG, tools, files, and progressive disclosure

Context engineering is the design of what information and capabilities are made available to a model at each step. It is broader than prompt engineering: it includes system/developer instructions, conversation history, retrieved documents, tool descriptions, memory, files, schemas, current task state, and summaries.

Do not place everything in the prompt. Large static context increases cost and can reduce attention quality. Retrieve or reveal information only when needed, summarize older state, and separate durable memory from short-lived working context.

For a digital-twin or résumé agent, parse source documents into structured or retrievable evidence rather than asking the model to invent autobiographical facts. Ground career claims in sources and keep private data scoped to the intended audience.

Progressive disclosure exposes a small capability summary first, then loads deeper instructions or tools only when relevant. Skills files and MCP/tool registries can use this pattern to reduce context overload.

INTERVIEW LENS

Prompt engineering changes wording; context engineering designs the whole information environment around the model.

OpenAI Agents SDK: Agent, Runner, function tools, sessions, guardrails, handoffs, and tracing

The OpenAI Agents SDK is a production-oriented SDK for building agentic applications with a small set of primitives. An Agent combines instructions, a model, tools, handoffs, and guardrails. Runner.run() executes the agent loop until completion or another stop condition.

A Python function can become a validated tool through @function_tool; schemas are inferred and validated. The SDK supports sessions for persistent conversation history, handoffs for transferring control to a specialist agent, agents-as-tools for manager/subagent patterns, MCP tools, human-in-the-loop, and built-in tracing.

Use the raw Responses API when you want to own the loop and state yourself. Use the Agents SDK when you want the runtime to manage turns, tool execution, sessions, handoffs, guardrails, or tracing.

OpenAI's current SDKs exist for Python and TypeScript. Keep model calls behind application boundaries so your domain logic is testable without a live provider.

OpenAI Agents SDK concept
from agents import Agent, Runner, function_tool

@function_tool
def lookup_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    return {"id": order_id, "status": "paid"}

agent = Agent(
    name="Support",
    instructions="Use tools for factual order status.",
    tools=[lookup_order],
)

result = Runner.run_sync(agent, "Check order A-42")
print(result.final_output)

OpenAI Agents SDK sessions, SQLiteSession, multi-turn context, and state ownership

Sessions let the Agents SDK maintain conversation history across runs without manually rebuilding the message list. A session identifier scopes which history belongs together.

SQLiteSession is a convenient durable local implementation for development and single-host workloads. Production architecture should consider concurrency, retention, encryption, deletion, tenancy, and whether a managed/distributed store is needed.

Conversation history is not the same as business state. An order status, approval, or workflow checkpoint should live in a domain database or durable workflow store rather than only in chat history.

Current Agents SDK continuation mechanisms have different ownership models. Avoid stacking multiple memory/continuation systems without understanding which layer is authoritative.

Session-backed conversation memory
from agents import Agent, Runner, SQLiteSession

session = SQLiteSession("customer-42", "agent_memory.db")
result = Runner.run_sync(
    Agent(name="Assistant"),
    "Remember that my preferred format is concise.",
    session=session,
)

OpenAI Agents SDK orchestration: code, asyncio.gather, agents-as-tools, and handoffs

Code orchestration gives the application explicit control: call several specialists, wait for their results, and synthesize them deterministically. Python's asyncio.gather() is useful when independent agent calls can run concurrently.

With agents-as-tools, a manager agent keeps control and invokes specialist agents as capabilities. With handoffs, control transfers to another agent better suited to continue the conversation/task.

Choose code orchestration when ordering, retries, fan-out, or business policy must be explicit. Choose model-directed delegation when the routing problem itself is semantic and bounded.

Multi-agent systems multiply failure modes. Add per-agent budgets, trace IDs, structured contracts, and evaluation of both individual agents and the end-to-end outcome.

Explicit parallel orchestration
results = await asyncio.gather(
    researcher.run(topic),
    competitor_analyst.run(topic),
    reviewer.run(topic),
)
report = synthesize(results)

OpenAI guardrails, structured outputs, sandboxes, MCP, hosted tools, and tracing

Guardrails validate agent input or final output and can stop an unsafe or irrelevant run. They supplement—not replace—authorization inside tools.

Structured outputs turn model output into a typed contract, often backed by Pydantic or Zod. Use them for planner results, classifications, research plans, and task handoffs.

Sandboxed execution isolates risky code/tool activity from the host. A sandbox reduces blast radius but still requires network, filesystem, credential, CPU/time, and package controls.

The Agents SDK can use function tools, MCP tools, and supported hosted tools. Built-in tracing records model generations, tool calls, guardrails, handoffs, and custom events, making the execution path inspectable.

Tracing is observability, not correctness. Pair traces with evaluations, policy checks, and domain metrics.

Deep research agent architecture: planner, search/retrieval workers, writer, evaluator, and delivery

A deep-research workflow decomposes an open-ended question into subquestions, collects evidence, tracks source provenance, synthesizes findings, and evaluates gaps before producing a final report.

A planner should output a structured research plan. Search/retrieval workers gather evidence independently. A writer synthesizes only supported claims, while an evaluator checks completeness, contradictions, and citation coverage.

Parallel search can reduce latency but increases duplicate work and cost. Deduplicate queries, cache results, and stop when marginal evidence no longer improves the answer.

Treat external web content as untrusted data. It can contain prompt injection; retrieved text should never acquire tool authority merely because the agent read it.

CrewAI: agents, tasks, crews, flows, YAML configuration, tools, and context

CrewAI organizes work through agents, tasks, crews, and flows. A Crew describes collaborative execution; a Flow adds explicit event/state-driven orchestration around steps and crews.

YAML configuration can separate role/task configuration from Python wiring, making behavior easier to review. Configuration is not validation: tool permissions, data contracts, and stop conditions still belong in code/runtime controls.

Task context lets one task consume outputs from earlier tasks. Tools give agents external capabilities. For research use cases, a web-search provider such as Serper can be wrapped as a tool, but provider credentials and result trust must be controlled.

Use CrewAI when role/task composition is genuinely useful. A single deterministic pipeline is simpler when every step is already known.

Memory can improve continuity but also retain stale or sensitive information. Define what is remembered, who owns it, how it expires, and how a user can correct it.

Custom tools should be narrow, typed, observable, and independently testable. The tool is part of your software system, not merely prompt text.

LangGraph state, nodes, edges, reducers, supersteps, checkpointers, replay, and time travel

A LangGraph application models execution as a graph. State is shared data; nodes compute changes; edges determine routing; reducers define how concurrent/iterative updates merge.

A superstep is a unit of graph execution in which eligible nodes run and produce state updates before the graph advances. Thinking in supersteps is useful for parallel branches and deterministic state merging.

Checkpointers persist state at execution boundaries. They enable durable threads, pause/resume, debugging, replay, and 'time travel' to a prior checkpoint for branching or investigation.

Persistence makes failure recovery possible but introduces data-retention, tenant-isolation, migration, and cleanup responsibilities.

INTERVIEW LENS

A checkpointer stores graph state/history; memory is the higher-level information the application intentionally carries across turns or threads.

Deep Agents: agent harness, planning, filesystems, subagents, skills, and progressive disclosure

Deep Agents is a LangChain ecosystem harness for complex, long-running tasks. It combines planning/to-do tracking, filesystem-backed context management, subagent delegation, memory, and optional sandbox execution.

Filesystem tools let the agent offload large artifacts from the immediate model context. Subagents receive isolated context for focused tasks and return concise results to the parent.

Skills package reusable domain instructions/workflows. Progressive disclosure means the agent sees enough metadata to select a skill and loads detailed instructions only when the skill is actually needed.

Agent harnesses are useful when tasks are genuinely long and tool-heavy. A simple support bot does not need a filesystem, to-do planner, subagents, and shell access.

An agent harness is more opinionated than a bare framework: it bundles planning, context management, files, delegation, and operational controls.

A browser-based sidekick combines an agent loop with browser tools such as Playwright MCP, general tools, durable task state, and an evaluator that checks whether the requested work is complete.

Middleware can intercept model/tool activity to add approval checks, context, logging, policy, model routing, or summarization without embedding those concerns in every tool.

Human-in-the-loop approval is especially important before sending messages, purchasing, deleting, publishing, changing permissions, or executing other high-impact actions.

The evaluator should check the user's actual goal and evidence, not merely whether the agent produced confident text.

Google ADK and A2A: agent development, tools, MCP, Agent Cards, and remote agents

Google ADK (Agent Development Kit) is Google's framework/toolkit for building and operating agents with support for tools, sessions/state, multi-agent patterns, evaluation, and integrations such as MCP.

A2A (Agent2Agent) is a protocol for agent-to-agent interoperability. An Agent Card describes a remote agent's identity/capabilities and how a client can communicate with it.

MCP and A2A solve different boundaries: MCP standardizes an agent/app consuming tools and context; A2A standardizes agents communicating/delegating across service boundaries.

Remote-agent interoperability creates trust issues: authenticate peers, constrain data sharing, validate task/result schemas, and define timeouts/cancellation.

Microsoft Agent Framework: the successor to AutoGen and Semantic Kernel

Microsoft Agent Framework is Microsoft's current multi-language framework for agents and workflows. It includes agents, a long-task agent harness, graph/functional workflows, sessions/memory, middleware, tools, MCP, human-in-the-loop patterns, and integrations.

Microsoft describes Agent Framework as the direct successor to AutoGen and Semantic Kernel for this generation of agentic applications. It combines AutoGen-style agent abstractions with Semantic Kernel's enterprise-oriented state, middleware, telemetry, and integration capabilities, then adds explicit graph workflows.

AutoGen remains important historically and in existing systems: it pioneered group-chat/event-driven multi-agent patterns. Semantic Kernel remains a supported SDK and middleware ecosystem, but new agent architecture decisions should evaluate Agent Framework and the official migration guidance.

A framework migration is not a search/replace. Re-evaluate orchestration semantics, state ownership, observability, tool schemas, and safety controls.

Choosing an agent framework: ten criteria that matter more than demos

Compare frameworks using: (1) control model, (2) state/persistence, (3) tool model, (4) structured outputs, (5) human approval, (6) durability/recovery, (7) observability/evaluation, (8) provider/protocol interoperability, (9) deployment/operations, and (10) ecosystem/team fit.

Also compare maintenance activity, license, API stability, security model, testing ergonomics, and migration cost. A framework that minimizes code in a tutorial can still maximize operational complexity later.

Prefer the smallest abstraction that solves the actual problem. Many production systems need one agent plus deterministic tools and workflows rather than a multi-agent society.

Advanced / Current

MCP architecture: host, client, server, local/remote deployment, and transports

In MCP (Model Context Protocol), the host is the LLM application the user interacts with. A host creates one or more clients, and each client connects to an MCP server that exposes capabilities.

The three core server primitives are tools, resources, and prompts. Tools are model-invoked actions, resources expose readable context, and prompts expose reusable prompt templates.

Local servers are commonly launched as subprocesses over stdio. Remote servers use HTTP-based transports such as Streamable HTTP. Transport choice affects authentication, deployment, lifecycle, and trust boundaries but should not change tool semantics.

Initialization includes protocol/capability negotiation. Clients should close connections and spawned processes cleanly; remote servers need authentication, authorization, rate limiting, logging, and tenant isolation.

INTERVIEW LENS

A host contains MCP clients; servers do not talk directly to the model.

Current documentation: MCP Python SDK concepts

Advanced

When to build an MCP server, FastMCP, marketplaces, and server testing

Build an MCP server when a reusable capability should be discoverable by multiple MCP hosts/agents and the protocol boundary improves interoperability. Do not create a server for a one-function internal call when a normal library function is simpler.

FastMCP-style SDK APIs reduce protocol boilerplate by deriving tool/resource/prompt schemas from typed functions. The important design work remains names, descriptions, input schemas, authorization, errors, idempotency, and least privilege.

MCP marketplaces/registries can improve discovery but should not imply trust. Review source, publisher, requested capabilities, network behavior, credentials, and update policy before connecting a third-party server.

Test an MCP server without a model first: list capabilities, call tools with valid/invalid arguments, read resources, verify errors, and test cancellation/timeouts. Then add model-driven integration tests.

INTERVIEW LENS

MCP standardizes the interface; it does not certify the safety of the server behind it.

MCP for context engineering: long-term memory, web search, Qdrant, agentic RAG, and progressive tool disclosure

MCP servers can expose specialized context services such as web search, document retrieval, long-term memory, market/reference data, or a vector database.

Qdrant is a vector search engine and has an official MCP server pattern for storing and retrieving semantic memories. A memory server still needs retention, tenancy, metadata filters, deletion, and data-quality rules.

Agentic RAG lets an agent decide when/how to retrieve rather than forcing retrieval on every turn. Evaluate retrieval decisions separately from answer quality.

A large server/tool catalog can overwhelm model context. Progressive disclosure can expose concise tool metadata first and reveal deeper instructions or specialist servers only when relevant.

Advanced

Researcher-as-tool and multi-MCP orchestration

A specialist agent can be exposed to a parent as a tool. The parent sends a bounded task and receives a structured result rather than sharing the specialist's entire internal conversation.

This pattern reduces context pollution and creates a clear contract between coordinator and researcher. It also lets the specialist use its own MCP servers, model, memory, and evaluation policy.

When multiple MCP servers are connected, namespace or describe tools clearly, enforce per-server credentials, and make tool-call traces identify which server handled each action.

Multi-server architecture should degrade gracefully. One failed search provider should not corrupt unrelated state or produce an unqualified confident answer.

Shipping agent applications: FastAPI backend, React frontend, traces, feedback, and operational controls

A production agent app is still a software system. A FastAPI backend can own authentication, agent sessions, tool credentials, long-running jobs, streaming, and audit logs. A React frontend presents conversation/task state without exposing provider secrets.

Expose a stable job/session API instead of keeping all state inside a single HTTP request. Long tasks need cancellation, retry/resume, timeouts, and progress events.

Add user feedback linked to trace/run IDs so poor outcomes can be converted into evaluation cases. Track task success, intervention rate, tool errors, latency, tokens/cost, safety failures, and user-reported corrections.

Deployment should include rate limits, secret management, health checks, backups for durable state, incident runbooks, and a kill switch for dangerous tools.

Hands-on

Eight capstone patterns from the course, generalized into reusable architecture exercises

1. Career digital twin: build a source-grounded personal agent from résumé/portfolio documents with a Gradio UI and strict no-invention policy.

2. SDR agent: generate outreach drafts using CRM-style data, but require human approval before sending and record the source facts used in each message.

3. Deep research: planner + parallel researchers + writer + evaluator, with citations and prompt-injection defenses.

4. Stock-research agent: use public/simulated market data to practice retrieval and structured ranking. Treat it as an engineering exercise, not investment advice or unattended real-money execution.

5. Four-agent engineering team: planner/architect, developer, QA, and reviewer working in a disposable Docker sandbox with tests as the acceptance oracle.

6. Browser sidekick: an agent uses browser/MCP tools for real tasks with approval gates before destructive or externally visible actions.

7. Agent creator: generate a new agent configuration from a schema, validate allowed tools/models/permissions, run it in a sandbox, and require tests before promotion.

8. Simulated trading-floor capstone: coordinate researcher/trader-style agents and multiple MCP servers against simulated accounts/data, emphasizing tool permissions, traces, evaluation, and fail-safe controls rather than autonomous real-money trading.

Advanced

Agent observability, evaluation, feedback loops, and production learning

Agent observability should connect user request → model turns → retrieval → tool calls → handoffs/subagents → final outcome. Preserve trace/run IDs across backend logs and external tool calls.

Evaluation belongs in CI and production feedback. Maintain deterministic checks, golden cases, adversarial cases, historical incidents, and graded task-success metrics. Re-run them when changing models, prompts, tools, retrieval, or orchestration.

Human feedback is most useful when tied to exact run artifacts. Convert recurring corrections into test/evaluation cases rather than relying on anecdotal impressions.

Track operational metrics such as success rate, failure category, human escalation/approval rate, tool error rate, loop length, latency, token/cost distribution, and safety-policy interventions.

26C / AI AUTOMATION COURSE GAP ANALYSIS

AI automation with n8n: business integrations, RAG ingestion, messaging, security, and governance

This chapter fills the remaining gaps found by comparing v9 with the comprehensive AI Automation / n8n course. It focuses on practical workflow engineering: platform selection, installation, business integrations, email and messaging agents, vector-database synchronization, web ingestion, debugging, self-hosting, MCP inside n8n, commercialization, and current privacy/AI-law concerns.

Foundation

Automation platform landscape: n8n, Make, Zapier, Flowise, and code-first frameworks

Automation platforms sit on a spectrum. n8n emphasizes visual workflows plus code, APIs, self-hosting, AI nodes, MCP, and custom integrations. Make uses visual scenarios made of modules, routers, filters, schedules, and webhooks. Zapier uses trigger/action workflows (Zaps) and increasingly combines visual automation with AI and code.

Flowise historically provided a visual low-code environment for LLM chains and agents. However, Flowise announced a wind-down in 2026 and froze active feature development on July 29, 2026. Existing deployments can still matter, but new architecture should treat Flowise as a legacy/migration choice rather than an actively evolving default.

Code-first frameworks such as LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, PydanticAI, Mastra, or CrewAI provide more control over tests, source control, type systems, deployment, and custom runtime behavior. Low-code tools usually accelerate integrations and operations; code-first tools usually provide stronger engineering control.

The correct question is not 'which tool is best?' but 'where should orchestration live?'. Business integrations, approvals, schedules, and webhooks often fit an automation platform; complex agent state and domain logic may belong in code.

INTERVIEW LENS

Compare platforms on hosting, integration breadth, state/control model, source control, observability, testing, security, and operating cost—not on screenshot aesthetics.

Foundation → Intermediate

LLM families in automation: ChatGPT/OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Llama, Mistral, Grok, and local/open-weight models

A business automation should depend on a capability contract, not a model brand. Compare models for instruction following, structured output, tool calling, context length, latency, language quality, price, data controls, regional availability, and evaluation results on your own tasks.

OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, and other hosted providers expose managed APIs. DeepSeek and Mistral offer their own model/API ecosystems. Llama refers to Meta's model family and is commonly run through hosted providers or local runtimes such as Ollama. Grok refers to xAI's model family.

The label open source is frequently used too loosely. Some models are open-weight under licenses that are not OSI open-source software licenses. Check the exact model license before redistribution, fine-tuning, or commercial use.

In n8n, use a native chat-model node when it supports the provider and features you need; otherwise the HTTP Request node can call a documented API directly. Maintain a provider adapter pattern so workflow business logic does not depend on one vendor's response shape.

INTERVIEW LENS

Provider flexibility is real only when the required capabilities—tools, JSON schema, streaming, embeddings, multimodality—are actually portable.

Intermediate

Test-time compute, reasoning models, and why TTS is an ambiguous abbreviation

Test-time compute means spending additional inference-time computation to improve an answer, for example through longer internal reasoning, repeated sampling, search, self-consistency, or verification. It trades latency and cost for potentially better quality on difficult tasks.

The course uses TTS for test-time compute, but this abbreviation is ambiguous because TTS very commonly means Text-to-Speech. In engineering documentation, write out test-time compute or use a locally defined abbreviation such as TTC to avoid confusion.

Modern reasoning APIs often expose a reasoning-effort control rather than exposing the internal reasoning trace. Higher effort should be justified by task complexity and measured with evaluations; it should not be the default answer to poor prompts, bad retrieval, or unreliable tools.

Reasoning tokens and repeated tool calls can materially increase cost. Record reasoning settings in experiment metadata and compare quality, latency, and cost together.

INTERVIEW LENS

Test-time compute is an inference-time resource trade-off, not model training.

Current documentation: OpenAI reasoning models

Skills covered

Intermediate / Current 2026

OpenAI API pricing, project setup, data controls, and what 'compliant use' actually requires

API pricing is generally usage-based and model/tool specific. Cost can include input tokens, cached input, output/reasoning tokens, hosted tools, storage, and other services. Do not hard-code today's prices into architecture assumptions; link to the provider's current pricing page and add budget/usage alerts.

Use separate projects or equivalent provider boundaries for environments/clients when appropriate. Scope API keys, rotate them, avoid exposing them to browsers, and record model/version and usage in observability.

Using an API does not automatically make an application GDPR-compliant. Compliance depends on purpose, lawful basis, controller/processor roles, contracts/DPA, minimization, retention, data subject rights, international transfers, security, and the application's own processing decisions.

OpenAI's current API data-control documentation states that API data is not used to train models by default unless the customer explicitly opts in. Default abuse-monitoring logs can retain customer content for up to 30 days, while eligible customers may use Modified Abuse Monitoring or Zero Data Retention subject to feature-specific rules.

Always verify endpoint-specific retention and regional-processing behavior before sending sensitive data; tool providers, MCP servers, or downstream APIs can have independent retention policies.

INTERVIEW LENS

Separate provider security/privacy features from your application's legal compliance obligations.

Current documentation: OpenAI API pricing · OpenAI data controls

Foundation → Intermediate

n8n installation, Node.js/npm, Docker, Cloud, version compatibility, and upgrades

n8n can be consumed as a managed cloud service or self-hosted. For local experimentation, npm can be convenient; for reproducible long-running deployments, Docker or a managed n8n offering is usually easier to operate.

A Node.js/npm installation is sensitive to supported Node versions. When a local install breaks after changing Node, verify the n8n version's requirements rather than repeatedly reinstalling packages. A version manager can help keep isolated Node versions.

Before upgrading production, read release notes, back up the database and encryption key, test critical workflows in a staging instance, and verify community/custom-node compatibility.

The web/cloud experience removes server maintenance but not workflow engineering responsibilities: credentials, permissions, test data, rate limits, retries, and third-party API changes still matter.

Foundation → Intermediate

n8n data model, items, expressions, mapping, and JavaScript in workflows

n8n nodes usually receive and emit items containing JSON data and, when relevant, binary data. Most workflow errors come from misunderstanding the current item shape rather than from the external API.

Expressions reference previous node output inside configuration fields. Use the mapping UI where possible, then inspect the generated expression. Avoid deeply nested expressions that hide business logic inside a text field.

Use the Code node when transformation logic is genuinely clearer as JavaScript or Python. Keep code deterministic, validate required fields, and return data in the structure downstream nodes expect.

n8n tracks item lineage across nodes. When custom transformations combine or split items, preserve the relationship so later expressions resolve the intended source item.

Deterministic workflow transformation
// Example Code node: normalize customer input
return items.map(item => ({
  json: {
    customerId: String(item.json.customer_id),
    email: String(item.json.email || '').trim().toLowerCase(),
    amount: Number(item.json.amount),
  }
}));

Intermediate

AI Workflow Builder, workflow JSON, import/export, templates, backups, and version control

n8n workflows can be exported as JSON. Exported workflows are useful for backups, code review, reproducible examples, template distribution, and migration between instances. Sanitize secrets and personal data before sharing.

AI-assisted workflow builders can generate a useful starting graph, but generated credentials, node configuration, expressions, and error paths still require review. Test the workflow with realistic and adversarial inputs.

For production teams, treat workflow JSON as an artifact: use naming/version conventions, review important changes, and maintain separate development and production environments where possible.

n8n also offers source-control/environment features on applicable plans. A one-way promotion model from development toward production reduces accidental overwrites and unsafe direct edits.

A downloadable JSON template is not automatically production-ready. It may encode obsolete node versions, unsafe permissions, missing retries, or assumptions about external account IDs.

Intermediate

Airtable, Google Sheets, and Google Cloud credentials in business automation

Airtable behaves like a collaborative structured-data application with API-accessible bases/tables/records. Google Sheets is a spreadsheet, not a transactional database. Both are excellent for operational prototypes and human-editable workflows when their limitations are acceptable.

Google integrations often require OAuth or service-account configuration through Google Cloud. Request the minimum scopes necessary and separate test from production accounts when possible.

Use stable record IDs rather than row numbers or human-readable names when later steps need to update the same entity. Expect concurrent edits and missing/renamed columns.

When scale, transactional guarantees, complex queries, or strict schema become important, move durable state to a real database and keep Sheets/Airtable as an interface or reporting layer.

Intermediate

Email automation with Gmail, OpenAI, Airtable/Sheets, summaries, classification, and replies

A robust email workflow separates ingestion → classification → enrichment → draft → approval/action → logging. The LLM should not directly send mail merely because it generated plausible text.

For booking or support automation, extract structured fields first, validate them, fetch business data from Airtable/Sheets/database, and then draft a response using only verified facts.

Daily summary workflows use a schedule trigger, fetch messages for a defined time window, classify/deduplicate them, summarize in bounded groups, and send one digest. Store a checkpoint or processed-message IDs so reruns do not duplicate work.

Auto-replying should be restricted to low-risk categories with deterministic rules and clear escalation. For sales, legal, account, payment, HR, or sensitive messages, draft and request human approval.

n8n's Gmail integration can participate in human approval flows for AI tool calls; use that pattern for high-impact actions.

INTERVIEW LENS

The safest design has the model draft or classify, while deterministic policy controls whether anything is sent.

Intermediate

Sentiment analysis, classification, confidence, and storing model-derived labels

Sentiment analysis is a classification problem. Define the labels and their business meaning before choosing a model. A three-class positive/neutral/negative scheme may be insufficient for urgency, churn risk, abuse, or complaint routing.

Prefer structured outputs containing label, confidence/score where meaningful, and optionally a short rationale. Validate the output before writing it to Airtable or another system.

Model-derived labels are probabilistic data, not objective truth. Store model/version and timestamp so decisions can be audited and reprocessed after prompt/model changes.

Use a labeled evaluation set before automating actions based on sentiment. Measure confusion by class, not just aggregate accuracy.

Intermediate

Integrating hosted and local LLMs in n8n: native model nodes versus HTTP Request

n8n supports multiple chat-model integrations, including hosted and local providers. Native model nodes simplify credentials and connection to AI Agent/chain nodes; the generic HTTP Request node handles providers or endpoints that do not have a dedicated node.

For DeepSeek, Groq, Gemini, Claude, Mistral, OpenAI-compatible services, or custom gateways, normalize response/error handling at a sub-workflow boundary. Record provider/model in the output metadata.

Ollama allows n8n to call local models, but network topology matters: a containerized n8n instance must be able to reach the Ollama host, and production needs explicit resource/availability monitoring.

Design fallback routing carefully. Silent provider fallback can change safety behavior, output schema, price, or jurisdiction.

Advanced

Automated RAG ingestion in n8n: Google Drive → parse → chunk → embed → vector store

A practical RAG ingestion workflow watches or periodically scans a source such as Google Drive, identifies new/changed/deleted files, parses content, creates chunks, embeds them, and upserts them into a vector store.

Use a stable source document ID and content/version hash. On update, replace stale chunks; on deletion, remove the document's vectors. Blindly appending embeddings creates duplicate and outdated evidence.

Store metadata such as source path/URL, tenant, permissions, revision, modified time, chunk index, and content hash. Retrieval filters must enforce access control before the model sees context.

When the embedding model changes, old and new vectors usually should not be mixed in the same index without an explicit migration strategy.

Pinecone, Qdrant, pgvector, Redis, and other vector stores differ in filtering, operational model, cost, and indexing behavior; the correct choice depends on scale and system architecture.

INTERVIEW LENS

A RAG pipeline is a synchronization system, not a one-time 'upload PDFs' button.

Advanced

Email agents with sub-workflows, vector retrieval, Google Sheets, and reusable tools

Break a large email agent into sub-workflows with explicit inputs and outputs: fetch customer context, retrieve policy documents, classify request, draft response, request approval, send, and record the action.

Expose sub-workflows as narrowly defined agent tools only when semantic tool choice adds value. Deterministic steps such as writing audit rows or enforcing a blocked-recipient list should remain deterministic.

Keep retrieval and transactional data separate: vector search can answer 'what policy applies?', while a database/Sheet lookup answers 'what is this customer's current booking?'.

Sub-workflows improve reuse and testing only if their contracts are stable. Define required fields, output shape, error behavior, timeout, and idempotency.

Intermediate

Prompt engineering for automation: role, objective, evidence, tool policy, output contract, and failure behavior

Automation prompts should define the objective and decision boundary, not merely a persona. Include the allowed evidence, tool rules, output schema, uncertainty behavior, escalation conditions, and examples of ambiguous cases.

Separate instructions from untrusted content. Email bodies, webpages, retrieved documents, and chat messages belong in clearly delimited data fields and must not be allowed to redefine tool policy.

For tools with side effects, tell the model when it may propose the action, while application policy decides whether it is actually authorized.

Prompts are versioned software assets. Evaluate prompt changes on a fixed dataset and inspect cost/latency changes alongside quality.

Automation-oriented prompt structure
SYSTEM:
You classify inbound support email.
Use only the supplied email and account facts.
Never send email or change account state.
Return JSON matching the schema.
If evidence is insufficient, set action="human_review".

UNTRUSTED_EMAIL:
{{ email_body }}

Advanced

Self-hosting n8n: PaaS/Render-style deployment, Docker/VPS, persistence, webhooks, TLS, and backups

A production n8n deployment needs persistent database storage, a stable encryption key, durable credentials, public callback/webhook URLs, TLS, backups, logs, and a tested upgrade path. Treat the instance as infrastructure, not just a visual editor.

A Render-style PaaS can simplify deployment, while a VPS/Docker setup gives more control. Verify whether the platform provides persistent disks/databases, long-running services, background workers, custom domains, and outbound/inbound network behavior appropriate for your workflows.

Configure the public base/webhook URL correctly behind a reverse proxy. A workflow that works through the editor but fails from a production webhook frequently has a URL, proxy, authentication, filesystem, or network-boundary problem.

For higher throughput, understand queue mode, concurrency, execution retention, and external binary storage. Use health monitoring and security audits.

Back up the database and encryption key together. A database backup without the key can leave stored credentials unusable.

Advanced

WhatsApp Business automation with n8n: inbound messages, templates, identity, and approval

WhatsApp automation should use the official business platform/provider integration rather than consumer-account scraping. Inbound webhook events contain identifiers that must be mapped to the correct customer/session before an agent acts.

Separate inbound classification from outbound messaging. Enforce recipient identity, consent/allowed use, template/session rules, rate limits, and business policy outside the model.

For an agent tool that sends a WhatsApp message, require structured inputs and human approval when the action is promotional, sensitive, financial, or otherwise consequential.

Never place access tokens in workflow text or exported JSON. Use the credential store and restrict access to the workflow/credentials.

Telegram agents: trigger nodes, voice/text input, email/calendar tools, and security boundaries

Telegram can be used as an agent front end through a bot and Telegram Trigger. The chat/user ID becomes part of the authorization boundary; do not assume anyone who can message the bot may invoke internal tools.

For voice messages, the workflow typically downloads audio, transcribes it, interprets intent, asks for confirmation when necessary, then invokes narrowly scoped tools.

Maintain an allowlist or identity mapping for privileged operations. Reject tool actions originating from unknown chats, forwarded content, group contexts, or ambiguous identities when the risk is material.

A 'bot that can automate everything' is a security smell. Separate read-only tools from destructive tools, add per-tool approvals, limits, and audit logs.

Advanced

Social-media automation, webhooks, scraping/crawling, schedules, and sub-workflows

A webhook is event-driven: an external service pushes data to a URL. Polling/schedules repeatedly ask for changes. Choose webhooks where reliable event delivery exists; use polling when the provider lacks webhooks or reconciliation is required.

Social-media workflows often combine content generation, asset preparation, approval, posting, and analytics. Keep platform credentials and publishing tools behind approval and rate-limit controls.

Web scraping should respect technical constraints, robots/terms where relevant, copyright, privacy, and applicable law. Build deduplication and change detection so scheduled crawls do not reprocess the same content unnecessarily.

Use sub-workflows for reusable publishing, enrichment, scraping, and notification logic. Define clear inputs/outputs rather than copying a cluster of nodes into every workflow.

Intermediate → Advanced

Debugging n8n: execution history, pinned data, Error Trigger, retries, HTTP diagnostics, and observability

Debug from the first failing boundary. Inspect execution input/output at each node, status/error details, credentials, HTTP status/body/headers, and the exact expression values used.

n8n execution history allows failed runs to be inspected and retried. Pinned or previous-execution data can reproduce downstream logic without repeatedly calling external systems.

An Error Trigger workflow can centralize failure notifications and operational metadata. Include workflow/execution ID, failing node, error class, correlation/business ID, and a link to the execution—but avoid leaking secrets into Slack/email alerts.

Use retry with backoff for transient errors such as rate limits or temporary network failures. Do not blindly retry validation errors or non-idempotent side effects.

For production, monitor failure rate, latency, queue/concurrency saturation, credential expiry, provider rate limits, and unusually expensive AI runs.

Current 2026 / Legacy

Flowise integration via webhooks and custom tools—and why new projects should plan migration

Flowise historically enabled visual construction of LLM chains/agents and could be connected to n8n through HTTP/webhook calls. A common pattern was n8n handling business-system integration while Flowise handled the LLM/agent graph.

Custom tools in Flowise could use JavaScript to call APIs or n8n webhooks, while n8n returned structured business data such as Google Sheets rows.

However, Flowise announced in July 2026 that it was winding down operations and that active feature development would cease. Existing self-hosted code may remain usable, but security maintenance, ecosystem vitality, and upgrade strategy become architectural risks.

For new systems, evaluate migration to n8n's current AI capabilities, LangGraph/LangChain, OpenAI Agents SDK, Mastra, PydanticAI, or another actively maintained runtime rather than creating new Flowise dependency.

Legacy integration knowledge is useful, but current architecture must account for product lifecycle risk.

Advanced / Current

MCP directly in n8n: MCP Client, MCP Server Trigger, instance-level MCP, and agent tools

Current n8n includes MCP capabilities on both sides of the protocol. An MCP Client or MCP Client Tool lets a workflow/agent consume capabilities exposed by an MCP server. An MCP Server Trigger exposes selected n8n workflow capabilities to MCP clients.

Instance-level MCP can expose appropriate n8n capabilities to supported clients. Keep the protocol boundary explicit: MCP is not authentication by itself and does not justify exposing every workflow or credential.

When n8n is an MCP tool provider, define narrow schemas and idempotent behavior, and separate read-only tools from side-effecting tools. Apply human approval to consequential actions.

When n8n consumes remote MCP servers, treat them like third-party integrations: review permissions, data retention, network destination, authentication, and tool descriptions for prompt-injection risk.

Professional / Commercial

Selling AI automation services: discovery, scope, value, pricing, maintenance, and support

Sell a business outcome, not 'an AI agent'. Start with discovery: current process, volume, failure modes, systems, permissions, human work, compliance constraints, expected savings/revenue, and acceptable risk.

Separate implementation fee, third-party usage costs, infrastructure, and ongoing maintenance/support. Pricing can be fixed-scope, time-and-materials, monthly managed service, or value-based; each requires explicit assumptions and change-control rules.

Define the support boundary: who owns API-account changes, expired credentials, provider outages, prompt/model regressions, data corrections, and incident response. Include monitoring and a rollback/disable mechanism.

Do not promise deterministic accuracy for probabilistic workflows. Define measurable acceptance criteria and human fallback for cases that exceed the automation's confidence or authority.

Professional / Current 2026

n8n licensing and selling workflows/services: Sustainable Use License boundaries

n8n is fair-code, not conventional OSI open source. The self-hosted Community edition uses the Sustainable Use License (SUL), while Cloud and commercial offerings have separate terms.

Current n8n guidance states that you can build and run workflows for clients on your own instance and charge for that work, including letting clients connect their own accounts, provided clients cannot access/build/configure the workflow logic. Giving external users automation-building/configuration capability, white-labeling, or providing n8n itself as a service can require a commercial license.

n8n's current terms also contemplate published/sold workflow templates and require that templates not contain credentials, personal/confidential data, or third-party rights violations.

Licensing changes over time and edge cases can be fact-specific. Verify the current license/terms and contact n8n for formal clarification before designing a SaaS or multi-client product around the license boundary.

COMMON TRAP: Do not infer licensing rights from an old tutorial or community post. Check the current official terms for the actual deployment model.

Advanced / Business

Market-ready RAG lead bot: qualification, retrieval, Google Sheets/CRM, and website embedding

A lead-generation bot should combine product/company knowledge retrieval with structured lead capture. Do not let the model invent pricing, availability, guarantees, or customer-specific commitments.

Collect only fields needed for the stated purpose. Validate email/phone data, record consent/source where required, and route the structured lead to Sheets, Airtable, or a CRM.

Website deployment can use a hosted chat URL, an embedded widget, or a custom frontend. WordPress/CSS branding changes presentation, not the underlying security model.

Measure useful business outcomes such as qualified lead rate, escalation rate, unsupported-answer rate, conversion downstream, and privacy/consent failures—not just chat volume.

Advanced

RAG data quality: chunk size, overlap, metadata, deduplication, updates, and evaluation

Chunking is a retrieval optimization problem. Small chunks improve specificity but can lose context; large chunks preserve context but can reduce ranking precision and waste context tokens. Overlap can preserve boundary information but increases duplicate content and storage.

Choose chunking using the document structure and evaluation queries. Headings, semantic sections, tables, code blocks, and page boundaries often deserve structure-aware splitting rather than a fixed character count.

Data quality includes parsing accuracy, stale versions, duplicate documents, missing metadata, access permissions, encoding/OCR errors, and source authority.

Evaluate retrieval with representative questions and evidence labels. Tune chunking, embeddings, hybrid search, filters, and reranking based on measured retrieval failures.

Related: RAG pipeline

Advanced

Firecrawl for web ingestion: scrape, crawl, map, Markdown, structured extraction, and RAG

Firecrawl is a web extraction service designed to turn websites into LLM-friendly data. Scrape processes one page, Crawl recursively processes multiple pages, and Map discovers URLs.

Markdown output is useful for RAG because it strips much visual boilerplate while preserving headings, links, lists, and content structure. Structured extraction can produce JSON when the use case is field extraction rather than document retrieval.

For RAG ingestion, preserve source URL, retrieval time, crawl depth/path, title, and content hash. Re-crawl incrementally and delete or deprecate pages that disappear.

Web extraction must respect privacy, copyright, access controls, site terms, rate limits, and robots/technical expectations where applicable. Publicly reachable does not mean unrestricted for every commercial use.

Advanced

LlamaIndex, LlamaParse, document preprocessing, PDFs/CSVs, and Google Colab

LlamaIndex Framework provides ingestion, indexing, retrieval, and agent/RAG abstractions in Python and TypeScript. Its ingestion pipeline applies repeatable transformations such as parsing, splitting, metadata extraction, embedding, and vector-store insertion.

LlamaParse is LlamaIndex's hosted document-processing platform for complex PDFs, scans, tables, charts, and many office/document formats. It can output Markdown, text, or structured JSON and is useful before chunking when raw PDF extraction destroys layout.

PDF parsing and CSV ingestion are different problems. CSV already has explicit row/column structure; preserve typed fields and metadata instead of flattening every table into undifferentiated prose.

Google Colab is useful for exploratory notebooks and demonstrations but is not a production ingestion runtime. Move stable preprocessing into a versioned service/workflow with tests and repeatable dependencies.

Advanced / Security

Jailbreaks versus prompt injection

A jailbreak attempts to persuade or manipulate a model into violating its behavioral/policy constraints. It primarily targets model behavior.

A prompt injection targets an AI application by embedding hostile instructions in untrusted content—webpages, emails, documents, tool output, database records—so the model treats data as instructions.

Prompt injection becomes dangerous when the model has tools or access to secrets. Defenses include instruction/data separation, least-privilege tools, allowlists, structured tool arguments, confirmation for side effects, data minimization, and treating retrieved content as untrusted.

No prompt-only defense reliably eliminates injection. Security belongs in application/tool authorization boundaries.

INTERVIEW LENS

Jailbreak targets model restrictions; prompt injection exploits an application's instruction/data boundary.

Advanced / Security

Data poisoning and backdoor attacks in AI/RAG systems

Data poisoning deliberately corrupts training, fine-tuning, evaluation, memory, or retrieval data to change model/system behavior. In a RAG system, poisoning can be as simple as inserting malicious or misleading documents into an indexed source.

A backdoor is a hidden behavior triggered by a particular pattern or input while normal behavior appears acceptable.

Protect ingestion with source authentication, access control, provenance, document versioning, validation, anomaly detection, review of high-impact sources, and the ability to remove/rebuild affected indexes.

Evaluation datasets themselves can be poisoned or contaminated. Restrict write access and version them like code.

Advanced / Governance

Copyright, intellectual property, generated content, scraped data, and licenses

AI output ownership and copyrightability vary by jurisdiction and by the amount of human authorship. Do not promise that every generated asset is protectable or exclusive.

A provider's terms may grant contractual rights to output while copyright law separately determines whether copyright exists. Those are different questions.

Input rights also matter: copyrighted documents, images, source code, and scraped sites can impose license, contract, privacy, or other restrictions on ingestion and reuse.

For commercial workflows, record source licenses/permissions where relevant, avoid asking models to imitate protected content unnecessarily, and add review for customer-facing assets with IP risk.

COMMON TRAP: This guide provides engineering/governance context, not jurisdiction-specific legal advice.

Advanced / Governance

GDPR / DSGVO for AI agents and automation: principles, roles, lawful basis, minimization, and data-subject rights

GDPR is the EU General Data Protection Regulation; DSGVO is its common German abbreviation/name. It applies to personal-data processing within its territorial scope, including many AI workflows.

Core principles include lawfulness/fairness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality, and accountability.

Determine controller/processor roles, lawful basis, purpose, retention, subprocessors, international transfers, security measures, and whether a DPIA is required. Provide mechanisms to support applicable access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability, and objection rights.

For RAG and memory, deletion must propagate to source databases, document stores, vector indexes, caches, and derived records where required. A 'delete row' button that leaves embeddings indefinitely is not a complete deletion design.

Avoid sending unnecessary personal data to an LLM. Redact/pseudonymize where possible and document provider retention/data-processing settings.

Current documentation: European Commission GDPR principles

Advanced / Governance

CCPA/CPRA privacy requirements for AI automation

CCPA is the California Consumer Privacy Act. CPRA amended and expanded the CCPA rather than creating a completely separate replacement law.

Relevant rights include knowing/accessing certain personal-information practices, deletion subject to exceptions, opting out of sale/sharing, correction, limiting certain uses of sensitive personal information, and non-discrimination for exercising rights.

For AI automations, maintain a data inventory: what information enters prompts/tools/logs/vector stores, why it is processed, where it is sent, how long it is retained, and how a verified request can find/delete/correct it.

Applicability and detailed obligations depend on the organization and processing context; engineering should support counsel/privacy teams with traceable data flows rather than making legal conclusions from a tutorial.

Advanced / Governance / Current 2026

EU AI Act in 2026: risk-based obligations, transparency, AI literacy, GPAI, and high-risk timelines

The EU AI Act uses a risk-based regulatory structure. By November 2026, prohibited-practice and AI-literacy provisions have already applied since February 2025, governance/GPAI obligations since August 2025, and major enforcement/transparency provisions apply from August 2, 2026.

For certain interactive AI systems, transparency obligations can require informing people that they are interacting with AI. The Act also contains marking/disclosure rules for specified AI-generated/manipulated content.

High-risk-system timelines are later and use-case specific. Do not label every chatbot 'high risk' merely because it uses an LLM; classify the actual use case and role (provider/deployer/etc.).

Engineering controls that support compliance include system inventories, model/provider documentation, logging, human oversight, access controls, testing, incident handling, content transparency, and change management.

The Act is evolving through guidance and implementation measures. Re-check current Commission guidance before launching a regulated use case.

Current documentation: EU AI Act overview · Article 50 transparency FAQ

Advanced / Governance

Alignment, censorship, bias, evaluation, and provider differences

Different models can refuse, frame, or prioritize content differently because of training data, fine-tuning, system policies, regional/legal requirements, and product safety choices.

Avoid reducing these differences to a single 'censorship score'. Define the application's required behavior and evaluate consistency, factuality, refusal appropriateness, demographic disparities, language performance, and failure modes.

For consequential classification or ranking, test slices across relevant groups and edge cases. Human oversight should have a clear ability to correct model output and feed recurring failures into evaluation datasets.

Provider comparison is empirical: run the same versioned tasks under documented settings and record model/version/date.

Advanced / Business

Lead scraping and enrichment: data quality, consent, rate limits, and governance

Automated lead collection combines crawling/search, extraction, deduplication, enrichment, and CRM insertion. The technical ability to collect contact information does not establish a lawful marketing basis.

Store source URL, collection time, extraction confidence, and any consent/legitimate-use metadata required by the business process. Remove obvious personal/sensitive data that the workflow does not need.

Respect platform/API terms, robots/access restrictions, rate limits, copyright/database rights, privacy law, and anti-spam/marketing rules applicable to the target jurisdiction.

Quality matters commercially: duplicate or stale leads can waste sales effort and create compliance risk. Validate emails/domains and maintain suppression/do-not-contact lists.

Capstone: production-grade n8n RAG support agent with ingestion, messaging, approval, monitoring, and governance

Ingestion: Google Drive or web sources → parse/Firecrawl/LlamaParse → normalize → chunk → embed → Pinecone/Qdrant/pgvector with source/version/permission metadata.

Interaction: web/Telegram/WhatsApp/email trigger → authenticate/identify user → retrieve allowed context → agent/classifier → structured result.

Actions: read-only tools can execute directly; email/calendar/CRM writes pass through deterministic validation and human approval where appropriate.

Operations: Error Trigger workflow, correlation IDs, execution dashboards, retry policy, provider cost tracking, health checks, backups, and a disable switch.

Security/governance: prompt-injection tests, poisoned-document tests, least-privilege credentials, retention/deletion workflow, privacy notices, source licensing, and applicable regulatory classification.

Business: define acceptance metrics, setup/maintenance scope, third-party costs, support responsibility, and the current n8n license model before selling it as a service.

Additional AI automation technology and platform profiles

Make
Cloud workflow automation platform

Definition: Visual automation platform based on scenarios and modules. Main characteristics: app modules, routers/filters, schedules, instant/custom webhooks, mapping, error handling, and AI-agent capabilities. QA/automation: useful for business-process integrations and event-driven automations. Name: Make is a brand name, not an acronym.

Zapier
Cloud automation platform

Definition: Platform for trigger/action workflows and AI-enabled business automation. Main characteristics: Zaps, large app ecosystem, field mapping, AI steps/agents, code and workflow-management features. QA/automation: useful for rapid SaaS integration and operational workflow automation. Name: Zapier is a brand name, not an acronym.

Flowise
Legacy visual LLM/agent builder

Definition: Visual low-code builder historically used for LLM chains and agents. Main characteristics: node-based flows, tools, agents, API/webhook integration and self-hosted OSS code. QA/automation: relevant for maintaining or migrating existing agent workflows. Name: Flowise is a project name, not an acronym. 2026 status: the maintainers announced a wind-down and code freeze in July 2026.

Airtable
Collaborative structured-data platform

Definition: SaaS combining spreadsheet-like interaction with structured tables/records and APIs. Main characteristics: bases, tables, records, views, automations and API access. QA/automation: useful as a lightweight operations datastore/interface, especially in prototypes and human-in-the-loop workflows. Name: Airtable is a brand name, not an acronym.

Google Sheets
Cloud spreadsheet platform

Definition: Google's collaborative spreadsheet service. Main characteristics: cells/tables, formulas, sharing, Apps Script/API access and real-time collaboration. QA/automation: useful for test data, operational review, simple data stores and workflow inputs/outputs; not a transactional database. Name: product name, not an acronym.

Google Cloud
Cloud platform

Definition: Google's cloud-computing and API platform. Main characteristics: identity/OAuth configuration, APIs, compute, storage, data and AI services. QA/automation: commonly used to create OAuth clients/service accounts for Google integrations and to host automation services. Name: GCP commonly means Google Cloud Platform, though Google now generally brands the platform as Google Cloud.

DeepSeek
LLM/model and API ecosystem

Definition: Family/provider of language and reasoning models available through hosted APIs and, for some releases, open-weight distribution. Main characteristics: text/reasoning/coding capabilities and API access depending on model. QA/automation: a provider option to evaluate for routing, cost, structured output and agent workflows. Name: DeepSeek is a brand/model-family name, not an acronym.

Mistral AI
LLM provider / model ecosystem

Definition: AI company providing hosted and open-weight model families plus inference/tooling APIs. Main characteristics: chat/reasoning/coding/multimodal models, APIs, lifecycle and regional options depending on model. QA/automation: useful as an alternative model provider and for provider-routing evaluations. Name: Mistral is a company/model-family name, not an acronym.

Llama
Open-weight model family

Definition: Meta's family of large language models distributed under Meta-specific licenses. Main characteristics: downloadable weights, local/hosted inference and broad ecosystem support. QA/automation: useful for local/private inference and comparing cloud vs self-hosted model behavior. Name: Llama is the model-family name; do not assume its license is equivalent to an OSI open-source software license.

Pinecone
Managed vector database

Definition: Managed vector search/database service for semantic retrieval. Main characteristics: vector indexing, namespaces/metadata filtering, managed scaling and retrieval APIs. QA/automation: commonly used in RAG pipelines; test metadata permissions, stale vectors, index migrations and retrieval quality. Name: Pinecone is a product/company name, not an acronym.

Firecrawl
Web extraction/crawling platform

Definition: Service for scraping, crawling, mapping and extracting website content into LLM-friendly formats. Main characteristics: Scrape, Crawl, Map, search/extraction and Markdown/structured output. QA/automation: useful for RAG ingestion, research, change monitoring and enrichment. Name: Firecrawl is a product/project name, not an acronym.

LlamaIndex
RAG/agent data framework

Definition: Python/TypeScript framework for loading, transforming, indexing, retrieving and using data in LLM/agent applications. Main characteristics: loaders, documents/nodes, ingestion pipelines, retrievers, indexes and agent/workflow integrations. QA/automation: useful for reproducible RAG ingestion and retrieval testing. Name: LlamaIndex is a project name, not an acronym.

LlamaParse
Document parsing platform

Definition: LlamaIndex's hosted document-processing system for PDFs, scans, tables, charts and other file types. Main characteristics: layout-aware parsing, Markdown/text/JSON outputs, OCR and structured extraction. QA/automation: useful upstream of RAG when raw text extraction loses structure. Name: LlamaParse is a product name, not an acronym.

Google Colab
Hosted notebook environment

Definition: Google's hosted Jupyter-notebook environment. Main characteristics: browser notebooks, Python runtimes, package installation and optional accelerators. QA/automation: useful for experiments, parsing/RAG prototypes and demonstrations; not a production workflow runtime. Name: Colab abbreviates Colaboratory.

WhatsApp Business Platform
Business messaging platform/API

Definition: Meta's official platform for business messaging through WhatsApp. Main characteristics: business identities, API/webhook messaging, templates/session policies and provider integrations. QA/automation: useful for event-driven customer communication when identity, consent and approval boundaries are tested. Name: WhatsApp is a brand name, not an acronym.

Telegram
Messaging platform / Bot API

18 / DEEP DIVE

Operations, Reliability & IoT Deep Dive

Production operations and physical systems: SLOs, alert design, distributed traces, incident response, recovery, capacity, Home Assistant, MQTT, sensor quality, Tuya, hardware safety, and time-series retention.

Advanced

SLIs, SLOs, SLAs, and error budgets

A Service Level Indicator (SLI) is a measured signal such as successful checkout rate or p95 API latency. A Service Level Objective (SLO) sets a target over a window, such as 99.9% successful requests in 30 days. An SLA is an external contractual commitment and may include remedies.

The error budget is the amount of unreliability permitted by the SLO. Teams can use budget consumption to decide whether to prioritize reliability work or continue shipping riskier changes.

Choose user-centered indicators. CPU at 40% is not an availability SLI if customers still cannot complete a payment.

INTERVIEW LENS

Define SLI/SLO/SLA separately and give one user-facing example.

Skills covered

Reliability EngineeringOperational Monitoring

Related: Reliability basics · Performance

Back to contents ↑
Advanced

Alert design, tuning, and noise reduction

An alert should indicate a condition that needs human action or urgent automated remediation. Every page-worthy alert needs an owner, impact description, starting diagnostic context, and escalation path.

Use thresholds based on symptoms or SLO burn where possible, not arbitrary infrastructure values. Add duration windows to avoid transient noise, deduplicate correlated alerts, and group related failures.

Review alerts after incidents: did the right alert fire early enough? Did irrelevant alerts fire? Did responders know what to do? Delete or downgrade alerts that nobody acts on.

INTERVIEW LENS

“Actionable and tied to user impact” is the core answer. Then discuss tuning and ownership.

Skills covered

AlertingOperational MonitoringInfrastructure Monitoring

Related: Alerting basics · Runbooks

Back to contents ↑
Advanced

Distributed tracing and correlation IDs

Distributed traces represent a request as a tree/graph of spans across services. A trace can show that an API request spent 20 ms in the gateway, 50 ms in the application, and 900 ms waiting for a downstream provider.

Propagate trace/correlation context across HTTP, queues, background jobs, and webhooks. Include the identifier in logs so engineers can move from an alert to a trace and then to relevant log events.

Sampling controls cost and volume. Keep higher sampling for errors or high-risk paths where possible.

INTERVIEW LENS

Use a multi-service example to show why logs alone become hard to correlate.

Skills covered

ObservabilityLoggingSystem Integration

Related: Observability basics · Webhooks

Advanced

Incident response: detect, mitigate, communicate, learn

A practical incident lifecycle is detect → assess severity → establish ownership/coordination → mitigate user impact → recover → verify → communicate → learn. During the incident, stabilization usually matters more than perfect diagnosis.

Keep a timeline of observations and actions. Assign communication separately when possible so responders are not interrupted by repeated status requests. Preserve evidence before restarting or deleting failing resources.

After recovery, analyze contributing factors, detection gaps, failed safeguards, and organizational/process conditions. Track corrective actions with owners and due dates.

INTERVIEW LENS

Say the first goal is impact mitigation, then root cause after stabilization.

Incident ManagementTechnical OperationsTroubleshooting

Intermediate

Runbooks, operational procedures, and safe automation

A good runbook includes trigger/symptom, prerequisites, safety warnings, commands or UI steps, expected outputs, decision points, rollback, verification, and escalation. Keep it versioned and test it during drills or real incidents.

If a runbook is executed frequently and deterministically, automate the safe parts. Keep explicit confirmation for destructive operations and preserve a manual fallback.

Link alerts directly to the relevant runbook and dashboards so responders start with context.

INTERVIEW LENS

Explain how runbooks evolve into automation while retaining guardrails.

Advanced

Backups, restore testing, RPO, and RTO

A backup is useful only if it can be restored. Test restoration on a schedule and verify integrity, permissions, encryption keys, and application compatibility—not merely that a file exists.

RPO (Recovery Point Objective) describes acceptable data loss; RTO (Recovery Time Objective) describes acceptable recovery time. They guide backup frequency, replication, and disaster-recovery design.

Document which systems are authoritative during failover and how writes are reconciled after recovery.

INTERVIEW LENS

Define RPO vs RTO and say that restore testing is mandatory.

Advanced

Capacity planning and infrastructure monitoring

Monitor resource saturation and demand trends: CPU, memory, storage, I/O, network, connection pools, queue depth, database locks, cache hit rate, and third-party quotas. Capacity problems often appear first as latency or queue growth.

Plan for expected growth and peak events. Load testing can estimate how utilization changes with throughput, but production telemetry is needed to validate the model.

Infrastructure health is supporting evidence, not the final user-quality signal. Pair it with application SLIs.

Connect infrastructure metrics to user-facing SLOs and bottleneck analysis.

Home Assistant integration model and operational testing

Home Assistant represents devices and integrations as entities with states, attributes, services/actions, events, and automations. Integrations may communicate locally, through MQTT, or through vendor/cloud APIs.

Test more than the dashboard: entity availability, stale state, restart/reconnect behavior, automation triggers/conditions/actions, network loss, credential expiration, and whether a failed integration recovers automatically.

For critical controls, keep physical/manual override and fail-safe actuator behavior. A home-automation UI should not be the only control path for a pump or valve.
