Intermediate → Advanced

MQTT topics, QoS, retained messages, and offline behavior

MQTT uses a broker and topic-based publish/subscribe model. Topic design should be predictable and avoid embedding secrets. Wildcard subscriptions can simplify monitoring but may expose more data than intended.

QoS levels trade delivery guarantees and overhead: QoS 0 is at-most-once, QoS 1 at-least-once, and QoS 2 exactly-once at the protocol exchange level. Applications still need idempotency because duplicate business processing can occur around reconnect/retry boundaries.

Retained messages let new subscribers receive the latest retained value for a topic. Distinguish retained state from event streams; retaining a one-time “open valve” command can be dangerous if a device reconnects later.

INTERVIEW LENS

Mention QoS and the retained-message safety issue for actuator commands.

Skills covered

MQTTIoTHome Assistant

Related: IoT basics · Idempotency

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate

Sensor validation, freshness, calibration, and plausibility

Sensor data should have a timestamp, unit, expected range, and freshness threshold. Validate impossible values, stale readings, sudden jumps, repeated frozen values, and disagreement with correlated sensors.

Calibration error is different from communication failure. A sensor can be consistently wrong while technically “online.” Record calibration history and compare against a trusted reference when accuracy matters.

Automations should degrade safely when a sensor is missing or implausible instead of blindly acting on the last known value.

INTERVIEW LENS

Give one example each of range, freshness, rate-of-change, and cross-sensor validation.

Intermediate

Tuya, hardware integration, and failure boundaries

Tuya ecosystems can involve devices, Zigbee/Bluetooth/Wi-Fi gateways, local LAN behavior, vendor cloud APIs, Smart Life/Tuya accounts, and third-party integrations. The exact boundary varies by device.

Troubleshoot layer by layer: power/device state → local radio/network → gateway/broker → vendor cloud → Home Assistant/integration → automation logic. This avoids blaming application code for a physical or connectivity failure.

Document device identifiers, firmware, integration method, power requirements, and recovery procedure. Hardware replacement should not require rediscovering the entire architecture.

INTERVIEW LENS

Use a layered troubleshooting approach from physical device to application.

Advanced

Physical automation safety: interlocks, timeouts, and manual override

Automating a physical actuator introduces safety and equipment risk. Define safe startup state, maximum run time, mutual exclusion/interlocks, sensor prerequisites, manual override, and behavior when connectivity or the controller fails.

Do not let a single unvalidated sensor directly drive a dangerous action. Require plausibility, freshness, and potentially independent confirmation. Log every command and resulting state where practical.

Test failure modes deliberately: stuck relay, valve not closing, sensor unavailable, broker offline, duplicated command, reboot during operation, and loss of internet/cloud service.

INTERVIEW LENS

Show defense in depth: software rule + hardware-safe default + timeout + manual override + observability.

Skills covered

Automation SystemsHardware IntegrationReliability Engineering

Related: Home Assistant · Sensor quality · AI safety

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate

Time-series retention, aggregation, and dashboard design

Time-series systems record measurements over time. Store timestamps consistently (usually UTC internally), retain units and sensor identity, and distinguish event time from ingestion time when delays are possible.

Long retention may require downsampling: keep high-resolution recent data and lower-resolution aggregates for older periods. Preserve raw data long enough for the investigations you actually need.

Dashboards should make thresholds, missing periods, anomalies, maintenance windows, and actuator changes visible. A chart that smooths away outages can be actively misleading.

INTERVIEW LENS

Discuss retention/downsampling and how you represent missing data distinctly from zero.

Foundation → Intermediate

Technical Operations as a discipline

Technical Operations sits between product/software, support, automation, data, and infrastructure. The work is to make systems operable day to day: monitor integrations, investigate incidents, validate data, automate repetitive procedures, maintain runbooks, and escalate product defects with evidence.

The strongest operational teams reduce manual work over time. Repeated incidents become tests, alerts, automated recovery, safer product behavior, or clearer documentation.

Operational ownership also means knowing when not to automate: destructive or ambiguous actions may require an approval gate or carefully constrained tool.

Skills covered

Technical OperationsOperational MonitoringTroubleshooting

Related: Observability · Runbooks · AI safety

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate

Operational monitoring vs infrastructure monitoring

Infrastructure monitoring asks whether resources such as hosts, containers, networks, disks, and databases are healthy. Operational/application monitoring asks whether the product workflow is functioning for users.

A healthy CPU graph cannot prove that payments are succeeding. Combine resource signals with application SLIs, synthetic checks, queue/backlog state, integration health, and business-level counters.

Monitoring should support investigation: dashboards need links or identifiers that lead to logs, traces, affected entities, and recent changes.

Skills covered

Operational MonitoringInfrastructure MonitoringObservability

Related: SLI/SLO · Alert design

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate → Advanced

Root cause analysis and contributing factors

Root-cause analysis begins after the immediate impact is controlled. Build a timeline, identify the technical failure, and then ask what conditions allowed it to occur and escape detection.

Avoid stopping at “human error.” Examine design, defaults, permissions, test coverage, monitoring, review, deployment, documentation, and organizational incentives. Complex incidents often have multiple contributing factors rather than one root cause.

Corrective actions should be specific and verifiable: add a constraint, automate a check, change a default, improve an alert, test recovery, or remove an unsafe capability.

COURSE EXPANSION / SOFTWARE FOUNDATIONS

Software systems, development models, and team collaboration

The course begins below the level of test cases: what software is, how applications are structured, how requirements evolve, which development models teams use, and how QA fits into a multi-role product organization. These foundations make later testing decisions easier to reason about.

Foundation

Software, applications, tiers, roles, and channels

Software is a set of instructions, data, and configuration that makes a computing system perform useful behavior. A software product usually includes more than executable code: interfaces, databases, integrations, configuration, infrastructure, monitoring, and operational processes all affect quality.

A single-tier application keeps interface, business logic, and data on one machine or process. A multi-tier application separates concerns—for example browser → API/service → database. Multi-tier designs introduce network latency, partial failure, authentication boundaries, caching, serialization, and version compatibility, so test strategy must cover each layer and the interactions between them.

A multi-role system gives different capabilities to users such as customer, operator, manager, and administrator. A multi-channel system exposes the same business capabilities through different channels such as web, mobile, API, kiosk, or support tools. QA should verify both channel-specific behavior and consistency of shared rules.

Architecture ideaWhat changes for testing
Single tierFewer network boundaries, but UI, logic, and storage may be tightly coupled.
Multi tierTest contracts and failure modes between frontend, services, databases, queues, and third parties.
Multi roleBuild an authorization matrix and validate positive and forbidden actions for each role.
Multi channelCheck that shared business rules remain consistent across web, mobile, APIs, and operational tools.
INTERVIEW LENS

Explain architecture only to the depth needed to reason about risk. A QA engineer should be able to identify layers, trust boundaries, data ownership, and likely failure points.

Skills covered

Software TestingSystem IntegrationAuthentication Testing

Related: SDLC & STLC · System integration · Cross-layer reconciliation

Back to contents ↑
Foundation

How requirements become software and testable behavior

Requirements begin as a need or problem, then become increasingly precise through discovery, analysis, design, acceptance criteria, implementation, and feedback. They can be functional—what the system must do—or non-functional, such as reliability, security, accessibility, performance, or compliance.

QA should ask where the requirement came from, who benefits, which rules are authoritative, what data is involved, and how success will be observed. Ambiguity discovered before implementation is cheaper than a defect discovered after release.

Trace requirements through stories, acceptance criteria, tests, execution evidence, defects, and release decisions. When requirements change, impact analysis should identify which tests, data, documentation, and integrations may also need changes.

INTERVIEW LENS

A strong answer shows that requirement analysis is defect prevention: clarify actors, states, inputs, business rules, failures, permissions, and measurable acceptance criteria before execution begins.

Skills covered

Requirements AnalysisTest TraceabilityAcceptance Testing

Related: Requirements analysis · Acceptance criteria · Traceability

Back to contents ↑
Foundation

Sequential, iterative, incremental, Agile, and DevOps delivery models

Sequential development moves through major phases in order, with feedback often arriving later. Iterative development revisits and improves a solution through repeated cycles. Incremental development delivers usable slices of functionality over time. Most modern products combine iterative and incremental behavior.

Agile approaches shorten feedback loops and treat changing requirements as expected. DevOps extends collaboration into build, deployment, infrastructure, observability, and operation. These models change when testing happens, not whether disciplined test design is required.

In sequential projects, late integration and large releases increase the importance of early review and formal traceability. In iterative delivery, QA should participate continuously in refinement, development, CI, exploratory testing, release, and production feedback.

ModelTypical strengthQA risk
SequentialClear phase boundaries and documentationLate feedback; integration defects may surface near release.
IterativeFrequent learning and refinementRegression grows if feedback is not automated or prioritized.
IncrementalValue delivered in slicesCross-increment integration and backward compatibility.
Agile/DevOpsShort feedback loops and shared ownershipSpeed can become chaos without automated checks, observability, and clear quality criteria.

Skills covered

Quality AssuranceTest StrategyDevOps

Related: SDLC & STLC · Agile testing · CI/CD

Back to contents ↑
Foundation

Roles in a software development team and how QA collaborates

Software quality is a whole-team responsibility. Common roles include Product Manager or Product Owner, Business Analyst, UX/UI designer, frontend/backend/mobile developers, QA engineers, automation engineers, data engineers, DevOps/SRE, security specialists, database administrators, technical writers, support, and operations.

QA collaborates differently with each role: clarify business rules with Product, testability and diagnostics with developers, accessibility and responsive behavior with design, data contracts with data teams, deployment and telemetry with DevOps/SRE, and real-world failure patterns with support and operations.

Titles vary by organization, so focus on responsibilities and decision boundaries rather than memorizing a fixed org chart.

Skills covered

Stakeholder CommunicationQuality AssuranceTechnical Operations

Related: Project communication · Technical operations

Intermediate

Design review as a testing activity before code exists

A design review evaluates proposed architecture, UX flows, data models, APIs, and operational behavior before implementation. QA can identify missing states, impossible recovery paths, inconsistent permissions, untestable requirements, or observability gaps while they are still inexpensive to change.

Review sequence diagrams, wireframes, API contracts, database models, retry behavior, caching, failure states, error messages, accessibility semantics, and rollout/rollback plans. Ask how each important behavior can be observed and tested.

Design reviews are especially valuable for distributed systems and physical automation because a missing safety or recovery path can be difficult to retrofit later.

COURSE EXPANSION / MANUAL QA

Manual testing workflow, defect reporting, and test-management tooling

The course spends substantial time on the mechanics of professional manual QA: turning scenarios into managed executions, producing actionable defects, using Jira/Trello/Qase/Zephyr, and communicating progress. This chapter adds that operational layer.

Foundation

Manual testing workflow: scenarios, cases, execution, and status

Manual testing is deliberate human evaluation of software without relying on an automated script for every action. It is especially useful for exploration, usability, new features, visual judgment, rapidly changing areas, and scenarios where human interpretation matters.

A practical workflow is: analyze requirements → identify risks → write scenarios → prioritize → create detailed cases where repeatability is useful → prepare environment/data → execute → record pass/fail/blocked/not-run status → report defects → retest fixes → run regression → summarize residual risk.

A scenario should describe what to validate; a test case adds preconditions, data, steps, expected results, priority, and evidence. Execution status must be trustworthy: 'blocked' means a dependency prevents execution, not simply that the test failed.

ArtifactPurpose
Test scenarioHigh-level behavior or risk to validate.
Test caseRepeatable steps/data with expected results.
ChecklistCompact coverage for stable or exploratory workflows.
Test cycle/runA specific execution set for a build, environment, or release.
DefectEvidence that observed behavior differs from expectation.
Test summaryScope, results, defects, residual risk, and recommendation.

Skills covered

Manual TestingTest PlanningTest Case ExecutionTest Reporting

Related: Scenarios and cases · Defects · Reporting

Back to contents ↑
Foundation → Intermediate

Prioritizing and executing test scenarios

Prioritize tests by business criticality, changed code, likelihood of failure, historical defects, security/data impact, usage frequency, and cost of failure. Priority is not the same as execution order in every situation: a blocked high-priority scenario may require testing another risk while the environment is repaired.

Before execution, confirm the correct build, environment, configuration, credentials, test data, and known limitations. During execution, preserve evidence for unexpected behavior and avoid changing unrelated variables when investigating a failure.

For regression, maintain a small high-signal smoke set for fast confidence and broader suites for deeper coverage. Remove obsolete tests; an ever-growing test repository can become harder to trust than a curated one.

Skills covered

Regression TestingTest PlanningRisk-Based Testing

Related: Risk-based testing · Manual workflow

Back to contents ↑
Foundation → Intermediate

Defect reports, evidence, triage, and lifecycle in practice

A useful defect report contains a concise title, environment/build, preconditions, exact reproduction steps, expected result, actual result, frequency, impact, severity, relevant data, and evidence. Screenshots show state; videos show sequence/timing; browser console and network logs can expose technical cause.

Defect types may be functional, UI/visual, data, integration, performance, accessibility, security, compatibility, installation, or documentation issues. Classification helps reporting but should not replace impact analysis.

During defect triage, the team confirms reproducibility, impact, severity, priority, ownership, duplicates, release risk, and next action. QA contributes evidence; Product contributes business priority; engineering contributes technical context.

AI can help rewrite a report, summarize logs, or suggest missing fields, but it must not invent steps, impact, or evidence. Always verify AI-generated defect content against the observed failure.

Defect report example
Title: Checkout submits duplicate payment after rapid double-click
Build: web-2026.11.06 / staging
Precondition: authenticated user with one item in cart

Steps:
1. Open checkout.
2. Enter valid payment details.
3. Double-click "Pay" rapidly.

Expected:
One payment request and one order confirmation.

Actual:
Two successful payment requests are recorded.

Evidence:
request IDs, video, network HAR, transaction IDs
Severity: Critical
Frequency: 3/5 attempts

Skills covered

Defect TrackingTest ReportingTroubleshooting

Related: Defect lifecycle · Evidence-driven debugging

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate

Using generative AI for scenarios, cases, and defect writing

Generative AI can accelerate brainstorming by proposing test scenarios from a requirement, expanding boundary and negative cases, converting prose into a template, or checking a defect report for missing evidence. It is a drafting assistant, not the oracle for product behavior.

Provide the model with the actual requirement, actors, business rules, constraints, known architecture, and output schema. Ask it to identify assumptions separately from confirmed requirements so invented behavior is visible.

Review generated cases for duplicates, impossible preconditions, wrong priorities, security/privacy issues, and unsupported assumptions. High-risk scenarios should still be derived from authoritative requirements and engineering knowledge.

Safer AI-assisted test design
Prompt pattern:
Context: <feature and users>
Authoritative rules: <acceptance criteria>
Risks: <payments, auth, data integrity...>
Task: propose test scenarios
Output: ID | scenario | risk | preconditions | expected result
Constraint: mark every assumption explicitly; do not invent product rules.

Skills covered

Prompt EngineeringTest PlanningAI Automation

Related: Prompt design · Requirement analysis · AI safety

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate

Choosing and using test-management and work-tracking tools

A test-management tool should support the team's actual workflow rather than force documentation for its own sake. Evaluate test-case structure, reuse, versioning, execution cycles, traceability, reporting, permissions, API/integration support, automation import, and total maintenance cost.

For a small project, a well-structured spreadsheet can be a perfectly valid test repository. Move to a dedicated tool when versioning, reuse, execution history, permissions, reporting, integrations, or traceability become painful—not simply because a specialized product exists.

Generic work trackers such as Jira or Trello are good at planning and defects; dedicated tools such as Qase or Zephyr Scale add richer test repositories and execution management. Azure DevOps may combine work tracking and delivery in Microsoft-centric environments.

Keep one source of truth for each artifact. Avoid copying the same defect or test result manually across several systems unless an integration maintains the relationship.

Intermediate

Zephyr Scale: test cases, cycles, plans, reuse, and traceability

A mature test repository separates test design from test execution. A reusable test case describes behavior once; a test cycle records its result for a specific build/environment. Test plans can group cycles for a release or larger objective.

Folders help navigation but should not become the only taxonomy. Use labels/components and links to requirements. Reuse common sequences with care: excessive nesting makes failures hard to interpret.

Parameterized and data-driven tests reduce duplication. BDD cases can be represented in Gherkin and exchanged with Cucumber-oriented automation. Import/export and bulk creation are useful for migration, but generated cases still need review.

Bidirectional traceability should let a reviewer move from requirement → tests → executions → defects and back. AI-assisted test generation can accelerate drafting, but human reviewers remain responsible for correctness and risk coverage.

Zephyr Scale
Test management application for Jira

Definition: A test-management product integrated with Jira for creating test cases, organizing test cycles and plans, tracking execution, and reporting coverage.

Main characteristics

  • Test cycles, plans, configurations, and execution results
  • Parameters and data-driven variants
  • BDD/Gherkin support and Cucumber-oriented workflows
  • Traceability to Jira issues and reports
  • Import/export, cloning, archiving, bulk operations, permissions
QA / automation relevance: Useful when teams want test design and execution tightly connected to Jira requirements and defects. It can centralize manual testing while also linking automation evidence.

Name / acronym: Zephyr Scale is a product name; 'Scale' describes the product line rather than an acronym.

Foundation → Intermediate

Test plan template: what a useful plan should contain

A test plan translates strategy into an executable approach for a specific release, product area, or project. Keep it proportionate: a small feature may need a short page; a regulated multi-system release may need a detailed controlled document.

Useful components include objective/scope, in-scope and out-of-scope behavior, requirements/risks, test levels/types, environments, tools, roles, data, entry/exit criteria, schedule, dependencies, defect process, reporting, deliverables, assumptions, and residual-risk/approval rules.

A plan is a living coordination artifact. Update it when scope, dates, environments, or risk change; do not preserve a false plan simply because it was approved earlier.

SectionQuestions to answer
ScopeWhat are we validating, and what is explicitly excluded?
RisksWhat failures matter most and why?
ApproachWhich manual/automated levels and techniques address those risks?
Environment & dataWhere, with which versions/accounts/datasets, and who owns readiness?
Entry/exitWhat must be true to begin and what evidence supports completion/release?
ReportingWho needs what information, at what cadence, and where is evidence stored?

Skills covered

Test PlanningTest StrategyTest Reporting

Related: Strategy · Reporting · Release readiness

Intermediate

Progress reports, completion reports, and audience-aware communication

A report should answer the questions its audience needs. A developer may need failing test names, traces, logs, and reproduction steps; a Product Owner may need affected capabilities and release risk; leadership may need trend, blockers, and decision options.

A test progress report describes work in flight: scope executed, remaining work, blockers, defect trends, environment health, and forecast. A test completion/summary report records final scope, results, unresolved defects, exclusions, residual risk, and recommendation.

Avoid green/red dashboards without context. A release can have a high pass rate while a single untested payment path remains unacceptable.

Test ReportingStakeholder CommunicationQuality Metrics

Foundation → Intermediate

Practical test design for sign-up, login, search, and common web elements

Practice on familiar features because they contain reusable patterns. A sign-up flow combines required/optional fields, formats, uniqueness, password rules, consent, verification, retries, and persistence. Login combines authentication, session management, lockout/rate limits, errors, and recovery.

Search requires exact/partial matches, case and accent handling, empty queries, no-result states, filters/sorting, pagination, special characters, performance, relevance, and permissions. Test both valid and invalid combinations.

Common website elements—forms, dropdowns, checkboxes, radio buttons, tables, pagination, modals, toasts, file controls, date pickers, navigation, and responsive menus—should be tested for behavior, accessibility, keyboard use, state persistence, and error handling.

FeatureRepresentative risks
Sign-upDuplicate account, invalid formats, verification bypass, weak password handling.
LoginCredential leakage, session fixation, lockout defects, ambiguous errors.
SearchIncorrect filtering, stale results, broken pagination, injection/encoding issues.
FormsLost state, validation inconsistency, inaccessible labels, duplicate submission.
TablesSorting/filtering mismatch, wrong row actions, pagination/data reconciliation.

COURSE EXPANSION / AGILE

Agile testing, Scrum, Kanban, stories, estimation, and delivery metrics

The existing guide discussed Agile indirectly through CI/CD and planning. This chapter adds the explicit Agile material from the course: values and principles, Scrum, user-story quality, estimation, charts, retrospectives, Kanban, and stabilization.

Foundation

Agile values, principles, whole-team quality, and frequent feedback

Agile is a family of approaches built around short feedback loops, collaboration, working software, adaptation, and continuous learning. It is not synonymous with Scrum, Jira, or 'no documentation.'

The Agile Manifesto emphasizes people and collaboration, usable software, customer partnership, and responsiveness to change while still valuing processes, documentation, contracts, and plans when they help. Its principles reinforce frequent delivery, sustainable pace, technical excellence, simplicity, and reflection.

For QA, the whole-team approach means quality is considered during refinement, design, coding, automation, exploratory testing, release, and operation. Early and frequent feedback reduces the cost of misunderstanding and makes testing a continuous activity.

Four Agile values — practical interpretation

EmphasisTesting implication
People and collaboration over rigid process/tool worshipUse tools to improve communication; do not let a workflow replace discussion about risk.
Working software over documentation as the primary proofKeep documentation useful, but validate behavior with executable/evidenced outcomes.
Customer collaboration over adversarial contract interpretationClarify examples and acceptance criteria with stakeholders instead of testing literal wording in isolation.
Responding to change over blindly following a frozen planUpdate risk, tests, and automation when product learning changes priorities.

Twelve Agile principles — QA-oriented summary

  1. Deliver valuable software early and continuously so feedback starts soon.
  2. Expect changing requirements and adjust tests and risk analysis accordingly.
  3. Deliver working increments frequently rather than delaying validation for a large release.
  4. Business and technical people collaborate continuously; QA helps translate between them.
  5. Build around capable, trusted people and give them the environment and information needed to succeed.
  6. Use rich direct communication when ambiguity is high, while preserving decisions that need durable documentation.
  7. Working software and observable outcomes are stronger progress indicators than artifact volume.
  8. Maintain a sustainable pace; permanent crunch degrades both code and test quality.
  9. Technical excellence, testability, automation, and good design improve the ability to adapt.
  10. Prefer simplicity: avoid unnecessary work, tests, abstractions, and process.
  11. Self-organizing teams often discover better implementation and testing approaches than centrally prescribed scripts.
  12. Regularly inspect how the team works and adapt process, automation, and collaboration based on evidence.
INTERVIEW LENS

Avoid defining Agile as 'working in sprints.' Explain feedback, adaptability, incremental value, and shared ownership of quality.

Foundation → Intermediate

Scrum framework: accountabilities, events, artifacts, and QA participation

Scrum is a lightweight framework for developing complex products through short iterations called Sprints. The core accountabilities are Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers; QA specialists may be members of the Developers group rather than a separate gate.

Key events are the Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective. Core artifacts are Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, and Increment, each with a commitment such as Product Goal, Sprint Goal, or Definition of Done.

QA contributes to backlog refinement, acceptance criteria, risk discussion, estimation, testability, automation, exploratory testing, and the Definition of Done. Testing should occur throughout the Sprint, not as a mini-waterfall at the end.

Scrum elementQA perspective
Backlog refinementClarify acceptance criteria, dependencies, edge cases, data, and non-functional risk.
Sprint PlanningIdentify test work, automation, environments, and risks that affect capacity.
Daily ScrumSurface blockers and integration/environment issues without turning the event into a QA status meeting.
ReviewUse working product and evidence to validate outcomes and gather feedback.
RetrospectiveImprove process, automation signal, defect prevention, and collaboration.

Foundation → Intermediate

Themes, epics, user stories, acceptance criteria, and INVEST

Agile product work is often organized from broad themes or initiatives into epics and smaller user stories. A user story is a planning/conversation device, not a complete specification; acceptance criteria and examples add testable detail.

INVEST is a heuristic for reviewing stories: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable. A story that cannot be estimated or tested is often too ambiguous, too large, or too dependent on hidden work.

QA should test the seams between stories as well as individual acceptance criteria. Splitting work into tickets does not split the user's end-to-end experience.

Story-to-test example
User story:
As a returning customer
I want to verify my phone with an OTP
So that I can recover account access.

Acceptance ideas:
- valid, expired, reused, and incorrect OTP
- resend cooldown and rate limit
- correct account binding
- safe error messages
- accessibility and keyboard flow

Intermediate

Planning Poker, estimation, and quality work visibility

Agile estimation is about relative uncertainty and effort, not predicting exact hours. Planning Poker is one collaborative technique: participants estimate independently, reveal simultaneously, and discuss large differences.

QA should ensure testing, automation, test data, environment work, accessibility, observability, and integration validation are visible in estimates. If 'development' is estimated while testing is assumed to be free, the plan is distorted.

Estimates improve through decomposition, historical data, and explicit unknowns. They should not be used as individual performance scores.

Skills covered

Test EstimationAgile TestingRisk Management

Related: Test estimation · Scrum

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate

Burn-down, burn-up, velocity, and interpreting Agile metrics

A burn-down chart shows remaining work over time. A burn-up chart shows completed work against total scope, making scope changes easier to see. Velocity summarizes the amount of estimated work a team completes across Sprints.

These are planning signals, not quality metrics and not suitable for comparing teams. A team can increase velocity while accumulating defects or technical debt. Pair delivery metrics with escaped defects, reliability, cycle time, and customer outcomes.

Watch for denominator changes: adding scope can make a burn-down look worse even when delivery is healthy, while closing low-value work can make velocity look better without improving the product.

Skills covered

Agile TestingData VisualizationQuality Metrics

Related: Quality metrics · Data analysis

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate

Kanban, stabilization/hardening, retrospectives, and documentation

Kanban visualizes flow, limits work in progress (WIP), and emphasizes managing cycle time and bottlenecks. It can be used for product work, defects, support, or test queues without fixed Sprints.

A stabilization or 'hardening' iteration concentrates on regression, defect resolution, integration, and release readiness. It can be a pragmatic temporary tactic, but repeated dependence on hardening may signal that quality activities are happening too late.

Retrospectives turn delivery experience into process improvements. Document decisions, meeting notes, release information, and testing strategy in a shared knowledge system such as Confluence—but keep documentation current and connected to actionable work.

COURSE EXPANSION / WEB SERVICES

Web architecture, XML/SOAP, and deeper Postman workflows

The course's API module starts with web and protocol foundations before moving into Postman projects. These sections fill the main gaps in the existing REST-focused material.

Foundation

Web applications, client/server communication, and Internet protocol layers

A web application commonly has a client (browser or mobile app), one or more web/API services, persistence, and external dependencies. The client resolves a hostname through DNS, establishes a network connection, often negotiates TLS for HTTPS, sends HTTP requests, and receives representations such as HTML or JSON.

QA does not need to be a network engineer, but understanding DNS, TCP/IP concepts, TLS, HTTP, cookies, headers, caching, proxies, and browser storage makes failures much easier to locate. 'The website is down' can actually be a DNS, certificate, gateway, API, database, or frontend problem.

Use browser developer tools and API clients to separate presentation failures from transport or backend failures.

Skills covered

Web TestingREST APIsTroubleshooting

Related: API fundamentals · Reverse proxies · Network troubleshooting

Back to contents ↑
Foundation → Intermediate

XML, JSON, SOAP, and REST-style web services

XML (Extensible Markup Language) represents hierarchical structured data using tagged elements and attributes. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) represents objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null in a compact syntax widely used by web APIs.

SOAP is a standardized XML-based messaging protocol commonly paired with WSDL contracts and enterprise web-service standards. Its historical name is Simple Object Access Protocol, although modern specifications generally treat SOAP as the protocol name. REST is an architectural style, not a wire protocol, and REST APIs commonly use HTTP plus JSON.

Do not reduce the comparison to 'SOAP is old, REST is new.' SOAP can provide strict contracts and standardized enterprise features; REST-style HTTP APIs are often simpler and more web-native. QA should validate the actual contract, authentication, namespaces/content types, errors, and business semantics.

DimensionXML / SOAPJSON / REST-style HTTP
RepresentationXML with elements/attributes/namespacesUsually JSON, but REST does not require JSON.
ContractOften WSDL/XSD-drivenOften OpenAPI/JSON Schema or documented conventions.
TransportSOAP can use HTTP and other transportsREST-style web APIs commonly use HTTP.
Testing focusEnvelope, namespaces, schema, faults, WS-* behaviorMethods, status, headers, schema, resource semantics.

Formats and protocols

XML
Structured markup/data format

Definition: Extensible Markup Language is a text format for hierarchical structured data using elements, attributes, namespaces, and schemas.

Main characteristics

  • Self-describing tagged structure
  • Namespaces for combining vocabularies
  • Validation with XSD and related schema technologies
  • Common in enterprise integrations, configuration, documents, and SOAP services
QA / automation relevance: Testers may validate XML payload structure, namespaces, encoding, XSD conformance, optional/repeated elements, and transformations.

Name / acronym: XML = Extensible Markup Language.

SOAP
XML messaging protocol

Definition: A standardized XML-based messaging protocol used by many enterprise web services, often with WSDL contracts and formal fault messages.

Main characteristics

  • Envelope/Header/Body message structure
  • XML payloads and namespaces
  • SOAP Fault error representation
  • Often paired with WSDL and enterprise WS-* specifications
QA / automation relevance: Validate message envelopes, namespaces, schema, authentication/security headers, operations defined by the service contract, faults, and business response content.

Name / acronym: Historically expanded as Simple Object Access Protocol; modern standards generally use SOAP as the protocol name.

Intermediate

Postman environments, authentication, assertions, dynamic data, and scheduled execution

A maintainable Postman project separates requests from environment-specific values. Store base URLs, non-secret identifiers, and environment configuration in variables; handle credentials using protected mechanisms rather than exporting them casually.

Authentication may use API keys, Basic Auth, bearer tokens, OAuth, or application-specific schemes. Assertions should validate status, headers, schema, and meaningful body values. Extract dynamic values—such as IDs or tokens—from one response and reuse them in later requests.

Collection variables can carry state across requests; environment variables distinguish staging from other environments. Pre-request scripts can prepare data; test scripts validate outcomes. Scheduled or CI execution turns a collection from a manual API client into repeatable regression coverage.

A practical API project should include positive, negative, authentication, authorization, boundary, idempotency, rate-limit, and cleanup scenarios, not only CRUD happy paths.

Postman dynamic data
// Postman test: capture an ID for the next request
pm.test("created", () => pm.response.to.have.status(201));
const body = pm.response.json();
pm.expect(body.id).to.be.a("string");
pm.collectionVariables.set("createdId", body.id);

// Later URL:
// {{baseUrl}}/items/{{createdId}}

23B / POSTMAN COURSE GAP ANALYSIS

Postman API testing: variables, scripting, workflows, mocks, runners, CI, and collaboration

This chapter fills the material that remained absent or too shallow after comparing the guide with the complete Postman course. It keeps the course's practical progression—from individual requests to automated collections—but updates the tooling to the current Postman v12 ecosystem where older practices have changed.

Foundation

Postman as an API client: app, web experience, request builder, response viewer, and troubleshooting

Postman is an API development and testing platform. At the most basic level, the request builder lets you select an HTTP method, enter a URL, configure authorization, query parameters, headers, cookies, and a request body, then send the request and inspect the response.

The response viewer exposes the status code, response body, headers, cookies, response size, response time, and test results. When a request fails, use the Postman Console and the actual request/response details before assuming the API is broken.

Postman can be used through its desktop and web experiences. The important QA skill is understanding the HTTP exchange and the execution context, not memorizing the location of a specific button in one UI version.

A response that unexpectedly contains HTML often indicates the wrong URL, a frontend route, authentication redirect, proxy/gateway response, or server error page. Inspect status, Content-Type, redirect history, and the final URL rather than trying to parse the body as JSON.

INTERVIEW LENS

Explain the request anatomy first: method + URL + auth + headers + parameters/body. Then explain how you inspect the response and diagnose transport versus business failures.

Current documentation: Postman basics · Response data

Skills covered

PostmanAPI TestingREST APIsTroubleshooting
Back to contents ↑
Foundation

HTTP methods and request anatomy: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, path, query, headers, cookies, and body

GET retrieves a representation; POST usually creates a resource or triggers processing; PUT generally replaces a complete resource representation; PATCH applies a partial modification; DELETE removes a resource; and HEAD requests the same metadata as GET without returning the response body.

Path parameters identify a resource inside the URL path, such as /users/42. Query parameters refine a request, for example ?page=2&sort=name. Headers communicate metadata such as content type, accepted formats, authorization, caching, and correlation IDs.

Cookies are state tokens attached to matching domains and paths. Request bodies can be JSON, XML, form-encoded data, multipart form data, binary content, or another media type. The Content-Type header describes the body format; Accept describes response formats the client can consume.

The same value should not be placed arbitrarily in a path, query, header, and body. The API contract determines where data belongs, and tests should verify both syntax and business meaning.

Request anatomy
GET /orders/42?include=items HTTP/1.1
Accept: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <token>

PATCH /orders/42 HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"status":"cancelled"}

Related: REST fundamentals · Authentication

Foundation → Intermediate

Reading API documentation, resource identifiers, and modeling real workflows

Before building requests, read the API documentation for base URLs, resources, identifiers, methods, required headers, authentication, request schemas, response schemas, pagination, rate limits, and error formats.

A resource identifier such as boardId, listId, or cardId is usually returned by one request and becomes input to later requests. This is the foundation of request chaining.

Real-world practice APIs such as GitHub- or Trello-style APIs are valuable because they force you to work with nested resources, authentication, pagination, and server-generated IDs instead of isolated toy requests.

A good API test suite reflects the business process behind the endpoints. CRUD coverage alone does not prove that the workflow is correct.

INTERVIEW LENS

Given unfamiliar API docs, identify the resource model, auth scheme, happy workflow, negative cases, state transitions, and cleanup strategy before writing tests.

Foundation → Intermediate

Collections, folders, request documentation, examples, import/export, and team ownership

A Postman Collection groups requests, folders, scripts, examples, variables, and workflow logic into a reusable API test asset. Organize collections by domain or API capability rather than placing every endpoint into one flat list.

Folder- and collection-level scripts let you apply common setup or assertions to many requests. Request descriptions and saved examples make the collection useful as executable documentation, not only as a private tester artifact.

Collections can be shared through Postman workspaces and exported/imported when required. In current Postman v12, the collection v3 format is designed for source-control-oriented workflows and stores human-readable YAML assets on disk.

Treat collections as code: review changes, name requests consistently, document prerequisites, keep credentials out of shared artifacts, and make cleanup repeatable.

Intermediate

Postman variables: scopes, precedence, local/shared values, dynamic values, and runtime data

Postman supports variables at several scopes. In current Postman documentation, precedence from broadest to narrowest is global → collection → environment → data → local. When the same name exists in more than one scope, the narrower applicable value wins.

Collection variables are useful for state shared within one collection. Environment variables separate deployment-specific values such as staging and production base URLs. Data variables come from iteration data. Local variables are temporary and disappear after the request or run.

Dynamic variables such as {{$randomEmail}} generate sample data. Scripts can set, get, and unset variables through objects such as pm.collectionVariables, pm.environment, pm.globals, pm.iterationData, and pm.variables.

Variable scope is a design decision. Avoid global variables for values that belong to one environment or workflow, because broad scopes create hidden coupling.

Variable APIs
const body = pm.response.json();

pm.collectionVariables.set("orderId", body.id);
pm.environment.set("accessToken", body.access_token);

console.log(pm.variables.get("orderId"));
pm.collectionVariables.unset("orderId");
INTERVIEW LENS

Know the precedence order and explain when collection, environment, data, and local scopes are appropriate.

COMMON TRAP: Using global variables for everything. It makes collections depend on invisible workspace state.

Intermediate / Current

Secrets, API keys, tokens, and Postman Vault

API keys, passwords, bearer tokens, refresh tokens, client secrets, and private credentials should not be stored as ordinary shared collection values or committed to source control.

Current Postman provides Postman Vault for secrets. Vault secrets can be referenced at runtime without exposing the value in a collection or request. Local Vault secrets remain local; Shared Vault behavior depends on workspace and plan controls.

Environment variables can still hold configuration, but a variable name and a secure secret are different concepts. For CI, inject credentials from the CI secret store or supported Postman authentication mechanism.

Rotate leaked keys, limit scopes, separate test credentials from production, and avoid logging tokens in the Postman Console or CI artifacts.

INTERVIEW LENS

A variable is not automatically a secret store. Explain the difference between configuration scope and secret protection.

Intermediate → Advanced

Authentication in Postman: Basic Auth, API keys, bearer tokens, JWT, OAuth 2.0, cookies, and auth inheritance

Basic Auth sends a username/password credential in an Authorization header using Base64 encoding; Base64 is encoding, not encryption, so HTTPS is mandatory. API key authentication sends a key in a configured header or query parameter.

Bearer authentication sends an opaque or structured access token. A JWT (JSON Web Token) is one possible token format; not every bearer token is a JWT, and a decoded JWT is not automatically trusted unless its signature and claims are validated by the server.

OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework in which a client obtains access tokens, often with scopes and expiration. Postman can request, refresh, and use OAuth tokens through the Authorization tab. OIDC (OpenID Connect) adds identity/authentication semantics on top of OAuth 2.0.

Authorization can be configured at request, folder, or collection level and inherited where appropriate. Test missing, malformed, expired, revoked, wrong-scope, wrong-audience, and cross-user access—not only the happy token path.

Cookie-based APIs also require testing domain/path rules, expiry, logout, session invalidation, CSRF protections where relevant, and whether the cookie is sent with the intended requests.

INTERVIEW LENS

Separate authentication, authorization, token format, and delegated authorization. JWT and OAuth are not synonyms.

Current documentation: Authorization types · OAuth 2.0

Intermediate

The Postman Sandbox: pre-request scripts, post-response scripts, the pm object, callbacks, and the console

Postman scripts run in the Postman Sandbox, a JavaScript runtime based on Node.js. For HTTP requests, pre-request scripts run before a request is sent; post-response scripts run after the response arrives and are the normal place for assertions and extracting dynamic data.

The pm object exposes request/response data, variables, tests, execution metadata, cookies, Vault access, visualizations, and request-sending helpers. Use the Postman Console for debugging logs and the exact network exchange.

Postman scripting is asynchronous. pm.sendRequest() can send HTTP requests from a script and supports callback- or promise-style coordination depending on the API usage. Do not assume ordinary browser or Node filesystem APIs are all available inside the sandbox.

Collection- and folder-level scripts can centralize common logic. Current Postman also provides reusable packages, which is cleaner than copying the same helper function into dozens of requests.

Postman scripting lifecycle
// Pre-request script
pm.variables.set("requestStartedAt", Date.now());

// Post-response script
pm.test("request succeeded", () => {
  pm.expect(pm.response.code).to.be.oneOf([200, 201]);
});

console.log("request id:", pm.info.requestId);

Related: Reusable scripts · Sending requests

Intermediate

API assertions with pm.test, pm.expect, Chai, arrays, nested objects, headers, cookies, and error behavior

Postman uses pm.test() to define named tests and pm.expect() for assertions. The Post-response environment includes the Chai assertion library, allowing readable BDD-style assertions.

Validate more than status codes: response data types, required fields, nested values, arrays, headers, cookies, business invariants, and error contracts. A 200 response can still contain incorrect business data.

Array assertions should make ordering assumptions explicit. Use find(), map(), filter(), or loops when the response contains dynamic collections rather than relying on hard-coded indexes.

Negative and boundary tests should prove that invalid input is rejected safely and predictably. Refactor duplicated assertions into collection/folder scripts or reusable packages.

Chai-style assertions
pm.test("order response is valid", () => {
  const body = pm.response.json();

  pm.response.to.have.status(200);
  pm.expect(body.id).to.be.a("string");
  pm.expect(body.items).to.be.an("array").that.is.not.empty;

  const paidItem = body.items.find(item => item.status === "paid");
  pm.expect(paidItem, "a paid item must exist").to.exist;

  pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get("content-type"))
    .to.include("application/json");
});

Intermediate

JSON Schema validation inside Postman

Postman can validate response bodies against a JSON Schema directly from a post-response script. Schema validation checks structure, types, required properties, enums, and other declared constraints.

A schema is not a complete test oracle. A payload can satisfy the schema while containing the wrong account balance, order total, ownership relationship, or state transition.

Use schema validation for contract stability, then add targeted assertions for business invariants and security-sensitive fields.

Schema assertion
const schema = {
  type: "object",
  required: ["id", "status"],
  properties: {
    id: { type: "string", minLength: 1 },
    status: { enum: ["pending", "paid", "cancelled"] }
  },
  additionalProperties: false
};

pm.test("schema is valid", () => {
  pm.response.to.have.jsonSchema(schema);
});

Related: General JSON Schema · Contract testing

Intermediate

Inspecting and visualizing responses with Postman Visualizer

The normal response viewer displays status, body, headers, cookies, timing, and test output. Postman Visualizer adds a programmable presentation layer for response data.

pm.visualizer.set() renders an HTML/Handlebars template using data such as pm.response.json(). This can turn large JSON responses into tables, summaries, charts, or domain-oriented views that are easier to inspect.

A visualization is a debugging and communication aid, not an assertion. Keep automated tests separate so a visually attractive output cannot substitute for a failed invariant.

Postman Visualizer
const template = `
<table>
  <tr><th>ID</th><th>Status</th></tr>
  {{#each orders}}
    <tr><td>{{id}}</td><td>{{status}}</td></tr>
  {{/each}}
</table>`;

pm.visualizer.set(template, { orders: pm.response.json() });

Intermediate → Advanced

Request chaining and workflows with pm.execution.setNextRequest()

A workflow extracts values from one response and passes them to later requests: authenticate → create board → create list → create card → move card → verify → delete. Variables carry state; assertions at each step make the dependency explicit.

Current Postman uses pm.execution.setNextRequest() to change the request that runs next during a collection run. The older postman.setNextRequest() API is legacy/deprecated material and should not be used in new scripts.

Use request IDs rather than request names for robust branching when names may change. Set the next request to null to stop a workflow, and always protect loops with an explicit termination condition.

One collection can support multiple workflows by branching based on data or variables, but excessive control flow can turn a collection into difficult-to-debug application code. Keep business workflow readable.

Workflow control
const body = pm.response.json();
pm.collectionVariables.set("cardId", body.id);

if (body.status === "ready") {
  pm.execution.setNextRequest("move-card-request-id");
} else {
  pm.execution.setNextRequest(null);
}
COMMON TRAP: An unbounded setNextRequest loop can create an infinite collection run.

Current documentation: Request workflows

Advanced

Sending requests from scripts: pm.sendRequest() and pm.execution.runRequest()

pm.sendRequest() sends an HTTP request defined directly in script code. It is useful for auxiliary calls such as obtaining setup data or checking a secondary service.

pm.execution.runRequest() executes a request already stored in a collection, avoiding duplication of its full request definition. Current Postman limits how often a referenced request can be executed from one script, so it is not a replacement for a normal collection workflow.

Use script-driven requests deliberately. When a critical action is hidden inside a pre-request script, the visible collection can become misleading. Prefer explicit collection requests for major business steps.

pm.sendRequest
pm.sendRequest({
  url: pm.environment.get("healthUrl"),
  method: "GET"
}, (err, res) => {
  pm.test("dependency is healthy", () => {
    pm.expect(err).to.equal(null);
    pm.expect(res.code).to.equal(200);
  });
});

Current documentation: pm.sendRequest · pm.execution

Intermediate → Advanced

Data-driven runs with CSV, JSON, iteration data, and current Postman datasets

Collection runs can execute the same scenario repeatedly using rows from CSV or JSON input. Values from iteration data are available through pm.iterationData and can drive request bodies, parameters, and expected results.

Data-driven tests are useful for boundary tables, roles, product combinations, and expected outcomes. Keep one row understandable as one scenario; a giant data file with hidden logic becomes harder to maintain than normal code.

Current Postman also has reusable datasets. Unlike one-off data files, datasets can be reused by collection runs, monitors, mocks, and scripts depending on plan and execution context.

Be aware of execution-context limitations: uploaded/local data files and cloud/scheduled/CLI execution do not all behave identically. Check the current runner documentation when designing CI data flows.

Iteration data
// iteration data supplied by CSV/JSON
const expectedStatus = pm.iterationData.get("expectedStatus");
const email = pm.iterationData.get("email");

pm.test("status matches data row", () => {
  pm.expect(pm.response.code).to.equal(Number(expectedStatus));
});

Current documentation: Data files · Datasets

Intermediate

Collection Runner, manual runs, scheduled runs, and monitors

Collection Runner executes multiple requests in sequence, supports iterations, environment selection, run-order control, and test result aggregation. It is the bridge between an individually sent request and a repeatable API suite.

Current Postman can schedule collection runs in the cloud. Scheduled functional runs are useful for recurring API regression without maintaining your own CI job.

Postman Monitors are better suited when the goal includes ongoing API health checks and failure alerts. Monitors execute on a schedule and track results over time.

For pull-request and build gates, CI remains appropriate because it ties the test result to a code change. For continuous external health validation, a monitor is often the clearer model.

INTERVIEW LENS

Distinguish manual Collection Runner, scheduled functional runs, monitors, and CI pipelines by purpose—not just by where the Run button lives.

Intermediate → Advanced / Current v12

Postman CLI versus Newman, collection v3, environments, reporters, and CI

Postman CLI is the current official command-line tool for running and managing Postman assets. It can run collections locally or in CI and supports current Postman capabilities beyond collection execution.

Newman remains the open-source command-line runner used by many existing pipelines. In Postman v12, Newman runs compatible collection v2.1 JSON exports but cannot run the newer v3 collection format. Postman recommends the Postman CLI for new CI/CD workflows.

The Postman CLI supports current collection operations such as running, migrating, importing, and linting collections. Reporter availability depends on protocol and collection format; for compatible HTTP collection runs it can produce CLI, JSON, JUnit, and HTML reports.

Keep collection, environment, and secret inputs explicit in CI. A nonzero exit should reflect meaningful test failure so the pipeline can act as a quality gate.

CLI examples
# Current Postman CLI
postman collection run ./postman/collections/orders   --environment ./postman/environments/staging.yml

# Existing Newman workflow for v2.1 JSON
newman run orders.postman_collection.json   -e staging.postman_environment.json   -r cli,junit

Advanced

Running Postman API suites in Jenkins, GitLab CI, TeamCity, and other CI systems

A Postman collection becomes a delivery control when the pipeline installs the CLI/runner, injects environment configuration and secrets, executes the suite non-interactively, and publishes machine-readable results.

In Jenkins, the same principle applies to freestyle jobs and Jenkinsfile pipelines. Publish JUnit results so Jenkins can track failures and trends; archive HTML or JSON reports when they improve diagnosis.

GitLab CI, TeamCity, GitHub Actions, and other CI systems differ in configuration syntax, but the API-testing contract is the same: reproducible tool version, protected secrets, deterministic inputs, meaningful exit status, and retained evidence.

Do not place secrets directly in a Jenkinsfile, repository YAML, or collection export. Use the CI system's credentials/secret mechanism.

Jenkins concept
pipeline {
  agent any
  stages {
    stage('API tests') {
      steps {
        withCredentials([string(credentialsId: 'postman-key',
                                variable: 'POSTMAN_API_KEY')]) {
          sh 'postman collection run ./postman/collections/api'
        }
      }
    }
  }
  post {
    always {
      junit allowEmptyResults: true, testResults: 'reports/*.xml'
    }
  }
}

Related: Jenkins fundamentals · Secrets

Intermediate

Postman mock servers, examples, recorded responses, and frontend/API parallel development

A mock server simulates an API so clients can develop and test before the real backend is available or when a specific response state is difficult to reproduce.

Postman mock servers can be created from collections or mocks and use saved examples to determine responses. This makes examples executable assets rather than documentation-only samples.

Mocks are useful for frontend development, deterministic error scenarios, and contract discussion. They do not prove that the real service is compatible; keep contract/integration tests against the real provider.

Current Postman supports public and private mock servers. Public mocks are reachable by anyone, so never expose sensitive example data or secrets.

INTERVIEW LENS

A mock isolates a dependency; an integration test proves the real boundary. You normally need both at different points.

Current documentation: Mock servers

PostmanAPI TestingAPI Contract TestingSystem Integration

Intermediate

multipart/form-data, file uploads, binary bodies, working directories, and automated upload tests

multipart/form-data is commonly used when one request contains files plus ordinary form fields. Postman can attach files to form-data parts or send a binary request body.

For reproducible shared collections, file paths must be handled deliberately. The Postman desktop app uses a working directory for files referenced by requests; teammates need compatible files/paths when running the same collection locally.

An upload test should verify more than the HTTP status: filename/metadata, content type, size limits, authorization, malware/content policy where applicable, final persistence, duplicate handling, and cleanup.

CLI/Newman automation must have access to the referenced file in its execution environment. Mount or check in safe fixtures deliberately; never depend on a developer's personal Downloads folder.

Current documentation: Postman working directory

Skills covered

PostmanAPI TestingTest Data ManagementCI/CD

Advanced

CSV responses, file outputs, and the boundary of the Postman Sandbox

Not every API returns JSON. For CSV responses, use pm.response.text() and parse the text with appropriate logic or a supported package. Assert headers, row counts, delimiters, encoding, and business values.

The Postman Sandbox is restricted and should not be treated as unrestricted Node.js with arbitrary local filesystem access. Some external packages that depend on Node built-in modules may not work as they would in a normal Node process.

If an automated workflow must write durable files, prefer the runner/CI layer (for example reporters and shell steps), a supported Postman feature, or a purpose-built helper service rather than hiding filesystem side effects inside request scripts.

This separation makes the collection portable between desktop, cloud, CLI, and team environments.

Related: Postman sandbox

Current documentation: Sandbox packages · Sandbox API

Advanced / Current

Reusing tests and helpers with collection scripts and the Postman Package Library

The simplest reuse level is a collection- or folder-level pre-request/post-response script. Common checks applied at collection level run for every request inside the collection.

For reusable JavaScript shared across multiple collections, current Postman provides a Package Library. Teams can publish internal packages containing helper functions and tests and import them into scripts.

Postman can also import supported external packages from registries such as npm or JSR, subject to sandbox limitations and organizational policy.

Prefer one maintained helper to copy/pasted assertions. Reuse should reduce duplication without hiding business-specific expectations behind a generic 'validate everything' function.

Team Workspaces, collaboration, permissions, shared API assets, and source-of-truth decisions

A Postman Workspace groups related collections, environments, API specifications, mocks, monitors, and other project elements. Shared workspaces let a team collaborate and see synchronized changes.

Current Postman supports workspace types for different collaboration models, including internal, partner, and public use cases depending on plan and organization configuration.

Treat visibility as a security boundary. Public workspaces and public mocks must never contain private URLs, credentials, customer data, or internal-only examples.

Decide whether the team's primary source of truth is Postman Cloud or a Git/native project workflow. Avoid two unsynchronized masters that drift from each other.

Current documentation: Workspaces · Collaboration

Intermediate

TDD and API-first testing with Postman

TDD (Test-Driven Development) is the practice of writing a failing test first, implementing the smallest change that makes it pass, and then refactoring. Postman can participate in a TDD/API-first workflow when executable API expectations exist before the endpoint implementation.

A Postman collection can encode examples and contract expectations early, while mock servers allow clients to work against agreed examples before the backend exists.

Do not confuse TDD with 'write Postman tests before release'. The defining feedback loop is test-first: red → green → refactor.

INTERVIEW LENS

TDD is a development feedback cycle, not simply regression automation.

Related: Mock servers · API contracts

API TestingPostmanTest AutomationTest Strategy

Intermediate

Testing headers, cookies, redirects, content types, and error handling

Protocol-level assertions are often the fastest way to catch broken contracts. Validate expected Content-Type, cache headers, correlation IDs, pagination links, rate-limit headers, and security-related headers when they are part of the API contract.

Use Postman's cookie APIs or cookie manager to inspect session cookies and domain/path behavior. For security-sensitive sessions, test expiry, logout, invalidation, and whether cookies have the expected protection attributes where observable.

Error handling deserves a stable contract: status code, machine-readable error code, human-readable message where appropriate, correlation ID, and no sensitive internal stack trace.

A test should not require every header to be identical. Assert the headers that communicate behavior or security guarantees.

Current documentation: Response data and cookies

API TestingPostmanSecurity TestingAuthentication Testing

Hands-on

Capstone Postman lab: authenticated Trello-style API workflow with CI and mocks

Build a collection around a disposable Trello-style or local training API. The workflow should authenticate, create a board, create TODO and DONE lists, create a card, move the card, retrieve it, verify state, and clean up every created resource.

Use environment variables for deployment configuration, collection variables for workflow IDs, Vault/CI secrets for credentials, and CSV/JSON iteration data for at least one data-driven scenario.

Add negative authorization, malformed input, boundary, missing-resource, duplicate-operation, and error-contract tests. Validate response schema plus business invariants.

Create one mock-server example for an unavailable or not-yet-built dependency. Run the collection through Postman CLI in CI and publish a JUnit-compatible result. Add a second scheduled/monitoring use case only if continuous health validation is actually valuable.

Finally, document which checks belong in Postman, which belong in browser E2E tests, and which belong in direct service/unit tests. The goal is a test architecture, not a Postman-only solution.

Capstone flow
Workflow:
1. Authenticate
2. POST /boards              -> boardId
3. POST /boards/{boardId}/lists -> todoId, doneId
4. POST /lists/{todoId}/cards   -> cardId
5. PATCH /cards/{cardId}         -> move to doneId
6. GET /cards/{cardId}           -> assert durable state
7. Negative auth / boundary cases
8. DELETE created resources
9. Run in CI with non-secret configuration

COURSE EXPANSION / PERFORMANCE

Performance engineering and Apache JMeter

The existing guide covered performance concepts at a strategy level. The course goes much deeper into load profiles, statistical interpretation, JMeter scripting, correlation, pacing, recording, CLI execution, and controllers. This chapter adds that practical layer.

Foundation → Intermediate

Performance testing types, load models, and test environments

Performance testing evaluates how a system behaves under time and load constraints. Common test types include load testing at expected demand, stress testing beyond expected limits, spike testing for sudden changes, endurance/soak testing for long-running degradation, and capacity/scalability testing to find practical limits.

A load profile defines user or request arrival patterns, ramp-up, steady-state duration, concurrency, transaction mix, think time, and data distribution. '1000 users' is not meaningful unless you define what those users do and how quickly they act.

The performance environment should resemble production where bottlenecks matter: service topology, database size, network path, caches, external dependencies, autoscaling, and resource limits. If the environment is intentionally smaller, document how that changes interpretation.

TestQuestion it answers
LoadCan the system meet objectives at expected traffic?
StressHow does it fail and recover beyond capacity?
SpikeWhat happens when demand changes suddenly?
SoakDo leaks, queues, or degradation appear over hours/days?
CapacityWhere are the sustainable limits and scaling breakpoints?

Skills covered

Performance TestingReliability EngineeringCapacity Planning

Related: Performance deep dive · Reliability · Capacity

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate

Response time, throughput, utilization, median, percentiles, and standard deviation

Response time is the elapsed time observed for an operation. Throughput is work completed per unit of time. Utilization describes resource usage such as CPU, memory, connections, or disk. Robustness is the ability to remain correct and recover under unfavorable conditions.

The arithmetic mean is sensitive to outliers; the median is the 50th percentile. Percentiles such as p90, p95, and p99 answer 'what response time was not exceeded by this percentage of observations?' Tail percentiles are often more useful than averages for user experience.

Standard deviation measures spread around the mean. It can help identify variability, but latency distributions are often skewed, so always inspect percentiles and error rates as well. A fast average can hide a severe long tail.

Why percentiles matter
Example latency sample (ms):
100, 105, 110, 115, 120, 130, 180, 250, 800, 1200

Median: around 125 ms
Mean: much higher because of the 800/1200 ms outliers
p90/p95: reveal the slow tail that the median hides

Skills covered

Performance TestingData AnalysisQuality Metrics

Related: Data analysis · Performance metrics

Back to contents ↑
Foundation → Intermediate

JMeter Test Plans, Thread Groups, samplers, assertions, listeners, and CLI execution

A JMeter Test Plan is a tree of elements. A Thread Group models virtual-user threads and controls count, ramp-up, and loops. Samplers send requests. Assertions validate results. Listeners display or save results.

Build and debug a script with small load first. For meaningful load generation, execute in non-GUI/CLI mode and keep expensive listeners disabled, then analyze result files and server-side telemetry.

A valid performance script should reproduce user/business behavior at the protocol level, not simply replay every browser request without understanding dependencies.

Tools and technologies in this topic

Apache JMeter
Load and performance testing tool

Definition: An open-source Java application for generating protocol-level load and measuring responses for HTTP and other supported protocols.

Main characteristics

  • Test Plans organized as trees
  • Thread Groups model virtual-user execution
  • Samplers issue requests
  • Assertions validate responses
  • Timers model pacing/think time
  • Pre/Post-Processors prepare or extract data
  • Controllers shape flow
  • CLI/non-GUI execution for real load
  • Listeners help debugging/reporting but heavy listeners should be avoided during large load
QA / automation relevance: Useful for repeatable API/web-service load, stress, endurance, and capacity tests. JMeter generates protocol traffic; it does not behave like a full browser rendering engine.

Name / acronym: JMeter is a project name from Apache; it is not an acronym.

Skills covered

Performance TestingJMeterCLI

Related: Load models · Metrics

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate

Parameterization, correlation, dynamic data, and DRY test design

Parameterization replaces hard-coded values with variables or datasets so virtual users can operate on realistic distinct data. In JMeter, CSV data sources and variables are common approaches.

Correlation captures a dynamic value from an earlier response—session ID, CSRF token, resource ID, timestamp—and injects it into later requests. Without correlation, a recorded script often works only once.

DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) means centralizing reusable values and logic such as a base URL, headers, or common authentication setup. DRY improves maintainability, but over-abstraction can make a performance script harder to inspect.

Correlation and parameterization
Flow:
1. POST /login
2. Extract $.token -> ${token}
3. POST /orders with Authorization: Bearer ${token}
4. Extract $.id -> ${orderId}
5. GET /orders/${orderId}

Data:
users.csv -> username,password for each virtual user

Skills covered

Performance TestingTest Data ManagementAPI Testing

Related: API chaining · JMeter architecture

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate

Timers, think time, recording, and realistic pacing

Real users pause between actions. Think time is the delay between business actions; pacing controls how often a virtual user repeats a journey. Without realistic pacing, a test may generate an impossible request rate.

JMeter timers add controlled delays. Choose constant, random, or throughput-oriented pacing based on the workload model. Keep server response time separate from artificial think time when reporting service performance.

Recording tools such as BlazeMeter can capture a browser session and generate a starting script. Treat that output as raw material: remove irrelevant resources, parameterize data, correlate dynamic values, add assertions, and validate that the script represents the intended business flow.

Tools and technologies in this topic

BlazeMeter
Performance-testing and test-recording platform

Definition: A commercial continuous-testing platform commonly used with JMeter-compatible scripts and browser/proxy recording workflows.

Main characteristics

  • Can record HTTP interactions for script generation
  • Supports cloud/distributed load capabilities
  • Integrates with JMeter ecosystems and CI workflows
  • Provides reporting and collaboration features
QA / automation relevance: Recording can accelerate a first script draft, but generated requests need cleanup, correlation, parameterization, pacing, and validation before they represent realistic load.

Name / acronym: BlazeMeter is a brand name, not an acronym.

Skills covered

Performance TestingLoad Modeling

Related: Load profiles · Correlation

Back to contents ↑
Advanced

Serial/parallel execution, controllers, and sampler-error behavior

JMeter threads execute their child elements in order unless controllers or plugins change the flow. Multiple threads run concurrently, so a test can model many independent virtual users while each user's journey remains sequential.

Controllers structure execution: Simple Controller groups elements; Loop Controller repeats children; Runtime Controller runs for a duration; Throughput Controller executes a branch according to a percentage/count rule; Once Only Controller runs initialization once per thread; Interleave Controller alternates child branches.

Thread Group settings define what happens after a sampler error: continue, start next loop, stop thread, stop test, or stop immediately depending on test intent. Choose deliberately—continuing after a failed login can produce meaningless downstream traffic.

Parallelism in a load tool is not the same as browser test parallelism. Validate that the load generator itself is not CPU/network constrained before blaming the system under test.

Skills covered

Performance TestingConcurrencyTroubleshooting

Related: Parallel test execution · JMeter
