COURSE EXPANSION / DATABASES

Database fundamentals and relational modeling for testers

The guide already had SQL, joins, transactions, indexes, and data quality. The course adds a more beginner-friendly database foundation: DBMS terminology, SQL command types, CRUD, keys, and ER diagrams.

Foundation

DBMS, relational databases, SQL command families, and CRUD

DBMS (Database Management System) is software that stores, retrieves, secures, and manages data. A relational DBMS organizes data into tables related through keys and queried with SQL.

SQL (Structured Query Language) includes several families: DDL (Data Definition Language) such as CREATE/ALTER/DROP; DML (Data Manipulation Language) such as INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE; DQL (Data Query Language), commonly SELECT; TCL (Transaction Control Language) such as COMMIT/ROLLBACK; and DCL (Data Control Language) such as GRANT/REVOKE. Exact categorization varies slightly by vendor.

CRUD means Create, Read, Update, Delete. CRUD is an application/data-operation model; it maps loosely to INSERT/SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE but is not itself a SQL standard.

AcronymExpansionTypical examples
DBMSDatabase Management SystemPostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite (embedded DB engine)
DDLData Definition LanguageCREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE
DMLData Manipulation LanguageINSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
DQLData Query LanguageSELECT
TCLTransaction Control LanguageCOMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT
DCLData Control LanguageGRANT, REVOKE
CRUDCreate, Read, Update, DeleteApplication-level data operations

Skills covered

SQLData ValidationDatabase Testing

Related: SQL overview · Transactions

Back to contents ↑
Foundation

Tables, rows, columns, primary keys, foreign keys, and referential integrity

A relational table contains rows (records) and columns (attributes). A primary key (PK) uniquely identifies a row. A foreign key (FK) references a key in another table and can enforce referential integrity.

QA should test uniqueness, nullability, default values, constraints, cascading behavior, orphan prevention, and how application errors map to database constraints. A UI may look correct while invalid relational state is being stored.

Foreign-key relationships are especially important when deletion or updates affect dependent records. Understand whether the intended rule is RESTRICT, CASCADE, SET NULL, soft-delete, or application-managed behavior.

Relational table example
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);

Skills covered

SQLData QualityDatabase Testing

Related: ERD & cardinality · Data quality

Back to contents ↑
Foundation → Intermediate

SELECT, WHERE, operators, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, LIMIT, and joins

For QA, SQL is often used to verify preconditions, compare expected state, investigate defects, and reconcile API/UI results. Start with read-only queries whenever possible in shared environments.

Core filtering includes WHERE, IN, comparison operators, BETWEEN, LIKE, and boolean AND/OR. LIMIT (or vendor-specific equivalents) constrains result size. INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE change data and require much more care.

INNER JOIN returns matching rows; LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left side and fills unmatched right-side fields with NULL. Multi-table joins are normal when business state is distributed across related entities.

QA reconciliation query
SELECT o.id, c.email, p.status AS payment_status
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE
  AND o.status IN ('PAID', 'PENDING')
ORDER BY o.id DESC
LIMIT 50;

Skills covered

SQLData ValidationAPI Testing

Related: Joins & transactions · Cross-layer reconciliation

Back to contents ↑
Foundation → Intermediate

ERD, entities, attributes, relationships, and cardinality

ERD (Entity-Relationship Diagram) visualizes entities, their attributes, and relationships. An entity represents a thing such as Customer or Order; an attribute is a property such as email, status, or created_at.

Cardinality describes how many instances can relate: one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many. Many-to-many relationships are usually implemented through a junction/association table.

Reading an ERD helps QA identify required relationships, orphan risks, uniqueness assumptions, cascade behavior, and useful SQL joins before writing tests.

Cardinality example
Customer 1 ──── * Order
Order    1 ──── * OrderItem
Product  1 ──── * OrderItem

OrderItem acts as the junction between Order and Product,
turning a conceptual many-to-many relationship into two
one-to-many relationships.

Skills covered

Database DesignSQLData Quality

Common entity and attribute classifications

  • Strong entity: has its own key and can exist independently in the model.
  • Weak/dependent entity: identification or existence depends on another entity.
  • Simple attribute: atomic value such as a status code.
  • Composite attribute: conceptually made of parts, such as an address; relational designs often store the parts separately.
  • Single-valued vs multi-valued: one value per entity versus multiple values; multi-valued data often becomes a related table.
  • Derived attribute: calculated from other data, such as age from date of birth; tests should verify the source and calculation rather than only the displayed value.

Related: Keys & integrity · Data contracts

COURSE EXPANSION / JAVA AUTOMATION

Java, Maven, Selenium WebDriver, TestNG, and Katalon

The existing guide intentionally emphasized Playwright and only covered selected Java/Selenium interview concepts. The course contains a full beginner automation track. This chapter adds the missing toolchain and execution fundamentals.

Foundation

Test automation: benefits, limits, myths, and relationship with manual testing

Automation is not 'manual testing done by a robot.' It is software that performs repeatable checks and produces evidence. It is strongest for deterministic regression, high-volume data combinations, repeated cross-browser/API checks, CI feedback, and setup/cleanup tasks.

Manual testing remains essential for exploratory investigation, usability, rapidly changing features, visual judgment, and situations where the oracle is unclear. Mature teams combine human investigation with automated feedback rather than treating them as competitors.

Common myths include: automation eliminates QA roles; every test should be automated; a large automated suite guarantees quality; recording tools remove the need for programming; and automation is maintenance-free. In reality, test code is production-like software with design, data, environment, observability, and maintenance costs.

A useful automation decision weighs execution frequency, business risk, stability, cost to automate, cost to maintain, diagnostic value, and whether a lower-level test can prove the same behavior more cheaply.

Good automation candidatePoor/conditional candidate
Repeated regression with clear expected resultOne-off exploratory investigation
API/business-rule combinationsHighly subjective usability judgment
Cross-browser critical flowUI changing daily with no stable contract
Data setup/cleanupScenario cheaper to execute manually than maintain in code

Skills covered

Test AutomationExploratory TestingTest Strategy

Related: What to automate · Manual workflow · Framework design

Back to contents ↑
Foundation

Java foundations for test automation: variables, types, control flow, methods, and objects

Java is a statically typed language commonly used in enterprise test automation. Testers should understand variables, primitive and reference types, operators, conditionals, loops, methods, return types, arrays/collections, classes, and objects before relying on a framework.

JDK (Java Development Kit) provides the compiler and development tools. The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) executes Java bytecode. Historically the JRE (Java Runtime Environment) described the runtime distribution; modern JDK distributions generally include the runtime components needed to execute Java.

A class defines structure and behavior; an object is an instance. A constructor initializes an object. Access modifiers such as public, protected, package-private, and private control visibility. These concepts support the OOP patterns explained in OOP fundamentals.

Class, object state, constructor, encapsulation
public class User {
    private final String email;

    public User(String email) {
        this.email = email;
    }

    public String getEmail() {
        return email;
    }
}

Maven, pom.xml, dependencies, and repeatable Java test builds

A Java automation repository needs repeatable dependency and execution rules. Maven stores project metadata in pom.xml, resolves libraries such as Selenium or TestNG, and exposes lifecycle phases that CI can run consistently.

Pin or deliberately manage dependency versions, avoid manually copying JAR files, and keep test execution reproducible from the command line. The IDE should be convenient, not required for the build to work.

Do not confuse Maven's POM (Project Object Model) with the automation POM (Page Object Model) pattern.

Foundation

Selenium WebDriver: navigation, browser management, page information, and cleanup

A WebDriver session represents browser automation state. Typical operations include opening a URL, navigating back/forward/refresh, reading title or URL, resizing/maximizing the window, managing cookies/timeouts, and interacting with elements.

Use driver.close() to close the current window and driver.quit() to end the entire browser session and release the driver process. Framework teardown should run even when a test fails.

Selenium has a different execution model from Playwright: element references can become stale after DOM replacement, and synchronization is usually expressed more explicitly.

Selenium lifecycle
WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver();
try {
    driver.get("https://example.test");
    System.out.println(driver.getTitle());
} finally {
    driver.quit();
}

See the existing Selenium technology profile for the framework definition, main characteristics, QA relevance, and naming note.

Skills covered

SeleniumBrowser AutomationJava

Related: Selenium vs Playwright · Selenium waits

Foundation → Intermediate

Selenium locators and common form controls

Selenium supports locators such as ID, name, class name, tag name, link text, partial link text, CSS selectors, and XPath. Prefer unique IDs or stable semantic/test attributes when available; CSS or relative XPath are useful when a simple attribute locator is insufficient.

Class-name locators accept one class token, not a multi-class CSS expression. Link-text locators work only for links. Deep absolute XPath is brittle because DOM structure changes often.

Dropdowns built with a native <select> can use Selenium's Select helper. Custom dropdowns require normal element interactions. For checkboxes and radio buttons, assert selected state rather than only clicking.

LocatorGood useRisk
By.idStable unique IDIDs may be generated dynamically in some apps.
By.nameStable form field nameCan match multiple fields.
By.cssSelectorFlexible attribute/structure selectionCan become coupled to styling/DOM.

Intermediate

Tables, alerts, pop-ups, dynamic elements, and waiting strategies

Tables should be queried by row/column meaning, not only physical indexes. Locate the row representing the business entity, then perform assertions or actions within that row.

JavaScript alerts, confirms, and prompts require switching to the alert context before accepting, dismissing, or entering text. Browser windows/tabs require explicit handle management; HTML modals are ordinary DOM elements.

Dynamic elements often appear, disappear, become clickable, or are replaced after asynchronous updates. Use explicit waits for the exact condition and re-locate stale elements rather than adding arbitrary sleeps.

Skills covered

SeleniumDynamic UI TestingSynchronization

Related: Waits and stale elements · Playwright dialogs/tabs

Intermediate

TestNG annotations, suite configuration, priority, data, and parallelism

@Test marks tests; configuration annotations such as @BeforeTest and @AfterTest run around a TestNG test context. Other scopes include suite, class, method, and groups—choose scope according to resource ownership.

testng.xml can define suites, classes, groups, parameters, and parallel execution. Priority controls order but should not be used to hide dependencies between tests. Prefer independent tests with explicit setup.

Data providers support parameterized scenarios. Parallel execution requires thread-safe drivers, data, reports, and cleanup.

TestNG lifecycle
public class LoginTests {
  @BeforeMethod
  public void setUp() { /* create isolated driver/state */ }

  @Test
  public void rejectsInvalidPassword() { /* assertions */ }

  @AfterMethod(alwaysRun = true)
  public void tearDown() { /* quit/cleanup */ }
}

TestNG
Java testing framework

Definition: A Java testing framework influenced by JUnit/NUnit and designed for configurable test execution, annotations, grouping, data-driven tests, dependencies, and parallel execution.

Main characteristics

  • Groups, priorities, dependencies, and parameters
  • DataProvider support
  • testng.xml suite configuration
  • Parallel execution and listeners/reporting hooks
QA / automation relevance: Often paired with Selenium and Rest Assured to organize Java automation suites, setup/teardown, grouping, data-driven execution, and CI runs.

Katalon Studio: test cases, suites, objects, and evidence

Katalon Studio packages many automation concerns into one interface: project setup, object repository, test cases, test suites, execution, screenshots, and reports. This can lower the entry barrier for teams that prefer an integrated tool.

The same engineering rules still apply: avoid brittle recorded flows, use meaningful abstractions, isolate test data, assert business outcomes, and keep source control/CI in the workflow.

A recorded script is a draft. Refactor repeated operations into reusable keywords/components and review generated locators before relying on them.

COURSE EXPANSION / MOBILE

Practical mobile testing: devices, interruptions, permissions, connectivity, and usability

The existing guide covered mobile strategy at a high level. The course adds a concrete checklist of mobile-specific failure modes. This chapter turns those into a reusable mobile test model.

Foundation

Mobile application types, device diversity, and test matrices

Mobile products may be native apps compiled for a platform, mobile web applications running in the browser, hybrid apps combining native shells with web content, or PWAs (Progressive Web Apps) with install/offline capabilities where supported.

Device diversity includes operating-system versions, manufacturers, screen sizes, densities, memory/CPU classes, notches/foldables, language/locale, accessibility settings, and network capabilities. A risk-based device matrix uses production analytics and target-market importance rather than testing every device equally.

Emulators/simulators provide fast broad coverage; real devices remain important for hardware, OEM behavior, push notifications, biometrics, power, cameras, Bluetooth/NFC, and real network conditions.

Skills covered

Mobile TestingCross-Browser TestingTest Strategy

Related: Mobile strategy · Compatibility matrices

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate

Input methods, orientation, lifecycle, and interruptions

Test touch gestures, physical/virtual keyboards, copy/paste, autofill, voice input where relevant, back-navigation conventions, and accessibility input. Inputs can behave differently by OS, locale, keyboard, and form configuration.

Rotate between portrait and landscape during meaningful states and verify layout, data preservation, media, keyboard, and navigation. Also consider tablets, split-screen, and foldable transitions when supported.

Interruptions include phone calls, alarms, notifications, app switching, screen lock, OS dialogs, low-memory termination, and background/foreground transitions. Validate whether work is saved, sessions expire correctly, and sensitive content is protected in app-switcher previews.

Skills covered

Mobile TestingState Transition TestingUsability Testing

Related: State transitions · Device matrix

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate

Permissions, notifications, device features, and power consumption

Request permissions only when needed and handle allow, deny, deny permanently, and later settings changes. Test camera, location, microphone, contacts, storage/media, Bluetooth, and notification permissions according to the app's features.

Push notifications should be tested for foreground/background/terminated states, deep links, duplicate delivery, ordering, localization, sensitive content on the lock screen, opt-out behavior, and expired sessions.

Power consumption can be affected by GPS, background polling, wake locks, Bluetooth scanning, media, and excessive network requests. Battery testing is comparative and scenario-based: monitor whether the app behaves responsibly over realistic use rather than expecting one universal number.

Skills covered

Mobile TestingSecurity TestingPerformance Testing

Related: Security · Performance

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate

Connectivity, interoperability, co-existence, installation, update, and recovery

Test Wi-Fi, cellular, offline mode, transitions between networks, captive portals, high latency, packet loss, and intermittent connectivity. Verify retries, duplicate prevention, offline queues, conflict resolution, and clear user feedback.

Interoperability means working correctly with related systems, OS services, accessories, and external apps. Co-existence means behaving correctly while other apps share resources such as audio, location, Bluetooth, storage, or network.

Installability testing includes clean install, upgrade, downgrade rules where supported, insufficient storage, interrupted update, permissions migration, preserved data, uninstall/reinstall, and app-store packaging/signing behavior.

Skills covered

Mobile TestingIntegration TestingReliability Engineering

Related: Failure handling · Reliability

Mobile analytics, performance, usability, and OS preferences

Use production analytics to prioritize device/OS coverage, common journeys, crash hotspots, network conditions, and performance problems. Analytics informs risk; it does not replace designed testing.

Mobile usability includes touch-target size, one-handed interaction, keyboard avoidance, navigation conventions, readable content, orientation, accessibility, interruptions, and graceful handling of slow networks.

Respect operating-system preferences such as dark mode, font scaling, reduced motion, language/locale, time format, accessibility options, and notification settings. Test startup time, scrolling, memory pressure, battery-sensitive flows, and perceived responsiveness.

COURSE EXPANSION / TEST DESIGN

White-box coverage and pairwise combinatorial testing

The original guide already covered the major black-box techniques. The course adds explicit structural coverage—statement, decision, condition, MC/DC, path, and loops—and pairwise combinatorial design.

Foundation

Black-box, white-box, and gray-box testing

Black-box testing derives tests from externally observable behavior without requiring knowledge of internal implementation. Equivalence partitions, boundary values, decision tables, state transitions, and pairwise testing are typical black-box techniques.

White-box testing uses knowledge of internal code structure or logic to design coverage, such as statements, branches, conditions, and paths. Gray-box testing informally describes testing with partial internal knowledge—for example an API tester who understands database schema and service architecture.

These approaches are complementary. Black-box tests can miss unexecuted logic; white-box coverage can execute every line while still missing incorrect requirements or missing functionality.

Skills covered

Software TestingBlack-Box TestingWhite-Box Testing

Related: Equivalence partitioning · Structural coverage

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate

Statement coverage and decision/branch coverage

Statement coverage measures whether executable statements were run. Decision coverage (often called branch coverage) checks whether each decision outcome such as true and false was exercised.

100% statement coverage does not imply 100% branch coverage. A line inside an if may execute while the false path is never tested. Coverage percentages reveal what executed, not whether assertions were correct.

Useful formulas are: statement coverage = executed statements / total executable statements; decision coverage = exercised decision outcomes / total decision outcomes.

Structural coverage example
def shipping_cost(total, premium):
    if premium or total >= 100:
        return 0
    return 10

# A test with premium=True executes the 'return 0' path.
# To achieve decision coverage, also exercise a case where
# the condition evaluates False and returns 10.

Skills covered

White-Box TestingUnit TestingCode Coverage

Related: Condition coverage & MC/DC · Unit testing

Back to contents ↑
Advanced

Condition coverage and MC/DC (Modified Condition/Decision Coverage)

Condition coverage checks whether each atomic boolean condition becomes both true and false. It differs from decision coverage because a compound decision can have both overall outcomes without independently exercising every condition.

MC/DC (Modified Condition/Decision Coverage) requires evidence that each condition can independently affect the overall decision outcome while other relevant conditions are held so the effect is observable. It is stricter than basic condition or decision coverage and is important in some safety-critical standards.

MC/DC test design should be systematic; brute-force testing every boolean combination gives full truth-table coverage but may be much larger than the minimal MC/DC set.

MC/DC intuition
Decision: A && (B || C)

MC/DC seeks pairs showing:
- changing A alone changes the decision,
- changing B alone changes the decision,
- changing C alone changes the decision,
while the other conditions are set so each condition's
independent effect can be observed.

Skills covered

White-Box TestingCode CoverageSafety-Critical Testing

Related: Statement/decision coverage · Decision tables

Back to contents ↑
Advanced

Path coverage and loop coverage

Path coverage asks whether distinct execution paths through control flow have been exercised. Complete path coverage quickly becomes infeasible because branches multiply and loops can create an unbounded number of paths.

Loop coverage focuses on meaningful iteration counts: zero iterations where possible, one iteration, typical multiple iterations, boundary counts, and values around maximum/minimum limits.

Use path/loop analysis to identify structural risk, then combine it with business-focused black-box tests. Chasing 100% path coverage is usually not practical for nontrivial programs.

Skills covered

White-Box TestingUnit TestingCode Coverage

Related: Algorithms · MC/DC

Back to contents ↑
Intermediate

Pairwise (all-pairs) combinatorial testing

Pairwise testing is a black-box combinatorial technique that selects a compact set of tests so every pair of parameter values appears together at least once. It is useful when many configuration dimensions make exhaustive combinations too large.

Example dimensions might be browser × operating system × locale × account role × payment method. Pairwise can dramatically reduce the matrix, but it assumes most interaction defects are caused by small combinations and does not replace risk-based tests for known three-way or higher-order interactions.

Always add explicit tests for critical combinations, boundaries, and production-heavy configurations even if a pairwise generator does not emphasize them.

When pairwise helpsWhen it is insufficient
Large configuration matricesA specific 3+ factor interaction is known to be risky.
Compatibility combinationsSafety/security rules require exhaustive combinations.
Inputs with many categorical valuesContinuous numeric boundaries need dedicated analysis.
Early broad coverageProduction analytics show a critical combination deserving more depth.

Skills covered

Black-Box TestingTest DesignPairwise Testing

Related: Compatibility matrices · Risk-based testing

COURSE EXPANSION / CAREER

Certifications, T-shaped development, freelancing, CVs, and interviews

The course closes with certification and career material rather than stopping at testing tools. This chapter captures that content while keeping the emphasis on evidence-based professional development.

Professional practice

Testing certification landscape: ISTQB, A4Q, and specialist paths

ISTQB (International Software Testing Qualifications Board) maintains widely recognized testing syllabi. CTFL (Certified Tester Foundation Level) is the foundational certification. Specialist and advanced tracks can cover areas such as Agile, mobile, performance, test analysis/management, automation, AI testing, and generative-AI-related testing depending on the current catalog.

A4Q (Alliance for Qualification) offers or supports professional qualification programs in testing and related digital disciplines. Certification catalogs change, so always verify current prerequisites, exam versions, and local exam providers before paying.

A certification can create a shared vocabulary and pass HR filters, but it is not evidence of production skill by itself. Pair certification with a portfolio, practical test artifacts, automation, debugging examples, and clear project stories.

Certification familyWhat it generally targetsHow to use it
ISTQB CTFLFoundation vocabulary, test process, design techniques, management basics, and tooling concepts.Good first credential when job postings explicitly value ISTQB terminology.
Agile / Mobile / Performance specialist tracksDomain-specific testing practices.Useful when the target role actually uses that specialty; verify the currently offered modules.
AI Testing / Generative-AI-related tracksTesting AI systems and/or using AI in testing, depending on the syllabus.Relevant to AI QA roles, but practical evaluation projects remain important.
Advanced Test Analyst / Test Management / Test AutomationDeeper specialization for experienced practitioners.Best after hands-on experience makes the advanced material concrete.
A4Q programsTesting and adjacent digital-professional qualifications.Assess recognition in the target market before investing.

Certification names, versions, prerequisites, and availability change. Always check the current official catalog before planning an exam path.

Skills covered

Career DevelopmentSoftware TestingProfessional Certification

Related: Interview answers · Study roadmap

Back to contents ↑
Professional practice

PMP, CAPM, BCS, TMMi, and adjacent professional frameworks

PMP (Project Management Professional) and CAPM (Certified Associate in Project Management) are project-management credentials from PMI. They are adjacent to QA rather than testing certifications and are more useful when a role includes planning, coordination, risk, and delivery ownership.

BCS, the Chartered Institute for IT (historically the British Computer Society), offers business-analysis and technology qualifications. Business-analysis knowledge is relevant when QA spends significant time refining requirements and business processes.

TMMi (Test Maturity Model integration) is an organizational test-process maturity model. It evaluates how systematically testing is managed and improved; it is not an individual automation framework.

Choose credentials based on target roles, job-market recognition, cost, and the gap they actually close. Accumulating unrelated certificates can dilute a focused profile.

Skills covered

Project ManagementBusiness AnalysisQuality Assurance

Related: Requirements analysis · Planning

Back to contents ↑
Professional practice

Building a T-shaped testing profile

A T-shaped professional has broad collaboration knowledge across adjacent disciplines and deeper expertise in one or a few areas. For QA Automation, the vertical depth might be Playwright/API automation while the horizontal breadth includes SQL, CI/CD, Linux, accessibility, performance, AI, and operations.

Breadth helps diagnose cross-layer failures; depth makes you independently productive. The goal is not to claim expert level in every tool, but to understand interfaces well enough to collaborate and know when specialist knowledge is required.

Skills covered

Career DevelopmentQA AutomationTechnical Operations

Related: Study roadmap · Project story

Back to contents ↑
Professional practice

Freelance and crowdtesting platforms: workflow, evidence, and professionalism

Crowdtesting platforms connect testers with short test cycles across devices, countries, and products. The course uses examples such as TesterWork, Test IO, Digivante, and BugFinders; platform availability, eligibility, payment rules, and project volume can change over time.

Success depends on reading cycle instructions carefully, matching required devices/locations, avoiding duplicate defects, providing reproducible evidence, respecting confidentiality, and submitting within the requested scope. A valid bug may be rejected if evidence or reproduction quality is poor.

Treat crowdtesting as project work: track time, payout rules, payment method/fees, device costs, accepted/rejected defect rates, and the opportunity cost compared with salaried or direct freelance work.

Related: Defect reporting · Professional communication

Professional practice

Writing a QA CV and cover letter around evidence

A QA CV should lead with target role, relevant years/level, core testing and automation tools, and evidence of impact. Separate professional experience from portfolio projects so recruiters can distinguish production work from self-directed learning.

Use bullets that describe what was tested or built, the tools/layers involved, and why the work mattered. Avoid skill dumps without evidence and avoid inflating seniority. Link a GitHub/portfolio when it demonstrates automation architecture, reports, CI, or documentation.

A cover letter should explain fit for the specific role: relevant domain, testing layers, technical stack, and motivation. It should not restate the entire CV.

Career DevelopmentTechnical WritingStakeholder Communication

Professional practice

Technical interview preparation: concepts, stories, and live reasoning

Prepare three layers: fundamentals (testing vocabulary and techniques), technical depth (automation/API/SQL/code/debugging), and experience stories showing decisions, trade-offs, incidents, and collaboration.

For scenario questions, state assumptions, identify risk, propose an approach, explain evidence, and discuss trade-offs. For coding questions, clarify constraints, work through edge cases, then analyze complexity. For behavioral questions, use concrete context and outcome rather than generic claims.

Practice explaining the same project at 30-second, 2-minute, and deep-dive levels. Interview quality is partly the ability to make your reasoning legible.

COURSE EXPANSION / HANDS-ON LABS

Hands-on projects that consolidate the course material

The source course repeatedly returns to practical projects. These labs reproduce the learning objectives without tying the guide to a fragile third-party demo or a specific version of a tool UI.

Hands-on

Lab 1 — Manual QA: booking, to-do, e-commerce, and UI flows

Choose a small public/demo application with forms, search, state changes, and navigation. Start from requirements you write yourself, then create a risk list, high-level scenarios, detailed test cases for critical flows, exploratory charters, and a defect report.

Use a spreadsheet for the first iteration if that keeps the workflow simple. Suggested columns: ID, requirement/risk, scenario, preconditions, data, steps, expected result, priority, execution status, defect link, and evidence. Move to Qase/Zephyr only when the repository, execution cycles, or traceability needs justify it.

Include at least one sign-up/login flow, one search/filter flow, one stateful CRUD-like flow, responsive/mobile checks, accessibility checks, and a deliberately injected defect.

Manual TestingTest Case DesignDefect ReportingExploratory Testing

Related: Web scenarios · Manual workflow · Test management

Back to contents ↑
Hands-on

Lab 2 — API project: authenticated CRUD workflow in Postman

Use a disposable training API or local service. Build a collection that authenticates, creates a resource, captures its ID, retrieves it, updates it, verifies persistence, and deletes it. Add negative and authorization tests.

Use environment variables for base URL/configuration and collection variables for dynamic IDs. Validate status codes, headers, schema, key business fields, error formats, and final state. Export/share only non-secret configuration.

Extend the lab with idempotency, rate limiting, malformed payloads, missing/expired credentials, and a simulated downstream failure. Run the collection from the command line or CI.

Trello-style CRUD learning flow
Workflow:
POST /auth -> capture token
POST /boards -> capture boardId
POST /boards/{boardId}/lists -> capture listId
POST /lists/{listId}/cards -> capture cardId
PATCH /cards/{cardId}
GET /cards/{cardId}
DELETE /cards/{cardId}

Then verify forbidden access with a second user.

Hands-on

Lab 3 — JMeter performance test from script to analysis

Define a target SLO and workload before opening JMeter. Create a small Test Plan with one Thread Group, HTTP defaults, requests, assertions, realistic test data, and timers. Debug with one or two users.

Parameterize users, correlate dynamic tokens/IDs, then run non-GUI load with a controlled ramp-up and steady state. Capture JMeter results plus application CPU, memory, database, queue, and error metrics.

Report throughput, error rate, median, p90/p95/p99 latency, resource bottlenecks, and the point at which objectives fail. Repeat after one change to show whether the bottleneck actually improved.

JMeter CLI
# Example non-GUI execution
jmeter -n -t checkout.jmx -l results.jtl -e -o report/

# Never interpret client-side numbers alone:
# correlate them with service/database/infrastructure metrics.

19 / DEEP DIVE

Interview & Study Toolkit

A bridge between the reference material and the simulator: answer structures, debugging heuristics, study order, and quick checklists for recurring interview scenarios.

Professional practice

A framework for technical interview answers

For scenario questions, use a compact structure: clarify → identify risk → propose approach → name evidence → discuss trade-off. This demonstrates engineering judgment better than listing tools.

For “what is X?” questions, define it in one sentence, contrast it with the nearest confusing concept, give a concrete example, then mention one limitation or trade-off.

For experience questions, separate what you have done professionally from portfolio/training experience. Credibility is more valuable than inflating years or tooling.

Answer pattern
Question: How would you test a payment API?

1. Clarify: payment types, idempotency, provider, auth, data source.
2. Risks: duplicate charge, wrong amount/currency, unauthorized payment, partial failure.
3. Approach: contract + business rules + integration + failure injection.
4. Evidence: request IDs, provider response, ledger/database state, logs.
5. Trade-off: mocks for deterministic failures + integrated provider tests for contract confidence.
INTERVIEW LENS

Use this structure when you do not know exactly what level of depth the interviewer expects.

Stakeholder CommunicationTechnical Documentation

Related: Project story · Requirements analysis

Back to contents ↑
Professional practice

A systematic debugging framework

Start with the observed fact, not a theory. Define what failed, when, for whom, and how often. Preserve the failing state and artifacts.

Localize by boundary: client/UI → network → API → service logic → database/cache → asynchronous jobs → external provider. Compare a working and failing request when possible.

Form one hypothesis at a time and choose a check that can falsify it. After finding the immediate cause, ask what allowed the defect to escape and how detection/recovery can improve.

INTERVIEW LENS

This framework works for flaky tests, production bugs, data inconsistencies, and IoT failures.

TroubleshootingRoot Cause AnalysisObservability

Related: Evidence-driven debugging · RCA

Back to contents ↑
Study roadmap

Recommended progression from fundamentals to advanced topics

A practical study order is: QA fundamentals → test design → API/SQL → Playwright basics → automation architecture → CI/CD/Docker → specialized testing → observability/reliability → AI systems/evaluation. Programming fundamentals should run in parallel throughout.

Do not try to memorize the 530 questions independently. Learn the underlying topic families, then use the simulator to practice retrieval and explanation. When a question is wrong, return to the linked section and write your own explanation.

For interview readiness, prioritize depth in your core stack (Playwright, TypeScript, API, SQL, CI/CD) while maintaining working knowledge of adjacent areas.

INTERVIEW LENS

Use the guide as reference and the simulator as active recall. The combination is more effective than passive rereading.

Reference

Compact checklists for common QA scenarios

New feature: requirements, happy path, negatives, boundaries, permissions, state, data, integration, accessibility, observability, rollback.

API: method/status, auth, schema, business values, errors, idempotency, pagination, rate limits, side effects, logs.

UI automation: stable locator, deterministic data, explicit assertion, no fixed sleep, isolated context, useful evidence.

Production incident: impact, timeline, recent changes, containment, logs/metrics/traces, communication, recovery verification, RCA actions.

LLM/agent: golden cases, structured validity, task success, grounding, tool safety, injection tests, latency/cost, human escalation.

Acronym and abbreviation reference

The table expands technical acronyms and abbreviations used in the guide. Brand names such as Git, Docker, Playwright, pytest, n8n, Jenkins, Caddy, and Redis are explained in the technology reference instead of being given invented acronym expansions.

TermExpansionMeaning / context
A11yAccessibilityA numeronym: 11 letters sit between “A” and “y”. Common shorthand in accessibility engineering.
A4QAlliance for QualificationProfessional qualification organization associated with software-quality and digital-skills certification programs.
ACIDAtomicity, Consistency, Isolation, DurabilityFour core transaction properties commonly associated with reliable relational database transactions.
AIArtificial IntelligenceUmbrella term for systems performing tasks associated with intelligent behavior; in this guide it often refers to generative and agentic AI.
APIApplication Programming InterfaceA defined software interface through which components request data or behavior from one another. APIs are not limited to HTTP/web services.
ARIAAccessible Rich Internet ApplicationsWAI-ARIA specifications add accessibility semantics to web interfaces when native HTML alone is insufficient.
ASGIAsynchronous Server Gateway InterfaceA Python interface specification between asynchronous web servers and applications/frameworks; FastAPI commonly runs on ASGI servers.
BABusiness AnalystRole focused on understanding business needs, processes, requirements, and stakeholder outcomes.
BCSBCS, The Chartered Institute for ITUK professional body historically known as the British Computer Society; offers technology and business-analysis qualifications.
BDDBehavior-Driven DevelopmentA collaborative development approach that describes expected behavior through concrete examples, often expressed with Given/When/Then.

CDContinuous Delivery / Continuous DeploymentContinuous Delivery keeps software releasable; Continuous Deployment automatically releases qualifying changes.
CIContinuous IntegrationFrequent integration of changes with automated verification.
CI/CDContinuous Integration / Continuous Delivery (or Deployment)Combined shorthand for automated software integration and delivery/deployment pipelines.
CLICommand-Line InterfaceA text-based interface operated through shell commands.

CRUDCreate, Read, Update, DeleteFour basic classes of persistent-data operations.
CSRFCross-Site Request ForgeryWeb attack in which a victim's authenticated browser is induced to submit an unwanted request; CSRF tokens may need correlation in recorded performance scripts.
CSSCascading Style SheetsThe web styling language used to control presentation and layout.
CSVComma-Separated ValuesA simple tabular text-data format; delimiters and quoting rules must still be handled explicitly.
CTFLCertified Tester Foundation LevelFoundation-level ISTQB testing certification.
DBMSDatabase Management SystemSoftware used to define, store, query, protect, and manage databases.
DCLData Control LanguageSQL command family associated with access control, such as GRANT and REVOKE.
DDLData Definition LanguageSQL command family for database structure, such as CREATE, ALTER, and DROP.
DMLData Manipulation LanguageSQL command family for data changes, commonly INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE.
DNSDomain Name SystemThe distributed naming system that resolves domain names to network records such as IP addresses.
DOMDocument Object ModelThe in-memory object/tree representation of an HTML or XML document exposed to browser scripts and automation.
DQLData Query LanguageCommon label for query operations, especially SELECT; categorization varies by database/vendor.
DRYDon't Repeat YourselfEngineering principle encouraging a single authoritative representation of reusable knowledge or logic.
E2EEnd-to-EndA test that validates a realistic workflow across multiple integrated layers.
ERDEntity-Relationship DiagramDiagram showing data entities, attributes, relationships, and cardinalities.
ETLExtract, Transform, LoadA data-pipeline pattern that extracts source data, transforms it, and loads it into a destination.
FKForeign KeyRelational-database constraint/column reference linking a row to a key in another table.
GILGlobal Interpreter LockIn CPython, a lock that allows only one thread at a time to execute Python bytecode in a process; it mainly affects CPU-bound threading.
GraphQLGraphQL query language/runtime (name, not an acronym)A typed API query language and execution model that lets clients request selected fields from a schema.
GUIGraphical User InterfaceVisual interface; for JMeter, GUI mode is useful for authoring/debugging but not recommended for heavy load execution.
HAHome Assistant (in this guide); High Availability in other operations contextsContext-dependent abbreviation. In IoT sections HA usually means Home Assistant; in infrastructure discussions HA can mean High Availability.
HITLHuman-in-the-LoopA system design in which people review, approve, correct, or handle selected automated/AI decisions.
HTMLHyperText Markup LanguageThe standard markup language for the semantic structure of web documents.
HTTPHypertext Transfer ProtocolThe application-layer request/response protocol underlying the web.
HTTPSHTTP over TLS; commonly “Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure”Encrypted/authenticated HTTP transport using TLS.
I/OInput/OutputData transfer between a program and files, networks, devices, users, or other external resources.
IDIdentifierA value used to uniquely or contextually identify a record, entity, request, test, or resource.
INVESTIndependent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, TestableHeuristic for evaluating the quality and readiness of Agile user stories.
IoTInternet of ThingsNetworks of physical devices, sensors, actuators, gateways, and software services.
IPInternet ProtocolThe network-layer protocol and addressing system used to route packets across IP networks.
ISTQBInternational Software Testing Qualifications BoardInternational organization that maintains testing certification schemes and syllabi.
JDKJava Development KitJava compiler, tools, and runtime components used to develop Java applications.
JREJava Runtime EnvironmentHistorical/runtime concept containing the components needed to execute Java applications; modern JDK distributions generally include runtime components.
JSJavaScriptCommon abbreviation for the JavaScript programming language.
JSONJavaScript Object NotationA lightweight text format for structured data.
JSONBJSON Binary (PostgreSQL type name)PostgreSQL’s binary/decomposed storage format for JSON values, optimized for indexing and processing compared with plain JSON text storage.
JVMJava Virtual MachineThe runtime abstraction that executes Java bytecode and provides services such as memory management and garbage collection.
JWTJSON Web TokenA compact token format for signed and/or encrypted claims; often used in authentication/authorization systems.
LANLocal Area NetworkA network covering a limited local area such as a home, office, or lab.
LLMLarge Language ModelA model trained to predict/generate language tokens from context; modern LLMs may also support multimodal inputs and tools.
MC/DCModified Condition/Decision CoverageStructural coverage criterion showing that each atomic condition can independently affect a decision outcome.
MCPModel Context ProtocolAn open protocol for exposing tools, resources, and prompts/context capabilities to AI applications.
MFAMulti-Factor AuthenticationAuthentication requiring factors from more than one category, such as password plus authenticator possession.
MLMachine LearningMethods that learn patterns or predictive behavior from data rather than relying only on explicitly programmed rules.
MQTTHistorically Message Queuing Telemetry TransportA lightweight publish/subscribe messaging protocol. Modern specifications generally use MQTT as the protocol name.
npmnpm package manager (officially treated as a name, not an acronym)The package manager and registry ecosystem commonly used with Node.js and JavaScript/TypeScript projects.
OAuthOAuth authorization framework (name, not a formal acronym)An authorization framework for delegated access. It is often informally described as “Open Authorization,” but OAuth is used as the protocol/framework name.
OIDCOpenID ConnectAn identity layer built on OAuth 2.0 that standardizes authentication and identity claims.
OOPObject-Oriented ProgrammingA programming paradigm organized around objects that combine state and behavior, commonly using encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism, and composition.
OpenAPIOpenAPI Specification (name, not an acronym)A machine-readable specification for describing HTTP APIs, their operations, parameters, schemas, authentication, and responses.
OSOperating SystemSystem software that manages hardware/resources and provides services to applications.
OTPOne-Time PasswordShort-lived authentication code intended for one-time use.
PKPrimary KeyColumn or column set that uniquely identifies a row in a relational table.
PMIProject Management InstituteProfessional organization that administers credentials such as PMP and CAPM.
PMPProject Management ProfessionalProject-management certification from PMI.
POMPage Object Model / Project Object ModelIn test automation, Page Object Model abstracts UI interaction. In Maven, pom.xml is the Project Object Model configuration.
PWAProgressive Web AppWeb application enhanced with installability/offline/device capabilities where supported.
QAQuality AssuranceThe discipline of preventing and detecting quality problems throughout software delivery and operation.
QoSQuality of ServiceA service-delivery level or priority concept; in MQTT it specifically identifies delivery guarantees 0, 1, or 2.
RAGRetrieval-Augmented GenerationRetrieving external information and supplying it as context before model generation.
RCARoot Cause AnalysisStructured investigation of causes and contributing conditions after a defect or incident.
RESTRepresentational State TransferAn architectural style for networked resource-oriented systems.
RPORecovery Point ObjectiveMaximum acceptable data-loss window measured backward from a disruption.
RTORecovery Time ObjectiveTarget maximum time to restore a service or capability after disruption.
SDKSoftware Development KitLibraries, tools, documentation, and examples provided to build against a platform or service.
SDLCSoftware Development Life CycleThe complete lifecycle for planning, designing, implementing, verifying, deploying, operating, maintaining, and retiring software.
SLAService Level AgreementA formal agreement or commitment about service performance/availability, often with business consequences.
SLIService Level IndicatorA measured signal of service behavior, such as successful-request rate or latency.
SLOService Level ObjectiveA target value or range for an SLI over a defined period.
SOAPSimple Object Access Protocol (historical expansion)XML-based messaging protocol standardized for web services; modern specifications generally use SOAP as the protocol name.
SOLIDSingle Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, Dependency InversionFive object-oriented design principles used to reduce coupling and improve maintainability.
SQLStructured Query LanguageLanguage family for defining, querying, manipulating, and controlling relational data.
SSLSecure Sockets LayerOlder cryptographic protocol family superseded by TLS. “SSL certificate” is still used colloquially, but modern HTTPS uses TLS.
STLCSoftware Testing Life CycleThe testing-focused lifecycle within the SDLC: requirement analysis, planning, test design, environment/data preparation, execution, defect management, reporting, and closure.
TCLTransaction Control LanguageSQL command family for transaction boundaries such as COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT.
TLSTransport Layer SecurityCryptographic protocol used to protect data in transit and authenticate endpoints; it replaced SSL.
TMMiTest Maturity Model integrationModel for assessing and improving an organization's test-process maturity.
TSTypeScriptCommon abbreviation for the TypeScript programming language.
TTLTime To LiveA lifetime/expiration value; commonly used for caches, DNS records, messages, and stored keys.
UATUser Acceptance TestingBusiness/user validation that software supports intended real-world use.
UIUser InterfaceThe interface through which a person interacts with a system.
URIUniform Resource IdentifierA general identifier for a resource. A URL is a kind of URI that also describes location/access.
URLUniform Resource LocatorA URI form that identifies where/how a resource can be accessed, such as an HTTPS web address.
USDISO 4217 currency code for the United States dollarA standardized currency code, not an acronym expansion.
UTCCoordinated Universal TimeGlobal time standard commonly used to store/compare system timestamps consistently.
V8V8 JavaScript engine (name, not acronym)Google’s JavaScript/WebAssembly engine used by Chromium and Node.js. “V8” is a product name rather than an expanded acronym.
VMVirtual MachineA software-defined computer environment with virtualized hardware and its own guest operating system.
W3CWorld Wide Web ConsortiumStandards organization responsible for many web specifications and accessibility standards.
WAI-ARIAWeb Accessibility Initiative – Accessible Rich Internet ApplicationsW3C accessibility specification that defines roles, states, and properties for accessible web UI semantics.
WCAGWeb Content Accessibility GuidelinesW3C guidelines for accessible web content, organized around perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust principles.
WebSocketWebSocket protocol (name, not an acronym)A protocol providing persistent full-duplex communication between client and server after an HTTP-based opening handshake.
WIPWork in ProgressWork that has started but is not yet finished; Kanban commonly limits WIP to improve flow.
WSDLWeb Services Description LanguageXML-based description format historically common with SOAP web services.
XMLExtensible Markup LanguageA text markup/data format using nested elements/attributes and explicit document structure.
XSDXML Schema DefinitionSchema language used to describe and validate XML structure and data types.
YAMLYAML Ain’t Markup LanguageA recursive acronym for a human-readable serialization/configuration language; originally “Yet Another Markup Language.”
IDEIntegrated Development EnvironmentSoftware that combines code editing, navigation, debugging, build/run support, and related development tools. VS Code is editor-centric but can become IDE-like through extensions.
PRPull RequestA proposed change submitted for review before merging into a target branch; often used as the trigger and gate for CI quality checks.
QAOpsQuality Assurance OperationsAn industry term for embedding quality engineering and test feedback into continuous delivery and operational workflows; not a formal universal standard.
TDDTest-Driven DevelopmentA development cycle in which a failing test is written first, the smallest implementation makes it pass, and the code is then refactored.
JUnit XMLJUnit-style XML test reportA widely consumed XML report convention used by CI systems to ingest test suites, cases, failures, errors, and timing. It is not limited to Java/JUnit tests.
HARHTTP ArchiveA JSON-based format for recording HTTP request/response activity, often used to exchange or inspect captured network traffic.
ADKAgent Development KitGoogle's name for its agent-development toolkit/framework; more generally, an SDK focused on building agents.
A2AAgent2AgentA protocol/interface model for agents to discover and communicate with other remotely deployed agents.
ZDRZero Data RetentionA provider policy mode in which eligible API data is not retained beyond what is necessary to serve the request; exact guarantees are provider-specific.
SSEServer-Sent EventsAn HTTP-based mechanism for a server to stream events to a client over a long-lived response; older MCP deployments may expose SSE-based transports.
GDPRGeneral Data Protection RegulationEU data-protection regulation; DSGVO is the common German abbreviation/name for the same regulation.
DSGVODatenschutz-GrundverordnungGerman name/abbreviation for the EU GDPR.
CCPACalifornia Consumer Privacy ActCalifornia privacy law that grants covered consumers rights and imposes duties on covered businesses; it was amended by the CPRA.
CPRACalifornia Privacy Rights Act2020 California ballot measure that amended/expanded the CCPA and added privacy protections and enforcement structures.
DPIAData Protection Impact AssessmentGDPR risk-assessment process required for certain processing likely to result in high risk to individuals.
DPAData Processing AgreementContractual terms defining personal-data processing responsibilities between relevant parties such as controller and processor.
PIIPersonally Identifiable InformationCommon security/privacy term for information that can identify an individual; legal definitions vary and GDPR uses the broader concept of personal data.
SULSustainable Use Licensen8n's fair-code license for the self-hosted Community edition, subject to its current terms and permitted-use boundaries.
GCPGoogle Cloud PlatformCommon historical abbreviation for Google's cloud platform; current branding generally says Google Cloud.
CRMCustomer Relationship ManagementSystem/process for managing customer and lead information, interactions and sales/service workflows.
PaaSPlatform as a ServiceCloud hosting model where the provider manages much of the application platform while the customer deploys code/services.
TTCTest-Time ComputeInference-time computation allocated to improve model output through reasoning/search/sampling/verification. Some courses use TTS, but TTS commonly means Text-to-Speech.
TTSText-to-Speech (commonly); sometimes course-specific Test-Time ComputeAmbiguous abbreviation. In mainstream speech/AI usage TTS usually means Text-to-Speech; spell out test-time compute when that is intended.
JDBCJava Database ConnectivityJava standard API for connecting to relational databases, executing SQL, managing transactions, and reading result sets.
Names that should not be expanded: Git, GitHub, Docker, Playwright, Selenium, pytest, Cucumber, Allure, Postman, Newman, Jenkins, Caddy, React, Redis, Gradio, Pydantic, LangChain, LangGraph, LangSmith, Gemini, Groq, OpenRouter, Tuya, and similar product/project names are not technical initialisms. n8n is a numeronym/brand name, not an acronym.
